# Sidecar compute: inference, the Harness, the compute balance, the gateway, secure enclaves, web search and fetch, mail and calendar, context history, connected services, listeners, automatic approvals

Status: design only, 2026-11-23. Nothing here is implemented, and no task may start from it before the owner's review. It extends [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) (the build at commit 5fb94cae, SHA-256 c069c784f4397bcb…, 26,965 lines) as [RECORD.md](RECORD.md) does: where this document is silent, DESIGN.md governs, and where they differ on a point this document owns, this document governs until a design-records track folds it in. [Appendix D](#appendix-d-amendments-to-designmd) lists every place this document amends DESIGN.md.

This document designs twelve additions to the sidecar infrastructure, asked for by the owner on 2026-11-23:

1. **Inference.** Local inference on the device with LiteRT-LM, or remote inference on Bittensor subnet providers, in a TEE (trusted execution environment) or not: every model carries its label, every person or network may limit inference to TEEs or to chosen providers, and every model has one canonical name, `<provider>-<model>-<effort>` (CO-18). It is exposed through an embedded agent harness, **the Harness**, whose output is a stream of typed events that apps render as UI components and the CLI renders as terminal text.
2. **The compute balance.** A prepaid USD balance per network, separate from the transfer balance, that pays for remote inference, enclaves and web searches, each with its own charges, and shows each service's spend, in all and over the last 7 days (CO-22). Users fund it with fiat credits and auto-renew. URnetwork pays the Bittensor providers in Gamma, and Parallel, which is not on Bittensor, per search in USDC.
3. **The gateway.** A local OpenAI Responses API endpoint in the daemon, with Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages beside it, that puts every model in the catalog and the compute balance behind one config entry for Codex, Claude Code and other harnesses, and leaves their own web search off, so they search through §21's MCP tool (CO-26).
4. **Secure enclaves.** TEE Debian VMs rented from Bittensor providers, each booting a measured image with `ur` inside, joining the user's network with an overlay IP address, and running its own Harness with full tools. Sidecar's networking runs the enclave's routes and default egress, a built-in minimal SSH reaches it, and a local Harness attaches to the enclave's Harness over that SSH and manages its agents (CO-23). A network may run its mail indexer in one (CO-20).
5. **Bundled git and the recURd skill.** A minimal git, in Go, that the Harness uses on EVS without a system git; and the recURd skill every Harness starts with: an agent name, regular work summaries in EVS, and an inbox per agent through which agents message each other.
6. **Web search.** A built-in `web_search` tool backed by Parallel's Search (CO-28), in every Harness, through MCP for external harnesses and as `ur search`, each search a charge on the compute balance. The device sends each query to Parallel's keyless gateway itself, through URnetwork's network, and pays for it with a one-search USDC authorization URnetwork signs, so no URnetwork server sees or intercepts a query; each person first acknowledges what stays private and what could be exposed (added by CO-16, CO-26 to CO-31 and CO-33, §21).
7. **Web fetch.** A core `web_fetch` tool on every leg that fetches one page through URnetwork's network and returns it in a structured form: metadata, an outline, the main text, links, tables and structured data (added by CO-17, §22).
8. **Mail and calendar.** The person's own agent summarizes their unread mail and adds events to their calendar, through a calendar link saved in EVS that no agent ever sees (added by CO-24, §23).
9. **Context history.** Every Harness run keeps its whole context history in EVS, sealed, and so does every call through the gateway, so a call's context can be rebuilt exactly and a run resumed, continued or forked on another device or in an enclave (added by CO-25, §24).
10. **Connected services.** The Harness signs in to OAuth and OpenID Connect services, Google's and Microsoft's first, with the person completing each sign-in on their own device and the redirect never reaching a URnetwork server; every credential is kept sealed in EVS, and agents use a connection only through tools, never seeing a token (added by CO-36 and CO-37, §25).
11. **Listeners.** The apps list every service reachable on the network as `ip:port (description)`: each device's listening sockets and its port maps and forwards, which each device's bridge discovers and keeps current, visible to the whole network and reachable by any of its clients under its policy (added by CO-38 and CO-39, §26).
12. **Automatic approvals.** A safety classifier on the device, never on a URnetwork server, looks for injected instructions in what a run has read; by default it lets an action that waits only because the run read untrusted content go ahead when it finds none, and asks the person otherwise, within limits, every automatic decision recorded (added by CO-40, §27).

Every search, model provider, enclave, connected service and the listeners list carries an honest disclosure of what is private and what could be exposed, shown before first use where CO-31, CO-33 and CO-34 ask (§2.8).

The research behind it is in two reports: [design/reports/Bittensor TEE inference and enclaves.md](design/reports/Bittensor%20TEE%20inference%20and%20enclaves.md) and [design/reports/Compute extension building blocks.md](design/reports/Compute%20extension%20building%20blocks.md), with their notes in `research_notes/`; web search's notes are in `research_notes/Parallel web search device direct/`, and the earlier Brave design's in `research_notes/Brave web search tool/`. Facts about Gamma come first from URnetwork's own on-chain work, mmm/BTCPAY.md §18 and server/controller/gamma_chain.go.

## How to read

- **Codes.** Sections use these codes, with DESIGN.md's id forms (`R-CODE-n`, `D-CODE-n`, `Q-CODE-n`): CCTX §1, CTRUST §2, CARCH §3, PROV §4, ATTEST §5, INFER §6, HARN §7, GW §8, BAL §9, GAMMA §10, ENC §11, SSH §12, GIT §13, CSRV §14, CSURF §15, CACL §16, CABUSE §17, CTEST §18, CPHASE §19, SKILL §20, SRCH §21, FETCH §22, MAILCAL §23, CTXH §24, CONN §25, LSTN §26, SAFE §27. Compute invariants are IC-1 to IC-23 (§2.4). Compute flows are CF-1 to CF-21 (§3.4). Metadata rows are `compute-1` to `compute-11` (§14.6).
- **Citations.** `§n` is a section here; `DESIGN §n` is a section of DESIGN.md; `owner decision N` is DESIGN.md's numbered record; `CO-n` is above; `[Rpt:bt]` is the Bittensor report and `[Rpt:bb]` the building-blocks report, each with the notes file named where a fact comes from one; `[Notes:pd]` is web search's notes folder, research_notes/Parallel web search device direct/, and `[Notes:bs]` the earlier Brave design's, research_notes/Brave web search tool/, cited for Brave's terms and for how Codex and Claude Code run hosted search, each with the file named, and `[Rpt:rs]` the report on search providers URnetwork could resell, design/reports/Resellable web search APIs.md; code is cited as `repo/path/file.go:LINE` relative to the urnetwork checkout.
- **Notation.** DESIGN.md's (`<net>`, `<root>`, the overlay block). Money is USD held as `model.NanoCents`, which server/model/subscription_model.go:167-175 defines as USD × 10^9 despite its name; this document writes it "nano-USD". One gamma is one US dollar of a subnet's service credit at 10^9 units (server/controller/gamma_chain.go:95-97).
- **Stages.** DESIGN.md's v0 and v1 are M0-M10. This document's milestones are M11-M16 (§19), all after M10's exit; M12 and M13 each come in two parts, a, which needs nothing new from another company, and b, which waits on one, and §19.3 sets the order they are built in. "Later" means outside M11-M16.
- **For the owner.** Appendix G lists the decisions still yours, first those that cost money, bind URnetwork to another company or are hard to undo, then every open owner question by what it blocks; Appendix H lists where this document changes a position you took before; Appendix I lists the residual risks the design accepts; §19.6 shows what a person can use with nothing new from another company, and what waits on whom. Every other answer and decision stands unless you say otherwise.
- **Reading order.** §20 to §27 design the additions asked for later, and §14 to §19 already serve, test and schedule them, so a first reading may take §20 to §27 before §14.
- **Dated facts.** What this document says of outside parties, their features, prices, models, harness releases and terms, is as of 2026-11-23 and informative; what URnetwork requires of a party is normative, and each milestone's entry re-checks the facts it builds on (§19.8).

## 1. Context, scope and requirements

### 1.1 Purpose and scope

This section states what the compute extension is, what it is not, the requirements that trace to the owner's statements and to DESIGN.md, and the DESIGN.md positions it changes. Mechanisms are in §4-§27. What it says of outside parties, their features, prices, models, harness releases and terms, is as of 2026-11-23 and informative; what URnetwork requires of a party is normative, and each milestone's entry re-checks the facts it builds on (§19.8).

### 1.2 What it adds, and to whom

| Consumer | Runtime (DESIGN §1.4) | What the compute extension gives it |
|---|---|---|
| A person in a URnetwork app (iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux) | sdk, the app process, never the VPN component ([owner decision 197](DESIGN.md#od-197)) | the Harness as UI components: chat with an agent on a local or remote model, each labeled, enclaves to create, list, attach to and remove, web search and fetch, mail summaries and calendar events (§23), connected services (§25), the network's listeners (§26), the compute balance, top-ups and auto-renew |
| A developer at a terminal | `ur` daemon | `ur harness` (the Harness in the terminal), `ur enclave`, `ur ssh`, `ur git`, `ur search`, `ur fetch`, `ur calendar`, `ur connect`, `ur listeners`, `ur compute`, and the gateway for the harnesses they already use |
| Codex, Claude Code and other harnesses | the daemon's gateway on loopback | every catalog model, local and remote, in a TEE or not, by canonical name, behind one provider entry, billed to the compute balance, each call recorded as a `model_call` with its attestation and its whole request and response (§8.9, §24.8); web search through MCP's `web_search`, since the gateway serves no hosted search (§21.7) |
| An agent in an enclave | `ur` inside a TEE VM | a full Debian with tools, a sidecar identity, an overlay address, EVS, the bundled SSH server, and a Harness others attach to; for the initial version the enclave is one of its sponsor's devices, with their access (CO-43, §11.4) |
| recURd | the record (DESIGN §16.8, RECORD.md) | Harness runs recorded natively with their whole context history (§24), model receipts with attested evidence (RECORD.md section 12's reserved level 4), agent names, status summaries and inboxes (§20) |
| The browser sidecar | `sidecar.wasm` (DESIGN §18.8) | the Harness with remote inference only, once the extension's Worker returns from Later; the page Worker gets no compute surface at launch (§15.4) |

What of this a person can use at the first release, with no outside party's act, and what waits on which company, is §19.6's table; §19.3 gives the order of the build.

### 1.3 Requirements

| Id | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| R-CCTX-1 | Inference runs on the device (LiteRT-LM) or at a remote provider the person's policy allows, in a TEE or not, each model labeled (§4.3) | CO-1, CO-18 |
| R-CCTX-2 | A model labeled as in a TEE is reached only after the requesting device verifies its TEE evidence itself, and fails closed, never falling back to another model, provider or label | CO-2, CO-18; directive (DESIGN §0) |
| R-CCTX-3 | Prompts, outputs, tool calls and files reach URnetwork's servers only as ciphertext; the servers see the metadata rows of §14.6 and nothing else | directive; I-2, I-18 |

### 1.4 Non-goals

- **Running GPUs.** URnetwork operates no inference or VM hardware; providers do (§4).
- **A plaintext path through URnetwork.** No catalog entry, setting or fallback sends a prompt through a URnetwork server in plaintext, whether its model runs in a TEE or not (R-CCTX-24), and none sends a prompt to a model the person's policy refuses (CO-18). A person's own API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic or Google stay out of the gateway (Q-GW-4). Web search is not inference: sidecar calls only the Search endpoint of Parallel's gateway, never its Task or Responses, whose answers a model writes (§21).
- **A general cloud.** Enclaves are TEE VMs for agent work, with the shapes §11.5 lists; no public load balancers, managed databases, object stores or GPU clusters beyond one enclave.
- **A training or fine-tuning service.**
- **Paying in crypto for compute.** CO-10 sets fiat; the crypto rails URnetwork runs for Pro (server/PRO-GRANT-CYCLE.md:23-36) do not fund the compute balance at launch (Q-BAL-6).
- **App UI.** As in DESIGN.md (owner rule 6), this document gives the event contract the apps render (§7.6), not their screens.

### 1.6 Decisions proposed

**D-CCTX-1 (proposed).** The compute extension is one subsystem of the sidecar infrastructure, built in the sidecar repo under the root prefixes `infer_`, `attest_`, `harness_`, `gateway_`, `compute_`, `enclave_`, `ssh_`, `git_`, `skill_`, `search_`, `fetch_`, `calendar_`, `oauth_`, `listeners_` and `safety_`, with one new server engine, `computeservice` (§14). *Why:* owner rules 1 and 2; DESIGN §4.5's placement pattern.

**D-CCTX-2 (proposed).** The products name it "compute": recURd's agents run on it, burner email does not use it, and the URnetwork apps show it as a tab beside the VPN. *Why:* CO-1 puts the Harness in the apps; the record is where its work lands.

### 1.7 Questions

**Q-CCTX-1.** Does compute ship to personal networks, Team networks, or both? *Options:* (a) both, from M11; (b) Team only first. *Answer:* (a). The compute balance is per network, and a personal network is a network; Team adds budgets per member (§16.4) and billing admins (§9.10). *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-42).

**Q-CCTX-2.** Is compute part of a tier? *Options:* (a) every tier, Community included, pays only from its compute balance; (b) Pro and Team only. *Answer:* (a). A prepaid balance carries its own fraud limits (§9.11), local inference is free (CO-9), and gating by tier would push a free user who only wants a TEE model into a subscription they do not need. Only the number of enclaves a network may run at once scales with its tier (§11.13). *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-42).

## 2. Trust model and invariants

### 2.1 Purpose and scope

This section extends DESIGN §2 to compute: a new trust boundary, who sees what, the compute invariants every other section keeps, key custody, what a TEE does not protect when a miner holds the machine, and the threats. DESIGN §2's boundaries, invariants I-1 to I-20 and "private from us" statement all still bind; this section adds to them.

### 2.2 Boundaries

DESIGN §2.4's TB1 (the device), TB2 (members) and TB3 (URnetwork's servers) stand. One is added:

```text
TB4 TEE providers: the provider company, whose software runs inside its TEEs (measured, or not, as §4.5 says)
    and whose API, validators and load balancers run outside them; the miners, anonymous third parties who own
    and physically hold the machines; the hardware vendors whose keys root the evidence (Intel, AMD, NVIDIA);
    and the services that publish their collateral (Intel PCS, AMD KDS, NVIDIA's RIM, OCSP and NRAS).
    Trusted: the vendors' roots, and inside a passing TEE the measured software, for confidentiality of what is
    sent to it. Untrusted: everything outside the TEE, the miner above all, for content. Since CO-18 also the
    providers without a TEE, which read what is sent to them, trusted with it by the person's choice alone.
outside (adds): the drand beacon (freshness only, §5.6); exchanges and custodians (TAO; no user data); the
    Bittensor chain, where URnetwork's deposits, hotkeys and spends are public (§10); Parallel, whose keyless
    gateway answers web searches, and Vercel, which hosts it, both reading each query, never who asked (§21);
    Coinbase's facilitator and Stripe, which see each search's payment; Base, where each search's payment is public
    (§21.5); the DoH resolver that resolves searched and fetched hosts' names, and the hosts of direct calls' providers, from an exit's address (§22.4, §6.6);
    the person's calendar provider, which keeps their calendar and, for sidecar's calls, sees an exit's address (§23);
    each connected service's provider, which issues a connection's tokens and, for sidecar's calls, sees an exit's
    address (§25)
```

An enclave is inside its member's TB1 like a cloud agent's VM (DESIGN §2.4, [owner decision 49](DESIGN.md#od-49)), and an agents' enclave is, for the initial version, one of its sponsor's devices, holding what their other devices hold (CO-43, §11.4); with one difference: its host operator, the miner, is outside the boundary unless it breaks the TEE, where a cloud agent's sandbox operator is inside, so a physical attack or a broken TEE there exposes everything the sponsor's devices hold (2.6).

### 2.3 Who sees what

| Party | Remote inference | Enclaves | Web search |
|---|---|---|---|
| URnetwork's broker (`computeservice`) | network, sidecar, agent id, model, provider, instance, token maxima and usage, sizes, times, charges (compute-1, compute-3); for a call without a TEE, also the request's hash, which it signs and keeps only until the call settles; never prompts, outputs or tool calls | network, sidecar, enclave id, shape, provider, VM ids, states and times, the bootstrap hash, which enclave is the network's indexer, for its reserve (§9.9), much as the mail edge's routing to it shows already, sealed provisioning bytes (compute-4, compute-5); never keys, files, commands or traffic | that a network's agent paid for a search, and in which minute, kept 72 hours; the amount, never the payee or nonce, which only the search signer, apart, sees, without the network (§21.5); the charge (compute-10); outcome classes, kept only as hourly counts across all networks (compute-11); never the query, the mode or the results |
| URnetwork's api and taskworker | lots, charges, balances, auto-renew settings, payments (compute-2, compute-3, compute-6) | the same | the charges (compute-3) |
| URnetwork's search signer (`searchsigner`), apart from the broker | — | — | each authorization's payee, amount and nonce until it settles or lapses, in memory; the nonces it issued, with their values and windows, a day past them (§21.5); never the network, sidecar or agent, the query, the mode or the results |
| connect relays | — | the enclave's overlay traffic as Required-mode ciphertext, as for any sidecar (DESIGN §2.5) | — |
| The provider's API, validators, gateways | URnetwork's account, the instance, ciphertext sizes and times, usage | the VM's lifecycle, its image or payload, launch data; network metadata at the host | — |
| Inside the provider's TEE | the request and response in plaintext, to the measured platform and the unmeasured serving code (§4.5) | everything in the enclave, to the enclave's own software | — |
| The provider company at AP (Chutes) | could change the unmeasured serving code that reads plaintext, and releases the disk keys; that code reads the member's cache salt, the same in each of the member's requests, so Chutes could link a member's requests to each other, never to the member (§6.6); trusted, as the AP label says | (Hippius, Lium at AP) its platform software and key service, and so what the enclave holds: for an agents' enclave, everything its sponsor's devices hold (CO-43) | — |
| The miner | ciphertext and timing; plaintext only by a physical attack (2.6) | encrypted memory and disk; the VM's network packets (metadata; contents too under `direct` for anything not encrypted); at setup over SSH, an exit's address, never the person's (§11.7) | — |
| A provider without a TEE (label `none`, CO-18) | the request and response in plaintext, with URnetwork's hotkey, an exit's address, a random `user` value and a cache salt that changes per run (§6.6); no field names the person, the device or the network, but the conversation itself may: the network's label in the Harness's `ur://` addresses, agent and enclave names, whatever the person writes, so a provider that keeps conversations can link one network's runs and may read its name | — | — |
| Other customers of the provider | timing of shared prompt-cache hits, closed by the cache salt (§6.6) | none (EPC-6) | — |
| NVIDIA (NRAS, until M15) | GPU evidence and URnetwork's address, never a person's | the same for GPU shapes | — |
| The chain | URnetwork's deposits, hotkeys, mints and spends per provider; no user | the same | — |
| Stripe, the stores | purchases, as for Pro today | — | — |
| Parallel, through its keyless gateway | — | — | each query (objective, queries, mode) and its results, an exit's address, URnetwork's payer address and the payment, and the time; it may keep them and train its models on them, not linked to a person (CO-31, §21.4); never the person, the device, the network or their addresses |
| Vercel, which hosts the gateway | — | — | the same request and answer, since TLS ends there; never the person, the device, the network or their addresses |
| Coinbase's facilitator; Stripe | — | — | each search's payment: URnetwork's payer address, the one-time deposit address Stripe issued, the amount and time, which the facilitator screens; never the query |
| The exit carrying a direct call, a search or a fetch | for a direct call: the provider's host name, the TLS stream's sizes and times, and the window client that sent it | — | the host's name (Parallel's gateway's, or the fetched site's), the TLS stream's sizes and times, and the window client that sent it; never an HTTPS page's content |
| The DoH resolver | for a direct call, the provider's host name, asked from an exit's address | — | the names of Parallel's gateway and of fetched sites, asked from an exit's address |
| Anyone reading Base | — | — | each search's payment from URnetwork's payer address to a one-time Stripe deposit address: $0.01 and its time |

Web fetch (§22) adds no party beyond the exit and the DoH resolver above: a page travels as any traffic through URnetwork does (DESIGN §2.5), the site sees the exit's address, and URnetwork's servers see neither the URL nor the page.

Mail and calendars (§23) add one party, the calendar provider, which sees the person's own account, what the device reads and writes, and an exit's address; the exit and the DoH resolver see its host name as they see a fetched site's; the model's provider sees the mail and events an agent reads, as its label says (§23.5); URnetwork's servers see the mailbox and each calendar link's `secret` repo as EVS ciphertext and a calendar call as traffic (§23.12).

Connected services (§25) add each service's provider, which sees the person's own account, URnetwork's app by its client id, the person's own address and browser at sign-in (and, for Google on Android, at each access token Google Play services mints, §25.8), and an exit's address for every refresh and call; the exit and the DoH resolver see its host names as they see a calendar's; the model's provider sees what an agent reads, by its label; URnetwork's servers see each connection's `secret` repo as EVS ciphertext, with its writes' times, and its calls as traffic, never a redirect, a code, a token or a result (§25.12).

Listeners (§26) add no party: each device's list reaches every admitted sidecar of its network as EVS ciphertext, of which URnetwork's storage sees the writer, the padded size and the write times, so when a device's services change, never which; a live ask is connect traffic between two sidecars (§26.11).

Automatic approvals (§27) add no party: the classifier runs on the device or in an enclave's daemon, its model comes signed with the release from URnetwork's release host, which sees a download as it sees an update's, and its verdicts are sealed record entries, so URnetwork's servers see neither what it read nor what it decided (§27.9).

The network's indexer enclave (§11.10) adds no party, but what an enclave holds then includes each member's incoming mail, in plaintext as it arrives, and every mailbox a member grants it: the provider company at AP and the machine's holder by a physical attack (2.6) could read them, and, for an incarnation set up over SSH, its sponsor, whose word for what the setup installed members take (CO-41); URnetwork's servers never can.

An agents' enclave adds no party either, but for the initial version it is one of its sponsor's devices (CO-43, §11.4), holding what their other devices hold: their vault with the record and every run, their mailbox, their calendar links' secrets and connections' tokens, and every repo they read. The provider company at AP, the machine's holder by a physical attack (2.6), and anyone who breaks the TEE or escapes the agents' container to the daemon could read all of it while an incarnation runs, and keep tokens that work until the person replaces them (§25.7); URnetwork's servers never can.

### 2.4 Compute invariants

- **IC-1.** A call to a model labeled A1, A2 or AP reaches only an instance that the provider itself lists for the model's pinned provider id, and whose evidence the requesting device read over its own TLS session and verified within 10 minutes against the newest signed policy and a current freshness ticket (§5); a failure refuses, and nothing goes to another model or provider.
- **IC-2.** Prompts, outputs, tool calls and files leave a device only sealed to a key bound in verified evidence (remote inference in a TEE), as EVS ciphertext, or over connect's Required mode (enclaves, SSH); a call to a model without a TEE leaves only to its provider, over TLS through `auto` egress (§6.6); a web search leaves only to Parallel's gateway, over TLS through `auto` egress, a calendar call only to its link's hosts, over TLS through the network's egress or, under `direct`, from the device's own address, or over the overlay to a private name the person set (§23.7), a connected service's call only to its connection's token and API hosts, over TLS through the network's egress or under `direct` (§25.8), and a fetch only to the site, through the network's egress, over TLS unless the site serves plain `http` (§21.5, §22.4); URnetwork's servers see the compute rows of §14.6 and nothing more.
- **IC-3.** An enclave gets keys and credentials only sealed to a key bound in evidence a device of its network verified, the bootstrap's binding included (EPC-1), or to a later ReaderKey its bound identity key signed: to its provisioning key, by its sponsor's device, or for the network's indexer enclave an Owner's or Admin's; an agents' enclave, admitted as one of its sponsor's devices only by an untagged consented device of the sponsor that verified that evidence itself, then takes every repo key, token and link secret the sponsor's devices take, as any of them does (IC-23, §11.4); for a mailbox grant to the indexer enclave, to the incarnation's ReaderKey, by a device of the granting member that verified that evidence itself and, for an incarnation set up over SSH, whose payload no evidence covers, its sponsor's signed setup statement binding that evidence and those keys, the member taking the sponsor's word for what the setup installed (§11.7, §11.10, CO-41).
- **IC-4.** The compute balance and the transfer balance never convert, and neither pays for the other's charges.
- **IC-5.** Local inference writes no charge, and the inference sends no request to a server; the run's context history syncs as EVS ciphertext, as every run's does (§24.5). A web search is not inference: it is charged as a search (§21.8), whichever model asked for it.
- **IC-6.** Every compute debit is one charge row naming its kind, its subject's opaque ids, its model or shape, its units and its amount, never content.
- **IC-7.** The local Harness starts no process, opens no host path outside its workspace, and reaches the network only through the sidecar's own transports; and it leaves in its workspace nothing a person's own git, shell prompt or editor would run there, writing no path in a worktree's `.git` but through the bundled git, which writes no command there (§7.5, §13.7).
- **IC-8.** An enclave's default egress is set by `ur` and enforced inside the enclave, failing closed; leaving through the provider's network takes an outward action.
- **IC-9.** The attestation policy is signed by the compute-policy key the release key certifies, and only moves forward; daily freshness tickets make a revocation bind within 72 hours, or within their signed horizon, at most 14 days, if the host that holds the unreleased tickets is taken too; no server can widen the policy by changing it, and by withholding it can only delay a revocation that long (§5.4).
- **IC-10.** The design gives users no gamma, TAO, alpha or USDC to hold, see or move; URnetwork's treasury, spend and payer keys never reach a user's device, which carries at most a signed one-search authorization, of at most the policy's ceiling, to the payee it named (§21.5); a modified client may name an address of its own, never one the sanctions screen lists, and so move USDC within the network's budgets and the broker's search cap (CO-29, §9.11).
- **IC-11.** A gateway token administers, signs and reads nothing but its own grant's budget state; it spends within that budget and the broker's defaults, on loopback, for at most an hour. I-7 admits it as it admits the telemetry token ([owner decision 463](DESIGN.md#od-463)).
- **IC-12.** An inbox message, an agent's summary or status text (§20.6), or a command on a Harness's attach link, is untrusted, and taints the run that takes it, unless its provenance, or the link's signed origin (§7.10), shows the member's own person (the device's input path, no run) or an untainted run on the member's untagged device or in the member's own agents' enclave, whose Harness keeps each run's taint outside the agents' container as a member device's does (CO-43, §11.10); cloud agents, other members, their enclaves and the Team inbox always taint (§20.7), and so does a record entry another tagged sidecar wrote, when a run takes it into its context, and an EVS version, read by `evs_read` or fetched by the bundled git, whose push shows a tainted run, such a tagged sidecar or another member, or no provenance the reader can read (§7.8, §13.6); every push from an enclave's agents' container is a tainted run's (§7.8); and an enclave that reaches out takes a tainted run's version into its container only once its sponsor releases it (§7.8).
- **IC-13.** The broker logs no request body, envelope byte or SSH byte; it keeps §14.6's rows and nothing else.
- **IC-14.** An enclave's SSH server listens only on its overlay address and accepts only the key of an admitted sidecar whose flow principal matches it (§12.5), `root`, which reaches all the daemon holds, only from the sponsor's own untagged devices; the enclave's Harness, the receiving end of every attach link and its origin checks run in the daemon's namespaces, outside the agents' container, which holds no key, token or link secret the daemon holds for the sponsor (IC-23) and no credential but hour-long gateway tokens (IC-11), and reaches the daemon only through the gateway and a socket whose every call is a tainted run's (§11.10).
- **IC-15.** A web search query reaches no URnetwork server: the device sends it to Parallel's gateway itself, over TLS through `auto` egress, paid by an authorization URnetwork's search signer signs, apart from the broker, for the device's own nonce, to the payee the gateway's challenge names once the payee passes the sanctions screen, within the policy's price ceiling and the network's budgets (§21.5).
- **IC-16.** A web fetch reaches only public addresses, by `GET`, with no cookies or credentials, through the network's egress; a URL an agent composed in a tainted run is fetched only with an approval, a person's or, on a site the member has used, the device's safety classifier's in auto mode (IC-22), except in an enclave, whose egress mode governs a run without the `private` mark (§7.8); no device fetches directly (§22.4, §22.5).
- **IC-17.** A call to a model without a TEE carries a btauth/1 signature the broker made over the request's hash, for a host and receiver the signed policy pins, after checking the network's floor, providers, budget and hold; the broker keeps the hash only until the call settles, at most 10 minutes and never in a log, to check the provider's receipt, and a random value in the request keeps the hash from confirming a guessed prompt (§6.6).
- **IC-18.** A calendar link's credential, its app password or secret address (an OAuth form's tokens being its connection's, IC-20), is read only by the calendar tools of its member's consented devices, their agents' enclaves among them (CO-43), from its own `secret` repo, where it is sealed again to those devices' ReaderKeys, so a Team's audit reader that holds the repo opens none (§25.6), and never enters an agent's context, a tool result, a record entry, an approval, an error or a log; a calendar write from a tainted run, or any write to an event that has attendees, whom its provider mails, is outward action 25, each event shown to the person or, for a batch IC-22 admits, read whole by the device's safety classifier (§23.6, §23.9).
- **IC-19.** A Harness or gateway model call is sent only after every item of its context is journaled as a sealed record entry of its run, mail as a reference to its mailbox that a rebuild re-renders and checks (§23.11), and each item of its response is journaled before the event that completes that item reaches the caller, so before any tool it asks for runs and before its stream ends; those entries leave a device, a person's own export or disclosure aside (RECORD.md sections 9 and 11), only sealed, as vault entries after DESIGN §16.7's secret rules, its hashing of addresses and numbers applying only where history leaves the member's devices otherwise (§24.9), the member's agents' enclaves reading them there as their other devices do (CO-43); web search results and `keep: false` details are kept only as stubs (§24).
- **IC-20.** A connection's OAuth credentials, its refresh tokens, its per-platform tokens and any client secret, are stored only in its own owner-bound `secret` repo, written there before their first use and after every rotation (CO-37); with its access tokens, which live only in the memory of the process that refreshed them, they are read only by the connection client of its member's consented devices that use them, the member's agents' enclaves among them (CO-42, CO-43), each token sealed again inside the repo to those devices' ReaderKeys, a Google token to its platform's alone, so a Team's audit reader that holds the repo opens none, and none enters an agent's context, a tool result, a record entry, an approval, an error or a log, or reaches a URnetwork server but as EVS ciphertext; a connection is made only by a person on an approval-capable device, its redirect landing on that device; a token goes only to its definition's token endpoints and to API hosts that both its definition and its record list, over TLS through the network's egress or, under `direct`, from the device's own address; a tainted run's write or send to a connected service is outward action 26, and a run that has read nothing untrusted needs no approval once the person has connected the service (CO-40); and a run that has read a `limited_use` service's data carries its mark, and its context reaches only the models that rule admits (§25).
- **IC-21.** A device lists only what its own OS tables and bridge state show, never connecting to a service to describe it; it publishes its list only as EVS ciphertext in its network's `listeners` repo, a person's device only once that person has acknowledged `listeners:publish` at its current version and, for a desktop, confirmed its own first list on it, a tagged sidecar only while an Owner's or Admin's acknowledgment for the network stands, and an entry its person hid, or bound to loopback alone, leaves the device only in a live answer to that person's own devices; the listeners rule admits a flow only to a `socket` or `map` entry in the set its host last published, less what its discovery has since removed, never to one of the host daemon's own listeners (DESIGN §17.6's rule 0), a forward, a port a narrower socket shares, or a source outside the network, and delivers it as the network's traffic, never at `127.0.0.1`; the host's hook decides every flow whatever a viewer's badge says (§26.5-§26.8).
- **IC-22.** An approval that exists only because a run is tainted, of kinds 23-26 alone, may be the classifier's: made on the requesting device, or in its enclave's daemon outside the agents' container, by the model and threshold the release pins, over every input that tainted the run and the whole of what the action would send, only where the person's setting and the network's allow `auto` for the kind, the person has acknowledged `approvals:auto`, and none of §27.7's rules or §27.8's limits holds; it is signed by that sidecar's own identity key on channel `auto`, its `auto_verdict` entry journaled before the effect, spendable only by its signer, never at a server gate or for a grant, and never shown as a person's approval; nothing the classifier reads leaves the device for it (§27.4-§27.9).
- **IC-23.** An agents' enclave's incarnation is, for the initial version, one of its sponsor's devices (CO-43): an untagged consented device of the sponsor that verified its evidence admits it, the admission naming the sponsor beside the enclave's tags, so it reads and writes what the sponsor's devices reach in EVS, their owner-bound repos included, while its network reach stays its tags'; it signs no admission, consent, share, suspension, revocation or key registration but its own, `IndexerSet`, config or approval but its own runs' automatic decisions (IC-22), and no device takes from it a version of the sponsor's harness config or enclave settings, so nothing it signs outlasts its revocation, which its stop, its loss and a compromise each are, every repo it read moving to a generation sealed without it (DESIGN §10.5); its agents' container holds none of the keys, tokens or link secrets its daemon uses for them (IC-14); in an enclave that reaches out, no run holds both the sponsor's private data and the container but by the person's kind 24 (§7.8); and the network's indexer enclave is no member's device (§11.4, Q-ENC-13).

### 2.5 Key custody

| Key | Holder | Who can misuse it |
|---|---|---|
| An enclave incarnation's identity, client, reader and SSH host keys | made in its VM at boot, bound in its evidence, never leaving it (§11.4) | the VM's software; its machine's holder by a physical attack (2.6), until the incarnation is revoked at its stop; with an agents' enclave's, everything its sponsor's devices read (CO-43) |
| The provisioning key of an incarnation | made in the VM, bound in its evidence, erased after use | the VM |
| An indexer enclave incarnation's mail-host key | made in its VM and attested by its identity key, as every receiver's is (DESIGN §13.8, §15.5), never leaving it (§11.10) | the VM's software; its machine's holder by a physical attack (2.6), until the incarnation is revoked |
| Chutes' instance E2E keys | made in Chutes' TEEs | the TEE's software, the serving code included (§4.5) |
| A device's SSH key | its keychain, registered with `KeyRegister` | as its identity key |
| Gateway tokens | the daemon's sealed store, as hashes; the harness's memory for an hour | same-user processes, within the grant's budget |
| The network's compute cache salt | derived from `K_sock` on each device, never stored | every admitted sidecar; it hides nothing from them |
| URnetwork's provider API keys | vault; the `computeservice` hosts | insiders; spends URnetwork's provider balances |
| API-key hotkeys K_P | a rate-limited signer on the `computeservice` hosts (§10.5) | insiders: at a gamma-native provider, URnetwork's whole account there (2 days of deposit, 3 of balance, its VMs) |
| The compute mint coldkey | vault; the taskworker hosts that mint | insiders: the mint float (7 days at most) |
| The treasury reserve | a 2-of-3 multisig on the owners' Ledgers | 2 owners |
| The compute-policy key; the staging key | two of the compute-policy key's four holders sign, on hardware tokens, under the release key's certificate for `ur-compute-policy` (DESIGN §2.6); the staging key on the CI host, certified for `ur-compute-policy-staging` alone (§5.4) | two of its holders; the staging key's holder, whose policies only staging and CI builds verify |
| Unreleased freshness tickets | a ticket host apart from ur.io's serving path and the broker, which posts each on its day (§5.4) | whoever takes it and the serving path both: a revocation withheld up to 14 days |
| URnetwork's x402 payer key (Base) | `searchsigner`, a rate-limited signer on hosts of its own, apart from `computeservice`'s (§21.5) | insiders: the payer float, at most two days of searches; the key could sign a transfer to anyone, which the watcher stops at the first |
| The treasury's USDC | Coinbase, its withdrawals whitelisted to the payer address alone (§21.5) | insiders with the exchange account, who can send it only to the payer address |
| A calendar link's secret (an app password or a secret address; an OAuth form's tokens are its connection's, in the next row); an iCloud app password, or a Fastmail one not limited to calendars, also opens the account's mail and contacts | its member's `secret` repo (§23.6); a device's memory during one call; OAuth access tokens in memory, an hour at most | the member's consented devices, their agents' enclaves among them (CO-43), each opening the copy sealed to it (§25.6); the provider that issued it |
| A connection's OAuth credentials: refresh tokens, per platform where the provider binds them to a client, and any client secret its client needs (§25.6) | its member's `secret` repo, one a connection; a device's memory during a refresh and its calls; access tokens in memory only, an hour at most | the member's consented devices that use them, their agents' enclaves among them (CO-43), each opening the copy sealed to it, a Google token only its platform's (§25.6); the provider that issued them; each within the scopes granted |

### 2.6 What a TEE does not protect

A pass in §5 means: genuine silicon, firmware at the policy's level, a measured image, a key held inside it, now. A miner holds the machine, and the 2025-2026 literature shows what that allows ([Rpt:bt] tee_attestation_verification.md):

| Attack | Cost | Effect | Seen by attestation |
|---|---|---|---|
| TEE.fail (October 2025), passive DDR5 interposer | under $1,000 | extracts Intel's PCK signing key, so forged TDX quotes verify as UpToDate on 4th-generation Xeon and later; steals keys from SEV-SNP VMs on Zen 4 and 5; reuses NVIDIA evidence, since GPU reports are not bound to a VM | no |
| DDRop (September 2026), active DDR5 interposer | ~$159 | takes over TDX VMs, forces debug, overwrites the launch measurement | no |
| Battering RAM (2025), DDR4 | ~$50 | replays SEV-SNP launch measurements | no |

Intel and AMD treat physical DRAM attacks as out of scope and plan no fix; NVIDIA excludes "sophisticated" physical attacks. Production confidential-AI systems answer with custody (Apple, Google and Meta run their own data centers; Meta logs host identities), and the Proof of Cloud Alliance (Phala, Secret, Oasis, Flashbots, Nillion) keeps a registry of chip identities verified on site. On Bittensor, where miners are anonymous, the design therefore:

- **labels** every use with its assurance, in the catalog, the apps and the security page: AP "in a TEE: protected from the provider's miners short of a physical attack; the provider itself is trusted", A1 "protected from the provider and its miners, short of a physical attack";
- **offers A2** where a custody registry covers a machine, and lets a network require it (§16.4);
- **revokes** chip identities and GPU serials found misbehaving, in the policy;
- **bounds what a broken machine exposes**: the network's indexer enclave holds only its grants and its incarnation's own keys; an agents' enclave, one of its sponsor's devices for the initial version (CO-43), holds what their devices hold, which a broken machine exposes whole, but none of their authority, so its reach ends at its stop or a compromise revocation (DESIGN §7.10), every repo it read moving to keys it never held, and the next incarnation's keys were never there (§11.4).

### 2.7 Threats

| Adversary | Threat | Mitigation | Residual |
|---|---|---|---|
| URnetwork's broker, breached or compelled | reads or alters inference; points the device at a TEE it controls, such as its own private chute on the same provider, whose evidence would verify; maps a direct model's name to another model or upstream, or drops its zero-retention flag | models pinned to provider ids in the signed policy, and a direct model's provider id, zero-retention rule and upstreams too, which the device checks against each receipt (§5.4, §6.6); instance lists and evidence read by the device over its own TLS through the tunnel; E2E to keys bound in that evidence; a random choice among the verified instances, refusing a prepare that narrows them (IC-1, IC-2; §5.5, §5.7) | denial; who used which model when, and how much (compute-1, compute-3) |
| The provider's API or gateway, for a TEE-labeled call | reads prompts; routes the call to a model without a TEE | the E2E path only; TEE model ids pinned by policy | sizes and timing |
| The provider's own platform software | reads plaintext inside the TEE | measured platform pinned (§5.4); the AP label shown | at AP, the provider can change the serving code (Chutes #75) or release disk keys; a network may require A1 (§16.4) |
| A provider without a TEE | reads, keeps or trains on conversations | its `none` label on every model and message; its disclosure, which the person acknowledges before the first call (§2.8, CO-34); the network's floor and provider list; the person's choice (CO-18); its retention and training terms at its gate (§4.7); sign-in mail's codes and links withheld from it (§23.4) | what the person sends to it |
| A prompt-injected agent, or a breached broker | acknowledges a disclosure for the person, or softens its text, so what the person sends goes where they never read it would | acknowledgments only by the person's own act on an approval-capable device, never a tool, a run, MCP, an RPC answer or a server; texts only from the signed policy, by id (§2.8) | a same-user process passing as the person at a terminal (TB1, owner decision 47) |
| A miner, without physical attack | reads, alters or replays | TDX or SEV-SNP; nonces; EPC-1 for enclaves | network metadata; `direct` traffic |
| A miner, with physical attack | forges evidence; reads memory | 2.6 | as 2.6 says: in an agents' enclave, everything its sponsor's devices hold, and tokens until replaced (CO-43) |
| A breach of an agents' enclave: a physical attack, a TEE flaw, or a kernel escape from its agents' container | reads everything its sponsor's devices hold (their vault and record, mailbox, calendar links, connections' tokens and repos), acts as that device while it runs (writes their repos, calls their connected services, spends within its budgets), and tries to stay | keys made in its VM, and an admission only after the sponsor's device verified its evidence (§11.7); an admission that signs no admission, consent, share, suspension, revocation or key registration but its own, config or person's approval, and whose versions of the sponsor's settings no device takes, so nothing it signs outlasts its revocation; at its stop, loss or compromise revocation every repo it read moves to keys it never holds, and a compromise revocation parks what it signed and lists the links and connections it could read to replace (§11.4, §25.7, IC-23); the agents' container holding no key, token or link secret (IC-14) | everything its sponsor's devices hold, while an incarnation runs, and tokens it took until replaced at their providers; accepted for the initial version (CO-43), disclosed (§2.8) |
| URnetwork's broker, breached, against an enclave | answers a device's evidence request from another VM of the same image on which it holds root, so the device admits the broker; adds a key or boot input the provider's image accepts; aims a new incarnation, the network's indexer above all, at a machine whose holder can attack it physically, by choosing placement or discarding VMs | under setup over SSH the evidence binds a secret the device sent only inside its verified session, and under EPC-1's second and third forms the measured init refuses or measures every key and boot input before any access service starts; in no form a key, console or command into a running guest; one VM per device authorization, the device starting each retry, counted on the card; the indexer only where the broker does not choose the machine, A2 or the provider's signed placement, and its keeper's new machines capped (§11.3, §11.6, §11.7, §11.10) | denial; for an agents' enclave, a targeted attack within its counted retries where neither A2 nor a provider's placement exists |
| The Owner or Admin whose device set an indexer incarnation up over SSH, or that device, breached | installs a payload that reads the mailboxes members grant and sends them out | members' devices seat such an incarnation only on its sponsor's signed setup statement, bound to its evidence, keys and B, and only from the member their grant accepted; each member sees who set it up, and how, before granting; EPC-1's other forms, which let every member check the payload, preferred where a provider offers them (§11.7, §11.10) | members trust that sponsor for what the setup installed, as CO-41 accepts |
| Another customer of the provider, or another member of a Team | learns prompts from cache timing | the cache salt, per member on the TEE path and per run on the direct path (§6.6) | none known |
| A prompt-injected agent | spends the balance; creates, stops or starts enclaves; spreads instructions by inbox; puts text into search queries; composes URLs to fetch | budgets; `enclave_create`, and a start through a tool, are outward, a tainted run's `enclave_stop` waits for the person, and no tool stops or starts the network's indexer enclave (§7.5); taint, wake limits per agent and per sender, and other members' messages waiting for a person's turn (§20.7); the secret check on queries (§21.6); listed URLs only, once tainted, without approval (§22.5) | spending within its budget; text that is no secret, in Parallel's logs and training data; a choice among listed URLs, which its own queries steer, 10 a person's turn (§22.5) |
