| A device of the network, or a prompt-injected agent in an enclave | reaches a service a member's device serves on every interface, such as a development server or a database with no password, by the listeners rule (CO-38) | `listeners:publish` read before a person's devices publish, each desktop's first list confirmed on it, and an Owner's or Admin's before tagged sidecars publish or the implicit document's rule opens; the rule opens exactly what the list shows, each entry with its program's name; hide by entry and by device; admins narrow the rule's sources, hosts and ports; loopback binds, `shared` ports, the daemon's own listeners and forwards never opened, and flows delivered as the network's, through `ur tun` where it runs, so the host's firewall and a service's own checks apply (IC-21, §26.7) | what a person leaves listed, by CO-38's choice; on a host without `ur tun`, a service its firewall keeps off the LAN (§26.7) |
| A page, mail or message written to pass the safety classifier | has a tainted run's action approved automatically: a composed URL carrying what the run read to a site the member has used, a command or message into the member's own enclave, a change to events without attendees on the person's unshared calendar, or a write to the person's own data at a connected service | the classifier over every input that tainted the run and over what would leave, raw and normalized; hidden characters ask; new destinations, other people and members, sends, secrets, amounts, interactive sessions and whole contexts always ask; one ask ends auto for the run; 10 a run and 50 a day; the record and the daily digest; `ask` per kind or by the network (§27.6-§27.10) | what it misses within those bounds: adaptive attacks pass classifiers like it most of the time, and the model is public, so text can be tuned against it offline (§27.3, §27.12); disclosed (`approvals:auto`) |
| A modified client, or a same-user process on a desktop | signs automatic decisions for actions §27's rules exclude | an automatic decision is spendable only by its signer and only for kinds 23-26, which no server gate sees; its `auto_verdict` entry and the digest show it on the person's other devices (§27.9) | as TB1: such a process already acts as the person there (owner decision 47) |

### 2.8 "Private from us" and disclosures

DESIGN §2.8's statement holds unchanged for compute, with "hosted models" no longer out of scope: URnetwork's servers never receive prompts, outputs, tool calls, enclave files or enclave keys in plaintext; they see the compute rows of §14.6. The disclosures add: what the TEE does not protect (2.6); what the AP label means, the provider itself trusted, wherever it applies (Chutes for inference today); that a remote call tells URnetwork which model a sidecar used, when, and for how many tokens; and that an enclave's `direct` egress leaves from the miner's address. A model labeled `none` runs outside any TEE, where its provider and the machines it runs on can read the conversation; the person chose it (CO-18). The exit carrying a direct call sees which window client sent it, so an exit and that provider together could tie one client's calls to each other; and URnetwork's charge rows and the provider's own records, both taken, tie each conversation the provider kept to its network and agent by time and token counts (2.7). The conversation itself may name the network and its agents, in the Harness's `ur://<net>/…` addresses and in agent and enclave names, so a provider that keeps it could link one network's runs and read the network's label; and on the TEE path Chutes' code reads the member's cache salt, which links that member's requests to each other (§6.6). Web search adds these, each in the disclosure a person acknowledges before their first search (§21.6): a query leaves the device for Parallel's gateway in plaintext, through an exit, so Parallel and Vercel, the gateway's host, read it and its results but not who asked, and Parallel may keep both and train on them, not linked to the person (CO-31); each search is a public payment on Base, so anyone can count URnetwork's searches and see their times, and Coinbase's facilitator and Stripe see each payment, never the query; and the exit carrying a search sees which window client sent it, so an exit and Parallel together could tie that client's queries to each other; and URnetwork's rows, which keep each search's network and minute for 72 hours, and Parallel's records, both taken, could tie a search to its network while searches are few. URnetwork's servers see neither queries nor results (§21). Mail and calendars (§23) add one: a calendar call leaves through an exit for the person's calendar provider, which sees the exit's address and acts on the person's own account, and the mail an agent reads goes to the model the person picked, as any prompt does.

Context history (§24) adds two things URnetwork's storage learns: which run a device, an enclave among them, opened, continued, forked or exported, from the entries it reads and their push times; and each large part's padded size, a fetched page's among them (§24.11).

**Disclosures (CO-31, CO-33, CO-34).** Each service and provider has an honest disclosure: what stays private and what could be exposed, in plain sentences a person can read in under a minute. CO-33 asks for one for each search, inference and enclave; CO-31 and CO-34 have the person read it before the first web search and before the first call to a model without a TEE.

| Part | Rule |
|---|---|
| Ids | one per service and provider (below); a new provider adds `inference:<slug>` or `enclave:<slug>` |
| Text | the signed policy's `disclosures` line (§5.4): per id an integer version, raised only when a fact changes, and a revision, raised at any other change of its words (A new version, below); per locale a one-line summary and the "Could be exposed" and "Private" lists, rendered in that order, as §21.6's are, English the reference and each translation read against it by a second person before the policy that carries it is signed. A device shows the person's locale where the policy has it, else English, and an acknowledgment covers its version in every locale. The compute-policy key signs it (§5.4), so no server can soften a text, and a change ships with the next policy, without a release. Devices render only the newest policy they verified, never text an event, a model, a tool or a server's answer carries |
| What asks | web search, a model whose provider is labeled `none`, the publishing of a person's devices' listeners (§26.6), a service's first connection and, at a new version, its next use (§25.12), the first automatic approval, which until then goes to the person rather than being refused (§27.11), and an enclave's creation on a provider, or its move there (kind 19, §11.7), wait until the person has acknowledged that disclosure's current version, or, on a tagged or cloud sidecar, an Owner or Admin has for the network (below), and a new version asks again (A new version, below). Local and TEE models ask nothing, since CO-34 asks only of models without a TEE: their lines show on every badge and in settings. At AP the miner stays out and the company inside is named and bound by E6's terms, as the owner accepted (Q-PROV-3, CO-35); an enclave asks although it is AP, since it holds what its sponsor's devices hold (CO-43) and may run root agents on the internet, and creating one is an approved act already |
| The acknowledgment | the person's, per network (Q-CTRUST-1): the key `compute.disclosures` of their harness config (`harness/config.json` in their vault, DESIGN §16.7), `{"<id>": <version acknowledged>}`, sealed as the vault is, so each of their devices reads it. Only the person writes it, on an approval-capable device, after the full text was shown: in the app's UI (`AckDisclosure`, §15.3) or with `ur disclosures ack <id>` on /dev/tty (§15.1). No agent, run, MCP tool, RPC `ui_response` or server writes it: DESIGN §16.6 refuses MCP's and the Harness's evs writes to the vault's `harness/` path, and a wider value written any other way applies only once the person confirms it (DESIGN §16.7). An agents' enclave, one of its sponsor's devices, reads the sponsor's from the vault as their other devices do (§11.4), never the network's. A person who changes their mind narrows `allow` or sets `tee_only` (§16.4) |
| The network's acknowledgment | for the network's tagged and cloud sidecars, which read no vault (Q-CTRUST-3, decided by CO-41): an Owner's or Admin's, kept in the ACL document's `compute` block as `disclosures`, `{"<id>": <statement>}` (§16.4). Each is a DESIGN §6.9 `Signed` statement, purpose `disclosure-ack` and SignedType `SIGNED_DISCLOSURE_ACK` 0x1809, naming the network, the id, the version, the locale and revision shown and the member, signed by the identity key of that member's approval-capable device once it has shown the whole text: in the app's network settings (`AckNetworkDisclosure`, §15.3) or with `ur disclosures ack <id> --network` on /dev/tty (§15.1), then saved into the document as any policy change is; a network with no document keeps the block alone, in a config record that sets no reach, so acknowledging changes no one's reach (§16.4), but for `listeners:publish`, whose acknowledgment alone turns on the implicit document's listeners rule for tagged sources (§26.6). A tagged or cloud sidecar takes an entry only if the statement verifies, its device was approval-capable (DESIGN §16.6) and its member an Owner or Admin in the network's AdminSet when it signed, and its version is current, or the previous one within a new version's grace (below); another config writer's save carries it unchanged, and any Owner or Admin may remove it, which only narrows. It covers `search:parallel` and the `inference:` ids, the uses such a sidecar may have, and `listeners:publish` as §26.6 says; a person's devices and the agents they run take only that person's, and an enclave its sponsor's (above). The apps' card for each tagged or cloud sidecar, and `ur status` on it, name each disclosure it relies on, its version, and who acknowledged it and when |
| The prompt | the run the person is attached to, the agent they talk to in the app or in `ur harness`, here or attached in an enclave (§7.10), raises a `ui_request` of kind `disclosure` (§7.6), naming the id and version, and waits until the acknowledgment lands; "Not now" fails the call: a search's error goes back to the model (§21.6), and a model's comes with §7.4's choice of another model or local |
| The refusal | any other caller gets `disclosure_required`, naming the id, its summary line and the fix (the app's settings, or `ur disclosures ack <id>`), and nothing leaves the device; a Harness run then stops, its stop reason naming the disclosure, so the person can acknowledge it and resume the run (§7.7, §21.6). Such callers are a child agent, a run its inbox woke, an enclave's agent with no session attached, an MCP call (§15.2), a gateway call (§8), `ur` without a terminal, an sdk call outside the Harness such as `Enclaves().Create`, which the app precedes with the text and `AckDisclosure` (§15.3), and a tagged or cloud sidecar whose network has not acknowledged the id (above), whose error names the fix for an Owner or Admin: the network's settings, or `ur disclosures ack <id> --network` |
| Where it is checked | on the device that would send: the router before a call (§6.4), the search tool before a search (§21.6), the connection client before a connection and before each call (§25.12), the device that files and runs a kind 19 (§11.7), the device or enclave daemon that would approve automatically (§27.9); in an enclave its daemon, from its sponsor's acknowledgments; on a tagged or cloud sidecar its daemon, from the network's. Not the broker (Q-CTRUST-2) |
| Always shown | every card of the service carries the summary line, which opens the full text: each search card; each model's badge in the selector and on each assistant message (§7.6); each enclave's card; kind 19's approval card (§16.3); the Connected services screen, the connect sheet and each kind-26 card (§25.12); each automatic approval's note, the day's digest and the Approvals settings (§27.11). Settings list every disclosure with its version and the version acknowledged, and for an Owner or Admin the network's and who gave it (§15.4); at a new version, every line of the disclosure, one that asks nothing included, is marked "changed" until the person opens it |
| A new version | a revision changes words alone (a fix, a clearer sentence, a translation): it asks no one, acknowledgments stand, and the lines change with no mark. A version changes a fact, and asks again: the person at their next attended use, the `disclosure` request marking what changed, and each Owner and Admin, by a notice in the apps, for the network's entry. So that a changed text stops no work, the previous version's acknowledgment counts on through the new version's grace, 14 days unless the policy's signers set 0, which they do when the change widens who reads or keeps what is sent; meanwhile the lines are marked "changed", and a "Not now" fails only the call it answers. When the grace ends, a caller with only the old acknowledgment gets `disclosure_required`, as before a first use. A running enclave is not stopped by a version at all (Q-ENC-8) |

| Id | Covers | Asks before | Its line shows on |
|---|---|---|---|
| `search:parallel` | web search (§21.6) | the first search (CO-31) | each search card |
| `inference:local` | local models (§6.5) | nothing | each `local-*` model's badge; the bot tab's model download |
| `inference:chutes` | Chutes' models, AP | nothing | each `chutes-*` model's badge |
| `inference:engy` | engy's models, `none` | the first call to any of them (CO-34) | each `engy-*` model's badge |
| `inference:saygm` | SayGM's models, `none`, its `-tee` ones included (Q-PROV-8) | the first call to any of them (CO-34) | each `saygm-*` model's badge |
| `enclave:hippius`, `enclave:lium`, `enclave:cathedral` | enclaves on that provider, AP | the first kind 19 there, and a member's first mailbox grant to an indexer enclave there (§11.10) | the create sheet, each enclave's card, kind 19's card |
| `listeners:publish` | a person's devices' listeners, published to every device of their network (§26.6) | the first publishing, once per network (CO-39), each desktop then confirming its own first list; for the network's tagged sidecars and, where it has no document, the listeners rule, an Owner's or Admin's for the network (CO-41) | the Listeners section, `ur listeners` |
| `connect:google`, `connect:microsoft`, `connect:custom` | a connected service (§25), `custom` for every person's own definition | the first connection to that service | the Connected services screen, the connect sheet, each kind-26 card |
| `approvals:auto` | automatic approvals of tainted runs' actions (§27) | the first automatic approval, once per network (CO-33, CO-40) | each automatic approval's note, the day's digest, the Approvals settings |

The texts, version 1, follow; search's is §21.6's (CO-31), the listeners' §26.6's, and automatic approvals' §27.11's. Each fact comes from §2.3, §2.6, §4.4, §4.5, §6.6, §11, §14.6 or §24.11; an enclave provider's text is checked again against its gate's findings before it ships (§4.7), and G-PROV-any re-reads every text against its provider each 90 days. The three enclave texts share one form, each filled with its provider's line.

```text
inference:local · version 1 · asks nothing
Summary: On this device: the model runs here, and no server takes part in a call.

Could be exposed
- Your conversation's history, kept in EVS so your devices can continue it. URnetwork's storage holds
  it encrypted, and sees its sizes and when it is written and read, so it can tell when this device is in
  a conversation and roughly how much is said, never what.
- What the agent's tools send out: a web search, which has its own disclosure, a page fetch or a
  calendar call.
- Hugging Face, which serves the model file, sees the download and the address it came from.
- Anyone who can use this device unlocked.

Private
- What you and the model said: no server takes part in a call, which sends no request and makes no
  charge.

inference:chutes · version 1 · AP: in a TEE, Chutes trusted · asks nothing
Summary: In a TEE that keeps Chutes' miners out, short of a physical attack; Chutes itself is trusted.

Could be exposed
- Chutes itself. The check does not cover its code that reads your conversation inside the TEE, and
  its platform holds the disk keys, so Chutes could change what reads it without the check showing it.
- Other customers' models can run in the same TEE, kept apart by Chutes' software alone.
- Chutes' code reads a value fixed for you at the head of each request, which keeps others out of your
  cache and lets Chutes tell your requests from others', never who you are.
- The machine's holder, by a physical attack on its memory that no check detects. Published attacks
  need under $1,000 in parts, and a holder who has done this once can fake the check on every
  machine they run.
- URnetwork's servers see the model, the token counts, the sizes, the times and the charge.

Private
- Your conversation is encrypted on this device to a key made inside a Chutes TEE whose evidence this
  device checked. URnetwork, Chutes' API and the miner who holds the machine see only ciphertext.
- Chutes sees URnetwork's account, never you, your device or your address.
- Other Chutes customers, and other members of your Team, cannot probe your prompts through its
  shared cache.
- One-time codes and sign-in or password-reset links in your mail stay on this device, unless you
  turn that off in settings.

inference:engy · version 1 · none: not in a TEE · asks before the first call
Summary: Not in a TEE: engy and the machines that serve its models can read everything in this
conversation.

Could be exposed
- Everything in the conversation, your prompts and files, the tools' results, and the mail and
  calendar items the agent reads, goes in plaintext to Cloudflare, where engy's TLS ends, to engy's
  gateway and to the machine that runs the model.
- engy promises zero data retention and no training on what you send. No evidence of where a request
  ran reaches this device, so that is a promise, not a proof. This device checks engy's signed receipt
  for each call, which says whether every machine that received it keeps no data, and stops using a
  model whose receipt says otherwise.
- One model, qwen3.6-35b-a3b, runs on independent operators' machines, whose retention engy cannot
  guarantee.
- What the conversation itself says: your network's name in the addresses the agent's tools use, and
  your agents' and enclaves' names, so engy could tell your conversations apart and link them.
- The exit that carries a call sees that it goes to engy, and its size and timing; with engy, it
  could link one client's calls to each other.
- URnetwork's servers see the model, the token counts, the charge and the minute. If engy kept a
  conversation, its records and URnetwork's, both taken, could tie it to your network.

Private
- Beside what the conversation says, engy sees only URnetwork's account, an exit's address and a
  random value per request: nothing this device adds names you, your device or your address.
- URnetwork's servers never see the conversation.
- One-time codes and sign-in or password-reset links in your mail stay on this device, unless you
  turn that off in settings.

inference:saygm · version 1 · none: not in a TEE · asks before the first call
Summary: Not in a TEE: SayGM, its miners and the services they call can read everything in this
conversation.

Could be exposed
- Everything in the conversation, your prompts and files, the tools' results, and the mail and
  calendar items the agent reads, goes in plaintext to SayGM's gateway, to the miner that serves the
  model and to the upstream service that miner calls, which the signed policy names for each model.
- Its "-tee" models too, named here without the mark: only SayGM's gateway can be checked, and
  nothing shows what reads a request behind it, or whether the request reaches a TEE at all.
- SayGM's terms set no limit on what it keeps or trains on. An upstream may keep or train on what it
  is sent, as its terms allow: Moonshot's do.
- SayGM's public records keep each request's model and token counts for good, naming no buyer.
- What the conversation itself says: your network's name in the addresses the agent's tools use, and
  your agents' and enclaves' names, so SayGM, its miners and its upstreams could link your conversations.
- The exit that carries a call sees that it goes to SayGM, and its size and timing. URnetwork's
  servers see the model, the token counts, the charge and the minute.

Private
- Beside what the conversation says, SayGM sees only URnetwork's account, an exit's address and a
  random value per request: nothing this device adds names you, your device or your address.
- URnetwork's servers never see the conversation.
- One-time codes and sign-in or password-reset links in your mail stay on this device, unless you
  turn that off in settings.

enclave:<provider> · version 1 · AP: in a TEE, <provider> trusted · asks before creating one there
Summary: A TEE on a machine a <provider> miner holds. Your own enclave is one of your devices and holds
what they hold, so <provider>, a physical attack or a breach there could expose all of it.

Could be exposed
- Everything your devices hold, while it runs: your vault and the record of every run, your mail, your
  calendar links and your connected accounts' tokens, and every repo you read. For now your enclave is
  one of your devices, with their access; a later version may narrow it.
- <provider> itself: <inside> sit inside the boundary and could read all of it.
- The machine's holder, a miner you do not know, by a physical attack on its memory that no check
  detects, or anyone who breaks the TEE or escapes its agents' container: all of the above, and the keys
  to act as this device until it stops, reading and writing your repos and calling your accounts.
  Tokens taken then work until you replace them at their providers.
- A holder who has done such an attack once can fake the check on every machine they run, this
  enclave's among them.
- Agents you run in it act as root on the internet through its egress: the sites they reach see what
  they send, and the exit that carries it sees where it goes and anything not encrypted.
- Its agents read every repo you read, and an agent in it that a page misleads can send out what it
  read. A run in it that reads your mail, calendars, accounts or vault uses none of its root tools
  unless you approve, and a run's writes after it read mail, a page or another outside source wait
  until you release them before its root tools see them.
- Under the default egress its agents reach web, mail and DNS ports and ports from 1024 up, not
  SSH's port 22; an exit of your own network carries the rest.
- If it is your network's mail indexer, it is no device of yours: it holds each member's incoming
  mail, in plaintext as it arrives, whether or not they granted it anything, and every mailbox a
  member grants it, which <provider>, or the machine's holder by a physical attack, could read. It
  then runs no agents and admits no login. If it was set up over SSH, your device cannot check what
  the setup installed and relies on the word of the Owner or Admin whose device did, whom your mail
  settings name. In a Team it starts taking mail a day after every member is told.
- Services that listen in it on every interface are listed to every device of your network, which
  can connect to them unless its policy narrows that; its agents' own services stay in your view
  until you map one.
- The machine's holder sees its traffic's size and timing, and, under direct egress, which you
  approve, where it goes and anything not encrypted.
- URnetwork's servers see its shape, provider, state, times, charges and how much it sends through
  URnetwork's network.

Private
- Its files, keys and agents' work are encrypted in memory and on disk: the machine's holder cannot read
  them short of that attack, and URnetwork's servers never see them or its commands.
- Its keys are made inside it and never leave it; your device checked its evidence before admitting
  it as yours.
- Its agents never hold your keys, tokens or links: its sidecar uses them for them, outside their
  container. It cannot add a device, consent, share, approve for you, or change your settings.
- When it stops, its keys end with it, and your repos move to keys it never held.
- By default its traffic leaves through URnetwork's network, so sites see an exit's address, not the
  machine's.

<inside>, by provider:
- Hippius (CPU, AMD SEV-SNP): Hippius' image, its platform software and the key service that
  releases its image's disk keys.
- Lium (GPU, Intel TDX with NVIDIA GPUs in confidential mode, whole machines): Lium's node software
  and the container it starts for you, which its evidence does not cover.
- Cathedral (CPU, AMD SEV-SNP sandboxes): Cathedral's sandbox platform, as its gate documents it.
```

### 2.9 Decisions proposed

**D-CTRUST-1 (proposed).** TB4 and IC-1 to IC-23 as above. *Why:* CO-2; CO-16; CO-17; CO-18; CO-20; CO-23; CO-24; CO-25; CO-38; CO-40; CO-43; the directive.

**D-CTRUST-2 (proposed).** Physical attacks are disclosed, answered by A2 where custody registries reach, never hidden behind "TEE". *Why:* 2.6.

**D-CTRUST-3 (proposed).** Every web search, inference provider and enclave provider has a disclosure, by id, its versioned text in the signed policy and its summary line on every card of the service; web search, providers labeled `none` and enclave providers ask before first use, and again at each version that changes a fact, once its grace ends, refusing with `disclosure_required` until acknowledged on an approval-capable device, in the app's UI or on /dev/tty, never by an agent, a run, MCP, an RPC answer or a server; local and TEE models ask nothing; the acknowledgment is the person's harness config key `compute.disclosures`, which an enclave takes from its sponsor, and for the network's tagged and cloud sidecars an Owner's or Admin's signed statement in the `compute` block, which each such sidecar's card names. *Why:* CO-31, CO-33, CO-34, CO-41; a breached broker must not soften a text, and no run may consent for the person.

**D-CTRUST-4 (proposed).** Version 1 of the texts is 2.8's, each fact taken from §2.3, §2.6, §4.4, §6.6 and §11 and checked again at each gate and by G-PROV-any; a changed fact is a new version, which asks again while the previous acknowledgment carries running work through its grace, 14 days unless the policy's signers set 0 for a change that widens who reads or keeps what is sent; a change of words alone, or a translation, is a revision, which asks no one. *Why:* CO-33's "honest"; D-CTRUST-2's rule against hiding behind "TEE"; a fix of wording must not stop a network's agents.

### 2.10 Questions

**Q-CTRUST-1.** Is an acknowledgment kept per network or once per person? *Options:* (a) per network, in each network's vault; (b) once, copied by the app into each of the person's networks. *Answer:* (a). The vault and its harness config are per network, and DESIGN keeps no store across a person's networks; CO-26 treats each network as one person or entity, whose policy may allow different providers, so its member reads and acknowledges there. A person in two networks acknowledges in each. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTRUST-2.** Should the broker refuse a call or a search whose disclosure the person has not acknowledged? *Options:* (a) no: the device checks; (b) yes, on a flag the device sends. *Answer:* (a). The acknowledgments are sealed in the person's vault, which no server reads, so the broker could check only a flag the device sets, which a modified client sets as easily as it skips the prompt. The check protects the person from surprise, which only the person's own device can do; it does not protect URnetwork from the device. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-CTRUST-3.** May a tagged or cloud sidecar, which reads no vault, use what needs a disclosure, such as a CI runner calling an engy model? *Options:* (a) no: it gets `disclosure_required`, saying that a tagged sidecar cannot acknowledge; (b) by its sponsor's acknowledgments, carried to it as an enclave's are; (c) by an admin's acknowledgment in the network's `compute` block. *Answer:* (c), decided by the owner (CO-41): an Owner's or Admin's acknowledgment, kept in the network's `compute` block, covers the network's tagged and cloud sidecars, enclaves keeping their sponsor's; the admin sees the disclosure text before accepting for them. §2.8 carries it: the signed statement, who may make it, where it is checked, what each such sidecar's card shows, and how a new version asks the admin again without stopping work. *Decider:* owner, decided (CO-41).

### 2.11 Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| People acknowledge without reading | high | a provider reads what the person did not expect | texts short enough to read in a minute; the summary on every card and message, so the fact is met again; each new version asks again |
| A new version stops unattended runs on a `none` provider until the person acknowledges | low | agents, gateway calls and listeners stop | only a changed fact makes a version, a change of words being a revision; the previous acknowledgment carries work through a 14-day grace, set to 0 only for a change that widens exposure; the apps show what changed; the error names the fix |
| An Owner or Admin acknowledges for the network's tagged sidecars without reading, or members do not expect a CI runner's prompts to reach a `none` provider | medium | a provider reads what members put through those sidecars | the whole text before the act, on an approval-capable device; each such sidecar's card names who acknowledged; the network's `assurance_floor` and `providers` still bind; any Owner or Admin withdraws it (§2.8) |
| A text drifts from its provider's facts | medium | a disclosure that is no longer honest | each gate and G-PROV-any's 90-day check re-read the text; a changed fact is a new version |

## 3. Architecture and flows

### 3.1 Purpose and scope

The component map, where each piece lives, and the end-to-end flows. It introduces nothing the other sections do not design; where they disagree, the owning section wins.

### 3.2 Component map

```text
DEVICE (ur daemon on desktops; the sdk in the app process; never the VPN component)
  Harness (§7) ─────────────┐        gateway (§8) ◀── Codex, Claude Code, others on loopback
    tools: workspace, git    │            │
    (§13), evs, search,      ▼            ▼
    agent_* (§20), enclave_*, ssh_exec (§12) ──▶ router (§6.4) ──▶ local engine (§6.5): engine process | app host
                                                   │
```

The dependency rule holds: these pieces import `connect` and the sidecar root, never `server` or `sdk` (owner rule 2).

### 3.4 Flows

| Flow | Path | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| CF-1 Local inference | Harness or gateway → router → engine (process or app host) → events; no server, no charge | §6.5 |
| CF-2 Remote inference | router → evidence over the device's own TLS (tunnel) → keys via the broker → verify → seal → broker (worst-case hold) → provider E2E → TEE → stream back → settle → check usage → record | §6.6, §9.7, §5 |
| CF-3 Gateway call | harness → loopback (Host, token, grant) → translate → CF-1, CF-2 or CF-15, a hosted search tool dropped or answered `unavailable` (§21.7) → translate back → `model_call` and the call's new session entries (§24.8) | §8, §21.7 |
| CF-4 Buy credits | app or `ur compute buy` → Stripe Checkout, or a store purchase whose account token names the network, or one bound as Pro's are → webhook, notification or the app's report (`Compute().StorePurchase`) → lot, credited once by its transaction or order id, a Play consumable then consumed | §9.5, §14.3 |
| CF-5 Threshold top-up | balance under T → `compute_auto_renew` → off-session PaymentIntent → lot, or email and retry | §9.8 |
| CF-6 Pay a provider | treasury buys TAO → `mint_gamma` into D_P → `spend_gamma` at S_P → provider credits URnetwork → reconcile | §10.4 |
| CF-7 Create an enclave | approval → keys → broker → provider VM → evidence → verify → sealed bundle → enroll, an agents' enclave as one of its sponsor's devices (§11.4) → `ur tun`, SSH, Harness → running | §11.7 |
| CF-8 Attach | local Harness → SSH to overlay address → `ur harness rpc` → events both ways | §7.10 |
| CF-9 SSH | client → overlay → server checks key, flow principal, rule → session → receipt | §12.5 |
| CF-10 An agent thread | `agent_send` → create-only write in the recipient's inbox → lease fires → Harness queues → reply in the thread → sender's lease fires → again | §20.7 |
| CF-11 Stop, start, remove an enclave | orchestrator and a member device; new incarnations through CF-7 | §11.11 |
| CF-12 Low balance | the balance, holds left out, under 24 h of burn → `compute_low` → threshold renew → grace → suspended → enclaves stopped but the indexer, which runs on its reserve and grace (§9.9), each card naming the balance → a top-up → their keepers start them again, else their sponsors (§11.7) | §9.9 |
| CF-13 Web search | tool → disclosure check → query check → request → `402` from Parallel's gateway → authorize (broker: asset, ceiling, budgets, daily and search caps, rate, hold; then the signer, apart: screen, sign) → paid retry → results → settle on Base → untrusted result; the outcome class with the next authorization | §21.5, §21.6, §21.8 |
| CF-14 Web fetch | tool → listed-URL rule, or approval → address checks → `GET` through the egress → extract → untrusted result | §22.4, §22.5 |
| CF-15 Remote inference without a TEE | router → floor and providers → hash the request → broker: the declared model's hold under the exposure rule, sign btauth/1 → egress → provider → stream back → settle from the provider's usage, looked up in three states → record | §6.6, §9.7 |
| CF-16 Manage a remote Harness | `harness_list` (`enclave_list`, the agents repo) → kind 24 on an approval-capable device when the run is tainted and the enclave's egress is not `none` → SSH to the enclave's overlay address → `ur harness rpc --manage` under the caller's signed origin, which the enclave's SSH server verifies outside the agents' container and joins to its Harness → `ur_list_agents`, `ur_launch_agent`, or a Pi command naming its agent, its text also in a thread (CF-10) → trusted, or untrusted and tainting, by its origin → `ur_subscribe`'s events nested under the enclave → the agent reports back in the thread with `agent_send`, to the person's `me` when the prompt carried the person's request → the person's devices show it, or the asker's lease fires, link up or not | §7.10, §20.7 |
| CF-17 Mail summary and calendar write | `mail_list` (unread) → taint, fsynced → `mail_read` → the model (local, TEE or direct) → `mail_summary` card → `calendar_add` → kind 25 on an approval-capable device, events switched → the link read into memory → DoH and the egress → CalDAV `PUT` (create-only) or the provider's API → `calendar_event` cards → record | §23.10 |
| CF-18 Continue a run | a member's device, their agents' enclave among them (CO-43): the run's nodes from the vault → verify writers, chains, parent links and blob hashes → rebuild the context at the chosen node and check its request hash → a new run whose first node names it → continue, recording as any run | §24.6, §24.7 |
| CF-19 Connect a service | `ur connect` on `/dev/tty`, the apps' screen, or an agent's `connection_request` card the person accepts → the disclosure → PKCE, `state` and `nonce` in memory → the system browser (loopback, the iOS session, `AuthorizationClient` or the Auth Tab) → the provider's sign-in and consent, from the person's own address → the redirect on the device: `state`, `iss` → the code exchange through the egress, from the connection's exit → the ID token's checks, the scopes granted → `connection.json` in a new `secret` repo → the `connection` event; tools then attach tokens in the daemon | §25.5 |

| CF-21 Automatic approval | a tainted run's outward call of kind 23-26 → `Sidecar.Authorize`: the version-5 action with field 70, the request filed tainted → `auto_ok`: the kind, basis and rules, the person's setting and acknowledgment, the network's block and evidence list, the run's inputs, the limits, the manifest's switch and the model's hash → the classifier on the device or in the enclave's daemon: the inputs' cached scores and the action's text, raw and normalized → allow: the `auto_verdict` entry, a version-3 decision on channel `auto` signed by the device, request and decision in one push, the effect, the run's note and the day's digest; ask: the `auto_verdict` entry and `approval_pending` to the person's approval-capable devices | §27.9 |

## 4. Providers

### 4.1 Purpose and scope

This section answers CO-13: which Bittensor subnets the compute extension can use for inference, in a TEE or not (CO-18), and for enclaves, as of 2026-11-23, by what test, and which it starts with. It defines the bar a provider must clear, the provider adapter every provider is reached through, and the gates that admit a provider to the catalog. How the device checks the evidence is §5; how URnetwork pays is §10. The full evidence is [Rpt:bt].

### 4.2 Requirements

| Id | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| R-PROV-1 | Every provider's label says whether a TEE protects the workload; enclaves always run in one | CO-2, CO-18 |
| R-PROV-2 | For a TEE label, the device verifies the TEE itself, from evidence bound to its own nonce and to the key it encrypts to | R-CCTX-2 |
| R-PROV-3 | For a TEE label, no hop outside the TEE, the provider's own gateway included, sees plaintext; for any label, no URnetwork server does | directive; CO-2, CO-18 |
| R-PROV-4 | The provider accepts Gamma | CO-10 |
| R-PROV-5 | The provider's terms let URnetwork buy on its users' behalf | derived |
| R-PROV-6 | Providers are reached through one adapter interface, so one can be added or dropped without touching the Harness, the gateway or the ledger | derived |
| R-PROV-7 | A provider without a TEE is reached from the device, its requests signed by URnetwork's broker over their hash, and its usage per request is readable by URnetwork | directive; CO-18, CO-10 |

### 4.3 The bar

A TEE provider enters the catalog when it meets every eligibility rule E1-E7, and carries the label A1, A2 or AP. A provider without a TEE enters when it meets N1-N5 below, and carries the label `none` (CO-18).

| Rule | Test |
|---|---|
| E1 TEE execution | inference runs in an Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP VM, with GPUs in NVIDIA confidential-computing mode; an enclave is such a VM |
| E2 Evidence | the device fetches a CPU quote and, for GPUs, NVIDIA SPDM evidence, bound to a 32-byte nonce the device chose (or a beacon nonce, §5.6) |
| E3 End to end | the key the device encrypts to is generated inside the TEE and bound in the quote's report data; the provider's gateway, validators and load balancers carry ciphertext |
| E4 Measurements | the provider publishes the measurements its images produce (MRTD and RTMRs, or the SEV-SNP launch digest), with enough of the build to review; URnetwork pins them in the signed policy (§5.4); each catalog model is bound to the provider's own id for it (Chutes: the `chute_id`), so the device asks for that model's instances and no other's |
| E5 Gamma | the provider's subnet has `SubnetGammaEnabled`, publishes a service, and credits gamma spent at it (§10) |
| E6 Terms | a written agreement allowing URnetwork's relay or rental for its users, a DPA, no training on data, notice before suspension |
| E7 Capacity | at least 2 instances per catalog model, or capacity for the enclave shapes offered, and an API that reports status |

| Label | Meaning | Who sees what |
|---|---|---|
| **A1** `tee` | E1-E4 hold, and every piece of code inside the TEE that handles plaintext is measured and pinned, so the provider cannot change what reads a request without changing the evidence | the miner is outside the boundary unless it mounts a physical attack (§2.6); the provider company is outside too |
| **A2** `tee+custody` | A1, and each machine's chip identity (Intel PPID, AMD chip id) is in a custody registry the policy names, such as the Proof of Cloud Alliance's | as A1, with physical attacks needing a data center's cooperation |
| **AP** `tee-platform` | E1-E4 hold for the provider's base image, but the provider's own unmeasured code (serving code, a tenant image) or a key service it runs sits inside the boundary | the miner stays out; the provider company is inside, trusted as a cloud is |
| **none** `no-tee` | N1-N5 hold; no TEE | the provider and the machines it runs on read the conversation; URnetwork's servers do not (§6.6) |

| Rule | Test, for a provider without a TEE |
|---|---|
| N1 Direct calls | a device can call the provider's inference API itself with a per-request authorization the broker makes without reading the request: btauth/1, which signs a hash of the body (§6.6), or an equivalent |
| N2 Usage | URnetwork can read each request's usage itself, keyed by the btauth/1 nonce or the body hash, never by an id only the device sees, and checks a receipt the provider signs where it offers one, so a device cannot under-report what URnetwork pays for; the lookup answers `unknown`, `in progress` or `finished`, so a call still running is never taken for one never served (§6.6) |
| N3 Gamma | as E5 |
| N4 Terms | as E6, with the provider's retention and training terms stated, since they bind what it does with prompts |
| N5 API | an OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API with streaming and tool calls |

Remote inference takes every label by default (CO-18); a network or a person may require AP, A1 or A2, or name the providers it allows (§16.4), and AP is the lowest TEE label (Q-PROV-3). Enclaves take A1 where a provider offers it and AP otherwise. Every surface shows the label: the catalog, the badge on each message (§7.6), the enclave card and the record.

| Others (Actual, Yugos, Cacheon, Instant, REAX, rec4ll, Pareton, hoτfloaτ, Apex, ComputeHorde, Green Compute, Weir, ByteLeap, Gittensor, Cortex) | no TEE | no TEE | — | — | some | — | **ineligible** |

Gone or moved since 2025: SN2's Inference Labs (to DaniLabs, 2026-10-16; its SGX prototype archived), SN19 Nineteen (now blockmachine), SN27 NI Compute (now Komms), SN39 Basilica (Covenant AI left 2026-04-09; now Kokoah), SN42 Masa (now CADmind), SN49 Polaris (deregistered by 2025-11-01). Netuids change hands, so the adapter names a provider by team and endpoint, and the netuid is a field of its gamma setup, re-read at each gate (§4.7).

**The providers chosen (CO-28).** Inference: Chutes, in a TEE (AP), and engy and SayGM, without one (`none`). Enclaves: Hippius, Lium and Cathedral. Web search: Parallel (§21). URnetwork builds an adapter for each, and each serves users once its gate passes (4.7), since the gates carry the directive's and §5's checks; no other provider is integrated unless the owner adds it, and any of them without gamma at launch is dropped from launch (CO-32), which today is Chutes.

**What this means.**

1. **Inference: Chutes is the one provider that meets E1-E4 today, at AP.** Its quote proves a genuine TDX VM booted Chutes' base image, binding the device's nonce and the instance's E2E key; it does not cover the serving code or the tenant image, which Chutes builds and which share one measurement across every account's chutes (a private finetune had the same RTMR1-3 as Chutes' own Qwen chute, 2026-11-17). So the miner is kept out, and Chutes is trusted. Its plain OpenAI path is worse still: Chutes' API reads every prompt there, and since 2026-11-04 the same API serves 9 non-TEE models from third parties that may keep data 30 days. Only its E2E path, with the device verifying the evidence and failing closed, meets R-PROV-2 and R-PROV-3. Chutes' own E2E clients (`chutes-e2ee`, `e2ee-proxy`) do not check attestation, so sidecar implements the client itself (§6.6), as the independent verifiers teep and chutes-litellm-proxy do.
2. **Chutes fails E5 and E6 today.** SN64 has not enabled gamma, and resale needs a written agreement. Both are the M12 gate (4.7), and a provider without gamma at launch is dropped from launch (CO-32), so remote TEE inference launches only if SN64 takes gamma or SayGM's pass-through (Q-PROV-1) is in place; engy, which takes gamma, carries the launch's remote models once G-PROV-engy passes, and SayGM, which takes it too, joins once G-PROV-saygm passes (Q-PROV-10, CO-35); until Chutes joins, a person or network whose floor is a TEE label has local models alone (§6.3, §19.2).
3. **Enclaves: no provider meets E1-E4 for a VM we image.** Hippius comes closest for CPU (a Debian VM with sudo, SEV-SNP, gamma); Lium for GPU (TDX with NVIDIA CC, gamma). In both, the provider company stays inside the boundary, so both are AP. Cathedral, the third chosen (CO-28), offers SEV-SNP sandboxes with egress modes and gamma, but is not yet generally available. §11.3 states what an enclave provider must offer to reach A1, the enclave platform contract.
4. **Targon cannot be used** for either: no inference, no evidence a renter can check, terms that forbid resale.
5. **Without a TEE (CO-18): engy first; SayGM once it signs usage per request and enforces an allowlist.** Both take gamma and btauth/1, so a device can call them directly with a request the broker signs (§6.6); engy's signed receipts make its usage checkable per request, while SayGM's public records name no buyer, nonce or hash (G-PROV-saygm). Their frontier models, served with miners' own upstream keys, stay out (Q-PROV-7), as do Chutes' models without a TEE and Terza, which no device can call directly.

### 4.5 What the TEE does not cover, provider by provider

| Gap | Chutes | Lium | Hippius | Design response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Serving code unmeasured | yes (issue #75, open): a chute's `serve.py` can change without changing the quote | the renter's container is unmeasured | n/a | the reason Chutes is AP, not A1 (4.3); catalog entries say "serving code not measured; Chutes trusted" |
| Multi-tenant VMs | yes: one VM held chutes of several accounts (2026-11-17) | only single-tenant when every GPU is rented | VMs are single-tenant | disclosed |
| Cross-account prompt cache | yes (issue #78, open): the KV cache is shared across all accounts; `cache_salt` ignored | — | — | a per-member cache salt at the head of every request's system text (§6.6), so a prefix shared with another network never hits |
| Physical attack by the miner | in scope (TEE.fail, DDRop, Battering RAM) | in scope | in scope | §2.6: disclosed; A2 where a custody registry covers the machine |
| Provider changes terms or prices | Chutes cut free TEE access on 2026-02-27 with no notice, and its terms let prices change when posted | — | — | hourly price reads (§9.6); the catalog drops a model whose cost passes its price |
| The live measurement list | Chutes' `/servers/tdx/measurements` is unsigned, and on 2026-10-12 an instance served on an image Chutes had stopped publishing | — | — | devices never read the live list: only the signed policy's reviewed profiles pass (§5.4), and a withdrawn profile is revoked there |

### 4.6 The provider adapter

Every provider is one Go value behind one interface, in `computeservice` (server side) and `infer_`/`enclave_` (device side), so the Harness, the gateway and the ledger never name a provider.

```go
// computeservice (server); device-side halves live in infer_provider.go and enclave_provider.go
type ComputeProvider interface {
	Id() ComputeProviderId                  // stable: "chutes", "engy", "saygm", "hippius", "lium", "cathedral"; never a netuid
	Catalog(ctx context.Context) (*ComputeProviderCatalog, error) // models, shapes, prices in gamma, capacity
	// inference
	InstanceKeys(ctx context.Context, modelId string) ([]*ComputeInstanceKey, error) // id, e2e public key, one-use nonces
	Evidence(ctx context.Context, modelId string, instanceId string, nonce []byte) (*ComputeEvidence, error)
	Invoke(ctx context.Context, call *ComputeInvoke) (*ComputeInvokeStream, error)   // ciphertext in, ciphertext out
	Usage(ctx context.Context, requestId string) (*ComputeUsage, error)              // the provider's own record
	// the direct path (§6.6), for providers without a TEE
	DirectTarget(modelId string) (*ComputeDirectTarget, error)                     // host, method, target, receiver, and the
	                                                                               // model's provider id, zdr and upstreams: as the policy pins them
	DirectUsage(ctx context.Context, nonce []byte, bodyHash []byte) (*ComputeUsage, error) // by btauth/1 nonce or body hash (N2)
	VerifyReceipt(receipt []byte, bodyHash []byte) (*ComputeUsage, error)          // a provider-signed receipt (engy: Ed25519)
	// enclaves
	CreateVm(ctx context.Context, spec *ComputeVmSpec) (*ComputeVm, error)
	VmEvidence(ctx context.Context, vmId string, nonce []byte) (*ComputeEvidence, error)
	VmStatus(ctx context.Context, vmId string) (*ComputeVm, error)
	DeleteVm(ctx context.Context, vmId string) error
	// money
	Payment() ComputeProviderPayment        // gamma: netuid, service hotkey, API-key hotkey (§10)
	Balance(ctx context.Context) (model.NanoCents, error) // what URnetwork has left at the provider
}
```

The device's half verifies (§5) and encrypts (§6.6); the server's half carries bytes on the TEE path and signs and settles on the direct path, holds URnetwork's credentials for the provider, and meters. A provider that offers inference only answers `ErrComputeNotOffered` for the VM calls, and the reverse.

### 4.7 Gates

| Gate | When | Passes if |
|---|---|---|
| G-PROV-chutes | M12's entry, and again whenever SN64 enables gamma, Chutes joining then (CO-32) | SN64 `SubnetGammaEnabled` with a published service that credits URnetwork's API-key hotkey; a signed agreement covering E6 (relay for end users, notice before suspension, a DPA, no training); the evidence and E2E endpoints answer as §4.4 says; each catalog model's `chute_id` recorded in the policy; Chutes' VM root CA (`sek8s-vm-root-ca`) pinned; the evidence endpoint open to URnetwork's tunnel without an account, at a rate the agreement fixes for URnetwork's addresses, which every device shares (§5.7); §18's attestation vectors recorded; the external audit of §5 and §6.6 done (§19.2) |
| G-PROV-hippius | user-facing enclaves on Hippius | EPC-1 to EPC-9 (§11.3), shown by §18's "rewritten bootstrap refused" test, and its tests of a host-added key or boot input and of another VM's evidence at setup, run on Hippius itself; for the indexer role, a placement URnetwork's broker does not choose, signed by Hippius, or A2 (§11.10); SN75's gamma service credits a test hotkey; E6; the external audit of §11.7 and §12 done |
| G-PROV-lium | GPU enclaves | as Hippius, for a whole-machine CVM with the renter's image measured |
| G-PROV-cathedral | enclaves on Cathedral | as Hippius: general availability; EPC-1 to EPC-9 (§11.3), by setup over SSH's one feature (Q-ENC-7) if not by launch data; how a guest requests its own report, and the image's measurements, documented; SN94's gamma service credits a test hotkey; E6 |
| G-PROV-engy | engy's models in the catalog | N1-N5 shown: btauth/1 on its inference routes under URnetwork's hotkey; signed receipts on btauth requests, and a usage record URnetwork's hotkey can read by btauth/1 nonce or body hash, which answers each nonce `unknown`, `in progress` or `finished`, a request it refused or never served `unknown` (N2); asked of engy but not required: a bound the broker signs and engy enforces, a model allowlist per hotkey or the model and a cost cap in the signed target, which would let each direct call hold its own model's worst case (§6.6); SN53's gamma service credits a test hotkey; written terms on serving URnetwork's users, resale, retention and training (N4), the models whose terms bar training on, keeping past the request, and any person reading what they are sent recorded in the policy's `limited_use` line (§5.4, §25.10), a model it serves without `provider.zdr` on operators' machines recorded only if those terms bind the operators; `provider.zdr` honored, and each model's provider id, aliases and zero-retention rule recorded in the policy's `direct` line (§5.4); from a sample of at least 50 of URnetwork's exits across its regions, signed calls succeed 99 times in 100 with no challenge from engy's edge (Cloudflare), by an exemption that edge sets for btauth/1-signed routes, their latency recorded; engy asked to check a nonce when a request's headers arrive rather than its body, so upload time stops counting against the window (§6.6); the external audit of §6.6's direct path done (§19.2) |
| G-PROV-saygm | SayGM's models in the catalog | as G-PROV-engy (N1-N5, and its edge measured from exits the same way), once SayGM adds: a receipt per response signed by its gateway's attested key, or a usage listing for URnetwork's hotkey, carrying the btauth/1 nonce or the body hash with the model, tokens and charge (N2), its public settlement records, keyed by request id alone, not sufficing; a model and upstream-route allowlist it enforces for URnetwork's hotkey whatever `X-GM-Providers` a device sends, since btauth/1 does not sign it, each model served only on routes whose terms allow URnetwork's resale, or the model bound into the signed request as its Gemini surface's path already binds it, with its routes pinned the same way; written terms on its own retention and training, with each listed model's upstreams pinned in the policy's `direct` line (§5.4); its btauth/1 window confirmed |
| G-PROV-any | each provider, every 90 days | E1-E7, or N1-N5 for a provider without a TEE, re-checked, and its disclosure's text (§2.8) against them, a changed fact making a new version; a failure takes the provider out of the catalog for new work, and running enclaves are told to move (§11.11) |

A gate that fails does not stop the milestone's other work: the Harness, local inference, the ledger and the gateway ship with what the catalog holds, and the remote models or enclave shapes behind the gate wait.

Every inference gate, a TEE provider's included, also records which of its models' written terms bar training on, keeping past the request, and any person reading what they are sent, for the policy's `limited_use` line, which a run that has read Google's data needs (§5.4, §25.10): at AP and without a TEE the provider reads the plaintext, so its terms are the only bar, and at A1 they bind what its measured code keeps.

### 4.8 Alternatives considered

| Option | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chutes' plain OpenAI API, for its models without a TEE | the rest of Chutes' catalog | the broker would hold Chutes' key and read every prompt (the directive), and Chutes signs no per-request authorization a device could carry (N1) | not in the catalog until Chutes offers one |
| Frontier models (Claude, GPT, Gemini) through SayGM or Terza | frontier models paid in gamma, inside CO-18's "all inference" | served with miners' own upstream keys, which Anthropic's (D.4), OpenAI's (3.1, 3.3(g)) and Google's terms bar reselling; SayGM's own terms bar access that circumvents provider policies; no upstream approval found | excluded; SayGM only for models whose upstream terms allow it, behind its enforced allowlist (G-PROV-saygm) |
| Chutes' TEE models through SayGM, paid in SN28 gamma | gamma for Chutes' models, which SN64 does not take | today SayGM's gateway and miner read each request, and only the gateway is verifiable (Q-PROV-8); an end-to-end pass-through to Chutes' encrypted invoke would keep Chutes' AP label, but SayGM has not built one and Chutes must consent to the resale | asked of SayGM and Chutes (Q-PROV-1 (d)) |
| URnetwork's own inference on Lium confidential pods, paid in SN51 gamma | gamma today; our own serving image | Lium's quote does not cover the container; whole 8-GPU machines at $30-100 an hour need steady load; a fleet to run | not taken (Q-PROV-1 (c), CO-32): CO-28 names Lium for enclaves alone |
| Pay Chutes in TAO or alpha, which it accepts | inference sooner | against CO-10 | declined: a provider without gamma at launch is dropped from launch (CO-32, Q-PROV-1) |
| Per-user Chutes accounts through "Sign in with Chutes" | no relay | users pay Chutes, not URnetwork (against CO-10); two bills | rejected |
| Non-Bittensor confidential inference (Tinfoil, Privatemode, NEAR AI, Phala) | better verification in places | CO-1 names Bittensor providers | out of scope; Tinfoil's open verifier and EHBP inform §5 |

### 4.9 Decisions proposed

**D-PROV-1 (proposed).** Eligibility is E1-E7 for a TEE label (A1, A2, AP) and N1-N5 for the label `none`; a network's floor and provider list choose among them, every label allowed by default. *Why:* CO-18; a label needs a test, not a brand; Q-PROV-3.

**D-PROV-2 (proposed).** Chutes, through its E2E path only, each catalog model pinned to its `chute_id`, is the TEE inference provider, labeled AP, gated by G-PROV-chutes, which needs SN64's gamma: without it Chutes is dropped from launch (CO-32) and joins when SN64 takes gamma, or through SayGM's pass-through (Q-PROV-1). *Why:* §4.4: the only provider meeting E1-E4; CO-32.

**D-PROV-3 (proposed).** The enclave providers are Hippius (CPU, AP), Lium (GPU, AP) and Cathedral (CPU, AP), each by its gate, Hippius expected first; Targon and the rest are not integrated. *Why:* CO-21; CO-28; §4.4; no provider meets the enclave platform contract (§11.3) today.

**D-PROV-4 (proposed).** Providers are named by team and endpoint; the netuid is configuration re-read at each gate. *Why:* netuids changed hands repeatedly in October and November 2026.

**D-PROV-5 (proposed).** Providers without a TEE are reached by the direct path (§6.6), and only those whose usage URnetwork can read per request (N2). *Why:* the directive; R-PROV-7; a device must not be able to under-report what URnetwork pays for.

**D-PROV-6 (proposed).** engy is the first provider without a TEE, then SayGM, once it signs usage bound to the request and enforces an allowlist of models whose upstream terms allow it, each by the direct path after its gate; engy's calls carry `provider.zdr`; frontier models resold through Bittensor providers are excluded. *Why:* CO-18; §4.4; the upstream providers' terms.

**D-PROV-7 (proposed).** The providers are those CO-28 names: Chutes, engy and SayGM for inference, Hippius, Lium and Cathedral for enclaves, and Parallel for web search; an adapter is built for each, each serves users after its gate, and no other provider is integrated without the owner. *Why:* CO-28; the gates (4.7) carry the directive's and §5's checks.

### 4.10 Questions

**Q-PROV-1.** What if SN64 has not enabled gamma by M12's entry? *Options:* (a) remote inference waits for it; (b) the owner allows paying Chutes another way until it does, by card (fiat) or in TAO or alpha; (c) URnetwork runs its own TEE inference on Lium, paid in SN51 gamma; (d) Chutes' TEE models through SayGM, paid in SN28 gamma, once SayGM carries device-encrypted requests to Chutes' encrypted invoke unread. *Answer:* decided by the owner (CO-32): "Any provider that does not accept gamma at launch will be dropped from launch." So (a): Chutes, and with it every TEE model, is out of the launch unless SN64 takes gamma by then, and joins when it does; (b) and (c) are not taken. (d) is asked of SayGM now, since SayGM is paid in SN28 gamma: the device would verify Chutes' instance evidence and encrypt to it as §6.6 does, SayGM's gateway and miner would carry only ciphertext, and the label would stay Chutes' AP with SayGM outside the boundary; it needs SayGM to build the pass-through and Chutes to consent to the resale in writing. URnetwork asks Chutes for gamma now, with the E6 agreement, since Chutes was reported among the seven initial gamma issuers (2026-09-28). *Decider:* owner, decided.

**Q-PROV-2.** Is AP acceptable for enclaves? *Options:* (a) yes, labeled; (b) no enclaves until a provider meets the platform contract (§11.3). *Answer:* (a). A miner, the anonymous party, stays outside the boundary under AP; the provider company inside it is a named business, as a cloud is. The label shows wherever an enclave is shown, a network can require A1 (§16.4), and the provisioning protocol is the A1 one (§11.7), so a provider that meets the contract later moves an enclave to A1 with no change but its label. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-PROV-3.** May remote inference run at AP, where the provider itself is trusted? *Options:* (a) never: no remote inference until a provider reaches A1; (b) yes, labeled AP everywhere, with A1 the target. *Answer:* (b). Chutes is AP (its serving code and tenant image are unmeasured and its platform releases disk keys), and no Bittensor provider reaches A1, so (a) means no TEE inference at all. Under (b) the miners, the anonymous parties, stay outside; Chutes, a named company with a DPA, is trusted as a cloud is; the label says so on every message; and a network that will not trust a provider sets its floor to A1 (§16.4) and uses local models. **This is the owner's call: CO-2 says "TEE", and AP is a TEE that excludes the miner but not the provider.** *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-PROV-4.** What would move Chutes to A1? *Answer:* the chute's image digest and serving code bound into the evidence (its issue #75: a measured RTMR3, or a signed image digest the per-VM certificate carries), single-tenant VMs or a per-tenant key, and a disk key released by measurement rather than by Chutes' platform. G-PROV-any re-checks it every 90 days, and URnetwork asks for it with the E6 agreement. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-PROV-5.** Does the catalog take inference providers off Bittensor (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter)? *Options:* (a) not at launch; (b) yes. *Answer:* (a). CO-1 names Bittensor providers and CO-10 pays them in gamma; frontier models reachable through a Bittensor provider come in under that provider's terms (§4.4). A provider off Bittensor would need the direct path (N1) and USD payment, which is Later. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-42).

**Q-PROV-6.** Should engy's calls always carry its `zdr` flag? *Answer:* yes. It sends them only to engy's confidential-computing workers or engy's own machines, whose non-retention is more than an operator's promise, at the cost of a 503 when none is free; the policy's `direct` line (§5.4), not the unsigned catalog, marks the one model without ZDR workers (qwen3.6-35b-a3b), which the router sends without the flag, labeled so, and requires zero retention of every other, so a breached broker cannot drop the flag; the device checks each receipt's `served.zdr` (§6.6). *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-PROV-7.** CO-18 says "all inference": should Claude, GPT and Gemini through SayGM be in the catalog? *Options:* (a) no, until an upstream provider approves the resale in writing; (b) yes. *Answer:* (a). SayGM's miners serve them with their own keys, which Anthropic's, OpenAI's and Google's terms bar reselling, and SayGM's own terms bar circumventing provider policies, so URnetwork would resell a chain each link of which forbids it; frontier models can come in when one of those providers, or a Bittensor provider holding their written approval, offers them. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-PROV-8.** Should SayGM's `-tee` models be labeled AP, since its gateway is attested? *Options:* (a) `none` until the device can verify every hop that reads a request, or encrypts past them; (b) AP. *Answer:* (a). The device can verify the gateway: its quote passes Intel's checks against current collateral, and a static quote and a CAA pin tie its TLS certificate to it. But the gateway's code is private, so what reads a request inside it is unknown; the miner's CVM and the model's TEE read it too, their evidence never reaches the client, and the client's nonce stops at the gateway; and the gateway alone decides when a `-TEE` request goes to Chutes' plain API. An end-to-end pass-through (Q-PROV-1 (d)) reaches AP without trusting any of them. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-PROV-9.** Until SayGM signs usage per request, should URnetwork use it through one hotkey per network, billing each network from its hotkey's `/balance`? *Options:* (a) no, it waits for G-PROV-saygm; (b) yes. *Answer:* (a). Every mint and spend is a chain event under its hotkey, so per-network hotkeys would publish each network's spending as a series anyone can read, undoing the pooling behind URnetwork's hotkey (§10); each would cost a mint; and a modified client could still buy models URnetwork excludes (Q-PROV-7), since nothing bounds the model a body names. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-PROV-10.** CO-28 chooses SayGM: may it serve users before it signs usage per request, on the usage its device reports, checked against SayGM's public settlement records? *Options:* (a) no, it waits for G-PROV-saygm; (b) yes. *Answer:* (a). The device would report SayGM's request id, which those records list but bind to no buyer, so a modified client could cite a cheaper request from the same seconds and URnetwork would pay the difference, with nothing to show which network did it; and with no allowlist the same client could buy, on URnetwork's hotkey, the frontier models Q-PROV-7 excludes. engy carries the launch, with Chutes once SN64 takes gamma (CO-32), while SayGM adds the two features G-PROV-saygm names. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

### 4.11 Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chutes never enables gamma | medium | no TEE inference under CO-10 | Q-PROV-1 (d)'s pass-through through SayGM, asked now; meanwhile engy's and local models, a TEE floor leaving local models alone (§19.2); admitting Chutes later is configuration (§10.10) |
| Chutes suspends URnetwork's account for one user's abuse (its terms make the integrator liable) | medium | Chutes' models stop | E6's notice clause; per-network limits and abuse response (§17); a second provider when one clears the bar |
| Emissions fall and providers raise prices or leave | high (Chutes' share fell from ~14.4% to 5.82% of emissions in 2026; its traffic fell ~84%) | price or capacity | hourly price reads; G-PROV-any; small provider balances (§10.5) |
| A published measurement list itself is malicious | low | a policy pins a bad image | URnetwork reviews each list change before it enters the signed policy (§5.4) |

## 5. Attestation and the policy

### 5.1 Purpose and scope

This section owns what a device checks before it sends a byte to a TEE, for models labeled A1, A2 or AP and for enclaves; a model labeled `none` has no evidence to check (§6.6): the evidence, the checks, the signed policy that says which measurements and firmware levels pass, the binding of a key to the evidence, freshness, caching, and what a pass is worth. It applies to inference instances (§6.6) and to enclaves (§11.7) alike. [Rpt:bt]'s attestation notes are the source of every check below.

### 5.2 Requirements

| Id | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| R-ATTEST-1 | The device that holds the plaintext verifies the evidence; no server's verdict is taken in its place | R-CCTX-2; the relay gap teep documents for NanoGPT |
| R-ATTEST-2 | The key the device encrypts to is bound in the evidence, together with a nonce the device trusts as fresh | R-PROV-2 |
| R-ATTEST-3 | Which measurements, firmware levels and vendor roots pass is set by a policy URnetwork's servers cannot widen | I-4's spirit; directive |
| R-ATTEST-4 | A failure refuses; nothing is retried on a lesser provider | R-CCTX-2 |
| R-ATTEST-5 | The result is recorded with the work it allowed | RECORD.md section 12 |

### 5.3 The checks

The verifier is `attest_*.go` in the sidecar root, on every leg but the VPN component, built on google/go-tdx-guest and google/go-sev-guest (Apache-2.0, vendored and pinned), and on a GPU verifier of its own (below).

```text
TDX quote (v4/v5)
  signature    ECDSA chain: quote → PCK certificate → Intel's platform CA → Intel's SGX root (pinned in the policy)
  collateral   TCB info, QE identity and the PCK CRL from Intel PCS, through the broker's cache (5.7); each item checked
               under Intel's signature and its own next-update time
  tcb          status UpToDate; a policy may allow SWHardeningNeeded for named advisories only; never OutOfDate,
               Revoked or ConfigurationNeeded
  body         the client's job, since Intel's library does not check it: TD attributes' DEBUG bit 0; SEPT_VE_DISABLE
               set; XFAM as the profile says; MRTD and RTMR0-2 equal to one profile of the policy's list, RTMR3 equal or replayed as it says; MRCONFIGID,
               MROWNER and MROWNERCONFIG as the scheme says (enclaves, 5.5); REPORTDATA as the scheme says
SEV-SNP report
  signature    VCEK (or VLEK) → ASK → ARK, the ARK pinned in the policy; certificates from AMD's KDS through the cache
  tcb          the reported TCB checked against the VCEK certificate's own TCB extensions, never the report's claim alone
               (the Trail of Bits finding on Meta's system); firmware at or above the policy's minimum per family: 0x1F
               (EPYC 7003), 0x1E (8004/9004), 0x08 (8005/9005), as CSA's Mior guidance gives (2026-11)
  policy       DEBUG 0; MIGRATE_MA 0; SINGLE_SOCKET as the profile says; PAGE_SWAP_DISABLE and ALIAS_CHECK_COMPLETE
               set where the platform info reports them (Heracles, BadRAM); SMT reported, not refused (StackWarp:
               disclosed); VMPL 0
  body         MEASUREMENT equal to a profile's; HOST_DATA as the scheme says; REPORT_DATA as the scheme says
Chutes' per-instance wrapper (scheme chutes-e2e-v1)
  source       the device fetches GET api.chutes.ai/chutes/{chute_id}/evidence?nonce= itself, for the chute_id the
               policy binds to the catalog model, through a TLS tunnel the broker relays byte for byte (5.7) and
               cannot read or alter; only instance ids in that answer are used
  certificate  the per-VM certificate chains to Chutes' VM root CA (`sek8s-vm-root-ca`, pinned in the policy); its
               SPKI's SHA-256 equals REPORTDATA[32:64]
  signature    the RSA signature over `attested_body` verifies under that certificate, and the body carries the
               device's nonce
NVIDIA GPU (SPDM evidence, Hopper and Blackwell)
  signature    the device certificate chain to NVIDIA's root (pinned), with OCSP not revoked
  freshness    the evidence answers the nonce the scheme derives (Chutes: from the client nonce and the instance key)
  state        CC mode on, not DevTools; debug off; measurements equal to the reference integrity manifest (RIM) for the
               driver and VBIOS; every GPU the profile names present
```

**The GPU verifier.** No pure-Go local verifier of NVIDIA evidence existed on 2026-11-23; NVIDIA's own SDK still calls NVIDIA's reference-value and OCSP services, and go-nvtrust sends the evidence to NVIDIA's NRAS ([Rpt:bt]). The Chutes path, which M15 builds (§19.3), verifies through NRAS at first, with the broker forwarding the request so NVIDIA sees URnetwork's address, not the person's; GPU enclaves' work in M15 then replaces it with `attest_nvidia.go`, a local check of the SPDM signatures and measurements against RIMs and OCSP answers fetched through the cache (Q-ATTEST-2). NRAS's answer is a signed token the device verifies under a key that chains to the NRAS root the policy pins (5.4), so the broker can neither forge it nor swap the signing key, either way.

**What a pass is.** A pass says: genuine Intel or AMD silicon (unless its keys were extracted, §2.6), firmware at the policy's level, booted into one of the measured images the policy lists, holding the key in the report data, now, and, for a provider like Chutes, an instance the provider itself lists for the model asked for. At AP it does not say what the provider's unmeasured code inside that image does with the plaintext (§4.5).

### 5.4 The policy

**Staging.** A staging key, which the release key certifies for its own namespace, `ur-compute-policy-staging`, alone, signs a staging policy, `compute-policy-staging.json`, which only staging and CI builds verify; a production build pins the production namespace alone, so no staging line ever reaches a user. A gated line (a provider's `tee`, `direct` or `custody` entry, the `search` line, a `services` definition) enters the staging policy first, for its gate's tests (§4.7, §19.2), and the production policy once the gate passes; the staging policy expires after 7 days, and the apps show a staging banner while one is in force.

The policy is one JSON document, `compute-policy.json`, signed under its own namespace, `ur-compute-policy`, by the **compute-policy key**: two of its four named holders sign each version on hardware tokens, and the release key, the offline two-person key that signs `SHA256SUMS` (DESIGN §2.6, §4.10), certifies that key for this namespace alone, for a year. Devices still pin one root, the release key, and check the certificate's namespace and expiry; no release signature can pass for a policy or the reverse; and the release ceremony stays rare while the policy changes about weekly, as providers roll images and texts change (Q-ATTEST-4). §14.10 gives the signing cadence and the rota.

```text

not_after      90 days after signing; a device whose newest policy has passed it refuses remote work and says why
roots          Intel's SGX root, AMD's ARKs (Milan, Genoa, Turin), NVIDIA's device root and the root its NRAS tokens
               chain to: by SHA-256 of the certificate
tcb            TDX: allowed statuses and advisories, and a minimum TCB evaluation data number; SNP: minimum firmware
               per family, required policy bits; per vendor, a maximum age for collateral and revocation lists,
               7 days where the vendor re-signs them at least weekly (5.7)
providers      per provider id: allowed CPU types (tdx, snp), the binding scheme (5.5), the label (A1, AP), the
               provider's own roots (Chutes' VM root CA), each catalog model's provider id (Chutes: its chute_id),
               and its measurement profiles: { id, guest version, MRTD, RTMR0-3 | SNP MEASUREMENT, GPU model and count,
               expires, and any register listed as replayed: its expected events in order, the last SHA-256(B),
               §11.7 }, each reviewed before it is added (below)
direct         per provider without a TEE (label `none`): its slug, its API host, its btauth/1 receiver hotkey,

               raised at any other change of its words; per locale, English first, a one-line summary and the
```

**Freshness tickets.** A withheld policy must not keep a revoked profile or chip in use, since withholding a revocation widens what passes. So the compute-policy key's holders pre-sign, at a weekly sitting, a ticket per day for the next 14 days, `{policy_version >= N, valid_through: day D}` under the same namespace, and the tickets are released one a day; a device refuses remote work once its newest ticket is 72 hours past its day, or names a policy version above the one it holds (then it fetches the newer policy first). An unreleased ticket is itself the capability a revocation must defeat, so the unreleased ones wait on a ticket host apart from ur.io's serving path and the broker, with its own account, keys and deploy, which posts each on its day; a breach of the serving path or the broker holds only tickets already released. Tickets are signed, so a device takes them from any path: ur.io, a mirror, or another device of its network, which passes on the newest it holds. A lapse stops the remote work a revocation protects: remote model calls, TEE or direct, enclave creates and starts, a member's device seating an indexer incarnation, and searches; local inference, fetches, calendar links and connected services run on until the policy's `not_after`. An urgent revocation is a new policy N+1 and a fresh run of tickets naming it, so it binds every device within 72 hours; a server that withholds tickets can only stop that work, never widen it; and were the ticket host taken as well, a withheld revocation would last at most the signed horizon, 14 days (IC-9, Q-ATTEST-5). DESIGN pre-signs DNSSEC windows the same way, but a leaked DNSKEY set widens nothing, where a leaked ticket keeps a revoked line alive, which is why the horizon here is short and the store apart.

Distribution: each `ur` release carries the policy current at its build; devices fetch newer ones from `https://ur.io/compute/policy/v1/<version>.json`, verify the signature and the counter, and keep the newest. The signature, not the host, is what a device trusts, so the path through Cloudflare (DESIGN §2.8's EX7) changes nothing. URnetwork's servers serve the file but cannot sign it, so a breached server can withhold a newer policy (devices then refuse remote work when `not_after` passes) but cannot widen one.

**Review.** A provider's new measurement profile enters the policy only after a person at URnetwork reproduces it from the provider's published build, where the provider publishes one (Chutes documents an offline replay in sek8s's `tdx-measurement-verification.md`), or, where it cannot be reproduced, records that it was taken from the provider's list with the list's hash. The policy records which (`reproduced` or `listed`) per profile, and the catalog shows it.

### 5.5 Binding schemes

| Scheme | Used by | Report data | The key bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| `chutes-e2e-v1` | Chutes inference | `REPORTDATA[0:32] = SHA256(nonce_hex ‖ e2e_pubkey_b64)`; `[32:64] = SHA256(SPKI of the per-VM TLS certificate)` | the instance's ML-KEM-768 E2E key |
| `ur-enclave-v1` | enclaves, TDX and SNP | 64 bytes: `SHA-512("urnetwork-sidecar-v1/enclave-attest" ‖ 0x00 ‖ nonce ‖ SHA-256(B) ‖ H)`, `H = SHA-256(provisioning key ‖ SSH host key ‖ identity key ‖ ClientKey ‖ ReaderKey)`, public keys each; at provisioning under setup over SSH, `‖ s` after H, s the 32-byte secret the device sent only inside its verified setup session (§11.7); TDX MRCONFIGID (or SNP HOST_DATA) = `SHA-256(B)` where the provider sets it (§11.7) | the provisioning key, and the incarnation's own SSH host, identity, client and reader keys, all made in the VM |
| `ur-enclave-session-v1` | each attach (§12.6) | `SHA-512("urnetwork-sidecar-v1/enclave-session" ‖ 0x00 ‖ nonce ‖ the SSH exchange hash)` | the live SSH session itself |
| `ur-enclave-ssh-setup-v1` | setup over SSH (§11.7): the report the provider's measured SSH server makes | `SHA-512("urnetwork-sidecar-v1/enclave-ssh-setup" ‖ 0x00 ‖ SHA-256(the installed SSH keys, sorted) ‖ enclave id ‖ the SSH exchange hash)` | the setup session, and the exact keys that can enter the VM |

The device never takes a key from anywhere but an instance whose evidence binds it, and never takes the instance from the broker: it reads the instance list and evidence for the model's pinned `chute_id` from Chutes over its own TLS session (5.7's tunnel), the broker supplies only the E2E keys and one-use nonces that need URnetwork's API key, and the device checks each key against the evidence of an instance in that list.
