| Route part of SN25's emissions straight into a provider's gamma, as Affine (SN120) sends 10% of its emission to SN51 gamma | no exchange, no TAO float | only root-whitelisted recipients (SN51 and SN53 on 2026-11-23); emission-dependent amounts | an option for Lium's GPU enclaves once G-PROV-lium passes; the owner's call |
| Pay providers in TAO or card where they accept it | available now | against CO-10 | declined: a provider without gamma at launch is dropped from launch (CO-32, Q-PROV-1) |

### 10.12 Decisions proposed

**D-GAMMA-1 (proposed).** One API-key hotkey and deposit per provider and environment, the hotkey in a rate-limited signer on the broker's hosts, the deposit owned by a compute mint coldkey with a float of at most 7 days, behind a multisig reserve. *Why:* R-GAMMA-3; at a gamma-native provider the hotkey is the account.

**D-GAMMA-2 (proposed).** Mint and spend just in time: 1 to 2 days of gamma in each deposit, 1.5 to 3 days at each provider. *Why:* buffers for a stale feed and a slow chain; small losses if a subnet dies.

**D-GAMMA-3 (proposed).** Reconcile charges, provider bills and on-chain spends daily per provider. *Why:* R-GAMMA-4.

**D-GAMMA-4 (proposed).** Users never touch gamma; the balance stays a closed loop. *Why:* CO-10; FinCEN's closed-loop exclusions.

**D-GAMMA-5 (proposed).** A provider's forecast is the largest of its trailing mean, the committed rate of the enclaves running on it plus its inference, and a floor set at its gate; the broker refuses a new call or enclave the provider's account cannot cover (`capacity`); reconciliation reports each provider's realized margin weekly. *Why:* deposits, caps and accounts sized to a forecast that is zero at launch, or that one GPU enclave can pass, would fail on first use; TAO's movement between purchase and mint can erode the markup unseen (10.6).

### 10.13 Questions

**Q-GAMMA-1.** Where does the treasury buy TAO? *Options:* Coinbase Prime; Kraken; an OTC desk. *Answer:* Coinbase Prime first (US custody, TAO since February 2025), Kraken as the second venue (TAO and SN64 alpha); OTC once monthly volume passes $250,000. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-GAMMA-2.** Who custodies the reserve? *Options:* (a) a self-custodied multisig like `ur-owner`; (b) BitGo. *Answer:* (a): an exchange or custodian cannot sign `mint_gamma`, and the owners already run a Ledger multisig for SN25. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-GAMMA-3.** How often does the treasury buy? *Answer:* weekly, sized to the next week's forecast plus the 7-day float, so price exposure stays near a week of spend. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-GAMMA-4.** Do you accept cost swings of about 15% a fortnight from weekly TAO buys? *Options:* (a) yes: the treasury buys TAO weekly (Q-GAMMA-3), and TAO bought for a week and a 7-day float is minted about ten days later on average; (b) keep CO-35's weekly rhythm as a weekly transfer of USD to Coinbase Prime, and buy TAO just in time for each mint, with a hot float of one to two days. *Answer:* (b). The accepted TAO/USD price fell 12.3% in under two weeks this month (10.6), which would turn the 1.20 markup into about 1.05 on a week's spend; (b) cuts the exposure to a day or two, at the cost of more and smaller trades. It changes what CO-35 confirmed, so the treasury buys TAO weekly until the owner takes it. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-42).

### 10.14 Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gamma is new and unaudited upstream; its calls changed four times in a month | high | the payment path breaks on an upgrade | the shape check; buffers; G-PROV-any |
| One price feed for all of gamma | medium | mints stop | the deposit's 1-2 days |
| The accounting of gamma is unsettled | medium | restatements | an accountant's opinion before M12's exit |
| TAO falls between a weekly buy and its mints (CO-35) | medium | a 12% fall turns the 1.20 markup into about 1.05 on a week's spend | the realized-margin page (10.7); Q-GAMMA-4's just-in-time conversion |

## 11. Secure enclaves

### 11.1 Purpose and scope

This section designs enclaves (CO-5, CO-7): what one is, what a provider must offer, the image, the shapes and the lifecycle, how an enclave is attested and given its keys, its networking and default egress, its storage, the software in it, and how it is stopped, moved and removed. SSH is §12; the Harness in it §7; its charges §9; which providers qualify §4.

### 11.2 Requirements

| Id | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| R-ENC-1 | Create and remove enclaves through the service, from the CLI, the apps and the Harness | CO-5 |
| R-ENC-2 | An enclave is a TEE Debian VM with full tools, booting a bootstrapped `ur` | CO-5 |
| R-ENC-3 | It joins the person's network with an overlay IP address | CO-5 |
| R-ENC-4 | Its routes and default egress are set by `ur`, never the provider's network | CO-7 |
| R-ENC-5 | It is reached over the bundled SSH, and a local Harness attaches to its Harness | CO-5 |
| R-ENC-6 | No key or credential reaches it before a verifying device of its network (its sponsor's, or for the network's indexer enclave an Owner's or Admin's, or for a mailbox grant the member's own) has verified its TEE and that it booted URnetwork's bootstrap untouched, or, for an indexer incarnation set up over SSH, a member's device has verified its TEE and its sponsor's signed statement that it did (CO-41) | R-CCTX-17 |
| R-ENC-7 | Its work survives the VM: what matters lives in EVS | derived |
| R-ENC-8 | An enclave is created on, or moved to, a provider only once its sponsor has acknowledged that provider's disclosure at its current version, which the create sheet, its card and kind 19's card show | CO-33 |
| R-ENC-9 | A network may run its mail and search indexer in one enclave, which its mail setup offers; it stays the indexer across incarnations and indexes a member's mailbox only by that member's grant | CO-19, CO-20 |
| R-ENC-10 | Enclaves run only on the Bittensor providers CO-28 chose, each after its gate; the reference provider serves development, CI and staging, never a user | CO-21, CO-28 |
| R-ENC-11 | A person's agents' enclave is one of their devices, with the access their other devices have and none of their authority, for the initial version; the network's indexer enclave is no member's device | CO-42, CO-43 |

### 11.3 The enclave platform contract

What a provider must offer before its enclaves enter the catalog:

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| EPC-1 Measured payload | either the VM boots an image URnetwork supplies, by URL and digest, measured at launch; or the provider's own published image runs URnetwork's bootstrap only after checking it against a value bound into the launch: SEV-SNP `HOST_DATA` or TDX `MRCONFIGID` = SHA-256 of the bootstrap bundle (11.7); or the provider's measured image extends a runtime register the guest's evidence carries (TDX `RTMR3`, or a PCR of an SVSM vTPM on SEV-SNP) with that SHA-256 before it runs the bootstrap, in both of these forms starting no access service before the bootstrap and refusing, or measuring into what its evidence carries, every key and other input the host supplies at boot, so no key the broker or the miner adds there enters the guest unseen; or, where the provider's measured image takes no configuration from the host, installs the SSH keys and the enclave id only once, through its attested channel and before its SSH server starts, gives its customer no later key, console or command into the guest, and has that server bind into a report, on request, the keys installed, the enclave id and its own session (`ur-enclave-ssh-setup-v1`, §5.5; or the keys and id measured into `RTMR3` or an SVSM vTPM PCR, the session bound beside them), URnetwork installs the bootstrap itself over that session (11.7's setup over SSH), the provider then inside the boundary (AP). Without one of these a miner can rewrite a VM's start-up data, which arrives from the host, and nothing the VM attests would show it. In every form, no key, console, command or agent channel the provider offers its customer, the broker included, reaches into a running guest: the provider offers none, or the image starts nothing that answers one, no login on any console (serial, virtual or vsock) among them |
| EPC-2 Guest attestation | the guest asks for its own quote or report, with 64 bytes of report data it chooses, at any time (Linux `configfs-tsm`, `/dev/tdx_guest` or `/dev/sev-guest`) |
| EPC-3 Root | root in the guest, or `CAP_NET_ADMIN` and `/dev/net/tun`, so `ur tun` can own the routes |
| EPC-4 Outbound | outbound TCP and UDP to the internet; inbound not needed |
| EPC-5 Lifecycle | an API to create (shape, image or payload, launch data), read status and delete; billing per second or minute |
| EPC-6 Single tenant | no other customer's workload in the VM |
| EPC-7 Gamma | as E5 (§4.3) |
| EPC-8 Terms | as E6 |
| EPC-9 Kernel | under EPC-1's first form the guest kernel is `ur-enclave`'s, which takes upstream kernel security fixes within 14 days of their release; under the others it is the provider's, whose measured image must take them as fast, each fixed image entering the policy as a new profile and its predecessor's `expires` set 30 days out (§5.4), so no incarnation outlives a known kernel hole by more than about six weeks (11.11) |

Status on 2026-11-23 ([Rpt:bt]):

| Provider | EPC-1 | EPC-2 | EPC-3 | EPC-4 | EPC-5 | EPC-6 | EPC-7 | EPC-8 | Gap to close |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hippius (SN75), CPU SEV-SNP | no: images are Hippius'; its measurements and launch data are undocumented | the raw report is shown; guest requests undocumented | sudo | yes (but 25) | OpenAPI | VM | yes | no published terms | bind the bootstrap (`HOST_DATA` or a vTPM PCR), or, for setup over SSH (Q-ENC-7), confirm its image takes nothing from the miner's host, installs keys only once and gives its customer no later way in, and add one feature: an SSH server whose report binds the installed keys, the enclave id and its own session, which needs no register (SEV-SNP has none without an SVSM vTPM); either way document how a guest requests its own report, and the image's measurements; terms |
| Lium (SN51), TDX + NVIDIA CC | no: the renter's container is unmeasured | node quotes with the renter's nonce | container; tun unknown | yes (but 25 and the provider's LAN) | API, CLI | only by renting every GPU | yes | none | measure the renter's image (its compose hash into RTMR3), or, for setup over SSH (Q-ENC-7), confirm the executor starts the renter's image by digest and installs its SSH key only through Lium's channel, and have the pod's SSH server bind the installed key, the enclave id and its own session into its quote (or measure the key and id into RTMR3); tun in the pod; whole-machine rental |
| Cathedral (SN94), SEV-SNP | unknown | unknown: only signed run receipts are documented | unknown | none, allowlist or internet | API | yes | yes | — | general availability; EPC-1 to EPC-3 shown; terms. SSH into a sandbox, not yet live, with the same one feature, would let it qualify by setup over SSH (Q-ENC-7); once set up, an enclave's SSH server is its own sidecar's (§12) |
| Chutes BYO TDX VM | yes (own image, attested key) | `GET /attest?nonce=` | — | no: isolated network, declared POST routes | — | — | no | — | open outbound networking (EPC-4); gamma. SSH comes with our image; not chosen (CO-28) |
| Targon (SN4) | no | no | `ubuntu` user | yes | yes | yes | no | no | everything but compute |

**No provider meets the contract today.** Hippius is closest: one launch-data binding, documented reports and terms away; or, by setup over SSH, a confirmation that its image takes nothing from the host and gives no later way in, and one feature: an SSH server whose report binds the installed keys, the enclave id and its own session, which needs no new register (Q-ENC-7). Lium may qualify the same way. URnetwork asks Hippius, Lium and Cathedral, the three CO-28 chose, for EPC-1 and EPC-2 now, with the gamma relationship as the opening, and Hippius and Cathedral for the launch-data binding above all, which lets each member's device check an indexer incarnation's payload itself, where setup over SSH has members take its sponsor's word (11.10, Q-ENC-9), and, for the indexer role, a placement the broker does not choose (11.10); none documents EPC-9's kernel cadence yet, which each gate asks; G-PROV-hippius (§4.7) is the contract. Until a provider passes, the enclave stack is built and tested against a **reference provider** in two parts: Google Cloud's Confidential VMs with Intel TDX (C3), where URnetwork boots its own image, measured into TDX's registers, B bound through the report data (11.7); and an AMD SEV-SNP host URnetwork runs itself, with its own firmware and KVM, since Google's SEV-SNP VMs (N2D) measure only Google's firmware at launch, keep the rest in a vTPM Google controls and document no `HOST_DATA` a customer sets, so they would exercise none of the SEV-SNP paths Hippius and Cathedral need: the whole image measured at launch, `HOST_DATA`, an SVSM vTPM's PCR, and setup over SSH through an emulated provider channel. The reference provider meets EPC-1 to EPC-6 but not EPC-7, so it serves development, CI and staging only, never a user (CO-21); every user-facing enclave, the indexer included, waits for a Bittensor provider that passes. The production policy (§5.4) lists none of the reference provider's profiles and the production catalog none of its shapes, so a user's device refuses its evidence and no network is offered it; its adapter runs in development, CI and staging, against a test policy only their builds trust. Until a provider passes, the catalog holds no enclave shape: the apps' enclave screen and the mail setup say that enclaves await a provider and offer none, `ur enclave create` answers `no_enclave_provider`, naming the gates, and a network's mail indexer stays a member's always-on device (DESIGN §15.6). A pilot on Hippius may run before its gate for URnetwork's own testing of the adapter, billing and gamma path, holding no user's keys or data, since without EPC-1 its miner could rewrite the bootstrap.

### 11.4 What an enclave is

An enclave is a name, its settings and a line of incarnations. Each incarnation is one VM at a provider and one tagged sidecar in the person's network.

| Part | Value |
|---|---|
| The enclave | an id and a name, its shape, egress and Harness settings, the sponsor's `models` key (`tee_only`, `allow`, §16.4), acknowledged disclosures (`compute.disclosures`, §2.8) and automatic-approval setting (`approvals`, §27.10) among them, which the enclave's daemon enforces for every agent and gateway grant there, kept in the member's vault (`enclaves/<id>.json`) and reaching each incarnation sealed at provisioning (11.7); an agents' enclave then reads them, and the sponsor's harness config, from the vault as their other devices do, taking a version only from a device of the sponsor that is no enclave (below), and the indexer enclave, which reads no vault and runs no agents, takes each change signed by an Owner's or Admin's device and sealed to its current ReaderKey, as DESIGN §16.8 seals an `ApprovalDelivery`; `compute_enclave` (compute-4) holds its id, shape, provider and states, never its settings |
| An incarnation | one VM and one sidecar, tagged `tag:enclave` and `tag:enclave-<id>`, `<id>` its enclave id in 32 lowercase hex digits, named with the enclave's name and sponsored by the member (DESIGN §7.7), never ephemeral; an agents' enclave's incarnation is also one of its sponsor's devices (below) |
| Its keys | identity key, ClientKey, X-Wing ReaderKey and SSH host key, generated inside the VM at boot and bound in its evidence (11.7); they never leave it and end with it |
| Admission | the person's device that verified the evidence files the incarnation's `SidecarAdmit`, as the effect of an approved `enclave_create`, a person's start or a tool's start under kind 19 (§16.3): for an agents' enclave, an untagged consented device of its sponsor, the admission naming the sponsor's `member_id` beside the enclave's tags and carrying capability bit 3, `enclave`, so the incarnation is one of the sponsor's consented devices (below); for the network's indexer enclave, an Owner's or Admin's device admitting a tagged sidecar it sponsors (DESIGN §5.6, §7.9), never consented for any member (Q-ENC-13); never an MCP tool, so DESIGN §16.6's rule that no tool changes enrollment holds |
| What lasts | the name; the private name `<name>.<net>`, which follows the running incarnation; the tags and every grant written to them; the agent names, whose cards each new incarnation takes over (§20.5); the work in EVS |
| What does not | the overlay address (each incarnation claims its own), the keys, the scratch disk |
| End | a stop revokes the incarnation: it signs its own `SidecarRevoke` before its VM is destroyed, and one lost without doing so is revoked by the sponsor's next device online as that daemon's housekeeping (DESIGN §7.10); as for any removed device, every repo it read then moves at its next generation to a key it never holds (cause `remove`, DESIGN §10.5) |
| Owner | the sponsoring member; a Team admin may stop or remove it (`compute:enclave admin`, §16.2) |

A key that leaks from one incarnation, by a physical attack on its machine or any other way, ends with that incarnation's revocation: the next incarnation, on another machine, has new keys, and nothing written after the revocation is wrapped to the old ones (I-15). An agents' enclave's access comes with its admission as its sponsor's device, and its network reach and every grant to it are written to its tags, so a new incarnation reaches what the last one did without anyone re-granting it. The tag carries the enclave's id, never its name: a create refuses a name another enclave of the network holds, so its private name stays its own, but a name is only a label, and no grant rests on it. The first admission under `tag:enclave-<id>` claims the tag for its admitting member, the enclave's sponsor (for the network's indexer enclave, which its `IndexerSet` names, its Owners and Admins, any of whom may admit its incarnations, 11.7), as a `tagOwners` row naming them would, and readers refuse an admission under a claimed tag by anyone else (Appendix D), so a grant written to the tag reaches only incarnations its owner admitted; `ur` and the apps write rules by the name and fill in the id.

**One of the sponsor's devices** (CO-42, CO-43; Q-ENC-14). For the initial version an agents' enclave, one whose role in B is `agents` (11.7), as every enclave but the network's indexer is, has its sponsor's access, as the owner asked ("full access like any other sidecar") and confirmed once told that a breach there exposes everything the sponsor's devices hold. Its incarnation's admission names the sponsor's `member_id` beside its tags, with capability bit 3, `enclave`, and an untagged consented device of the sponsor signs it after verifying the evidence itself (11.7), so DESIGN §8.5's `consented(d, M)` holds for it by its `scoped` clause; where `self_admit` is off, an Owner's or Admin's cosign joins it, as for any new device of the member, so a keeper's restarts wait for one (Appendix D). Readers then take it as one of the sponsor's devices for EVS: it reads and writes what they reach, the sponsor's owner-bound repos (the vault with the record and every run, the mailbox, and the `secret` repos of their calendar links and connections, whose link secrets and tokens their devices seal to it as to each other, §23.6, §25.6) and every repo a rule, grant or kind default opens to the sponsor or their devices, a Team's included. Its network reach stays its tags': `dial`, `route`, `ssh` and listeners rules name `tag:enclave` and `tag:enclave-<id>` as before (§16.5, §26), since its agents' traffic leaves with its address. It holds none of the sponsor's authority: as a read_only device signs none, it signs no `SidecarAdmit`, `AdmissionConfirm`, `OwnerConfirm`, `Suspend`, `Delegation`, `EvsShare`, `RecoveryBind`, `IndexerSet`, owner-bound `RepoAdmin` add or DROP, no `SidecarRevoke` but its own, and no `KeyRegister` or `KeyRevoke` but for its own SSH keys (11.7); it writes no config head whatever the sponsor's role and counts toward no k of n; it is not approval-capable, so every approval its agents need goes to the sponsor's approval-capable devices (DESIGN §16.6), but the automatic decisions its daemon makes for its own runs (§27.9); and no device takes from it a version of the sponsor's harness config or of `enclaves/`, which only their other devices write. So a breach of one incarnation exposes what the sponsor's devices hold while it runs, and nothing it signs outlasts its revocation: its stop, its loss and a compromise each revoke it (11.11), every repo it read then moving to keys it never holds (DESIGN §10.5), and a compromise revocation parks what it signed and lists the links and connections it could read for replacing (§25.7). Readers refuse a `SponsorSet` naming such an incarnation, so its access never passes to another member, and the sponsor's leaving or removal revokes it with their devices. Its agents' container holds none of this (11.10), and in an enclave that reaches out no run holds both the sponsor's private data and the container but by the person's approval (§7.8). The network's indexer enclave is no member's device (11.10, Q-ENC-13). **Later.** A later version may narrow what an agents' enclave reaches, by per-repo or per-connection shares in place of its sponsor's whole access (§19.5).

### 11.5 The image and the shapes

**The image.** `ur-enclave`: Debian 13, built reproducibly with mkosi from pinned package snapshots; signed releases, versioned with `ur`. It holds `ur` (enclave build), a pinned PiG, the system git, OpenSSH's client tools, build-essential, Python 3, Node.js LTS, Go, Rust (rustup), the usual network and debugging tools, nothing listening, no login on any console (serial, virtual or vsock), and an init that reads nothing from the host but B (11.7). Its expected measurements are computed offline for each provider's firmware and VM layout (`sev-snp-measure`, TDX measurement tools, or dstack-mr), published with the release, logged to Sigstore's Rekor, and pinned in the policy (§5.4) as `reproduced`. On a provider that offers EPC-1's second form, the same contents travel as a signed payload the provider's measured init checks against `HOST_DATA` or `MRCONFIGID`.

**Shapes.** Prices are the provider's times the 1.20 markup (§9.6), set in the catalog at each gate:

| Shape | vCPU | RAM | Disk (scratch) | Accelerator | First provider |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cpu-2` | 2 | 8 GiB | 64 GiB | — | Hippius (after G-PROV-hippius) or Cathedral (after G-PROV-cathedral) |
| `cpu-4` | 4 | 16 GiB | 128 GiB | — | Hippius or Cathedral |
| `cpu-8` | 8 | 32 GiB | 256 GiB | — | Hippius or Cathedral |
| `gpu-1` … `gpu-8` (H200, B200, B300) | per machine | per machine | per machine | NVIDIA CC | Lium (after G-PROV-lium); whole machines only (EPC-6) |

### 11.6 Lifecycle

```text
state         entered when                                          charged
requested     enclave_create approved (§16.3)                       no
creating      the broker asked the provider for a VM                no (absorbed by URnetwork if it fails)
attesting     the VM published evidence; a device is verifying it   no
provisioned   the device sent the sealed bundle                     no
joining       the enclave enrolled and is joining the network       no
running       its sidecar is admitted, its address claimed, SSH and the Harness up   enclave_run per second
stopping      stop asked, or the balance hit suspension (§9.9)      yes, until the VM is gone
stopped       the incarnation revoked, its VM gone; name, tags, grants   no (no disk is kept, 11.9)
              and agent names kept
deleting      remove asked                                          until the VM is gone
deleted       revoked, keys erased                                  no
failed        attestation refused, provider error, VM lost         no further charge; the person told why
```

Transitions run in the broker's orchestrator (`computeservice`, §14) and on the creating device; each one is a record entry (11.12) and an `enclave_status` event (§7.6). A failed attestation destroys the VM and is never retried on the same machine. The orchestrator never retries alone: each create or start authorizes one VM, bound by its incarnation number in B (11.7), and a retry is the device's own, a new incarnation under the same approval, at most 3 tries in all, each counted on the enclave's card and in the record, the person asked past that, so a broker cannot discard VMs until one lands on a machine it chose. Each state before `running` has a timeout, past which the VM is destroyed and the state is `failed`: `requested` and `creating` 15 minutes each, `attesting`, `provisioned` and `joining` 10. From `requested` the network holds the enclave's first 10 minutes (§9.7), released if it never runs; VMs on their way count against 11.13's limits as running ones do, and failed tries against a daily cap of their own, so what URnetwork absorbs for VMs that never run is bounded per network.

### 11.7 Provisioning

```text
 1 approval  enclave_create (O, §16.3) is approved on an approval-capable device; that device runs 2-9 (for a start,
             the person's device that asks does)
 2 device    makes the bootstrap bundle B = {enclave_id, incarnation number, network_id, role (agents or indexer,
             11.10), image version, the image's payload root hash, broker url, the device's sidecar_id};
             POST /v1/enclaves {shape, provider preference, SHA-256(B)}
 3 broker    picks a provider meeting the shape and the network's floor (§16.4); creates the VM with the image
             (EPC-1's first form) or the payload, with SHA-256(B) as launch data where the provider sets it
 4 enclave   its measured init reads B, checks it against the launch data where set, checks the payload against B's
             root hash before running it (EPC-1's second form), and generates in memory the incarnation's identity
             key, ClientKey seed, X-Wing ReaderKey, SSH host key and a one-use X-Wing provisioning key P
 5 device    sends a 32-byte nonce n through the broker; the enclave answers with its quote or report, GPU evidence
             for GPU shapes, and the public keys, the report data being
             SHA-512("urnetwork-sidecar-v1/enclave-attest" ‖ 0x00 ‖ n ‖ SHA-256(B) ‖ H), ‖ s after H under
             setup over SSH (below), with
             H = SHA-256(P ‖ SSH host key ‖ identity key ‖ ClientKey ‖ ReaderKey), public keys each
 6 device    verifies (§5): roots, TCB, measurements = ur-enclave's profile for this provider, B's payload root hash =
             the policy's for that image version, launch data = SHA-256(B) where set, or, under EPC-1's third form, the register replayed from the provider's event log with SHA-256(B) as its event (for a vTPM, a quote over the PCR with the device's nonce as qualifying data, signed by an attestation key the device binds by credential activation to the endorsement key the SVSM's report binds), the report data as above (which
             binds B even where the provider sets no launch data, since the measured init computes it), GPU evidence;
             on any failure the VM is destroyed and the state is failed
 7 device    files the incarnation's SidecarAdmit for the attested identity key, with the enclave's tags and, for an
             agents' enclave, the sponsor's member_id and bit 3 (11.4); mints a single-use tagged auth key for its
             client (DESIGN §7.8); seals to P the auth key, the network's genesis anchor and the settings, and sends
             them through the broker
 8 enclave   opens them, erases P, enrolls (ur connect --token, from memory), binds its client under the attested
             ClientKey, claims an address, starts ur tun with its settings, files KeyRegister for its SSH host key,
             starts its SSH server and Harness, and takes over its agents' cards
 9 device    checks the KeyRegister names the attested host key; marks the enclave running; the record gets the
             AttestationResult
```

**Resuming.** Steps 2-9 run on one device but do not depend on it: each step's state (B, the nonce, under setup over SSH the session's secret, the keys the evidence bound) is kept sealed in the sponsor's vault with the enclave's settings (`enclaves/<id>.json`, 11.4), so if the device stops, a phone its OS suspended among them, any untagged consented device of the sponsor, or its keeper, resumes from the last step done, the apps prompting by notification, within that state's timeout (11.6).

**The provider's disclosure** (CO-33). Each kind 19, a creation or a start that changes an enclave's provider or shape, names its provider (§16.3), and that provider's disclosure gates it (§2.8). Before the request is filed, the requesting device checks that the sponsor has acknowledged `enclave:<provider>` at its current version, asking the person where one is attached and answering `disclosure_required` to anything else, an MCP call and an agent with no person attached included; the approval card shows the disclosure's summary line, which opens its text; and the device that runs steps 2-9 checks the acknowledgment again before step 2, and in step 6 accepts evidence only from the provider the approval named, so no broker can place an enclave where its sponsor has not read what is exposed. A start on the same provider and shape, a keeper's included, asks nothing (Q-ENC-8).

**Setup over SSH** (EPC-1's fourth form). On a provider whose measured image takes nothing from the host, whose attested channel installs the device's one-use SSH key and the enclave id only once, before its SSH server starts, with no later key, console or command for its customer, and whose SSH server binds into a report on request the keys installed, the enclave id and its own session's exchange hash (`ur-enclave-ssh-setup-v1`, §5.5; or measures the keys and id into `RTMR3` or an SVSM vTPM PCR, binding the session beside them), steps 3 and 4 change. The broker creates the VM with the provider's image, the device's one-use key and the enclave id, through the provider's API. The device dials the VM's SSH port through `auto` egress, so the miner and the provider's edge see an exit's address, never the person's; since `auto` carries no privileged port but a short list (11.8), the form needs the provider's setup server reachable at a port from 1024 up, its own or one the provider maps to it, which the gate checks, and a provider that answers only on port 22 does not qualify by this form; it logs in, asks for the server-bound report, and verifies three things: the provider's measurement profile; exactly its key and this enclave's id installed; and the binding to its own session. So it knows the session ends inside the VM made for this enclave, which only its key can enter; a genuine VM of the same image holding other keys, or a relay splicing another session's report, fails. Only then does it copy over the session B, the payload and a 32-byte secret s it draws for this incarnation, and run them; the payload keeps s in memory, appends it to step 5's report data (§5.5) and erases it with P, so step 6 refuses evidence from any other VM, which never received s, though it runs the same image and answers through the broker. The payload first checks that no key but the one-use key is installed, then stops the provider's SSH server and every provider agent that takes commands (a firewall does not reach a vsock or serial channel), removes the one-use key and installs 11.8's rules, and only then makes the incarnation's keys as step 4 does; steps 5-9 follow, step 6 checking the provider image's profile in place of ur-enclave's and launch data, and, where the keys are measured into a register, that it still holds exactly the one-use key and the enclave id. The bootstrap of EPC-1's second and third forms likewise stops the provider image's own access services before it makes keys. The form rests on the provider's image and channel, so the provider is inside the boundary (AP); a person's device or the keeper sets up each incarnation this way, as for the other forms, the network's indexer enclave included (CO-41). No evidence covers a payload installed over SSH, so for the indexer the device that set an incarnation up, its sponsor's, signs a **setup statement**: a DESIGN §6.9 Signed of purpose `enclave-setup` (`SIGNED_ENCLAVE_SETUP` = 0x180A, DESIGN §6.11; Appendix D) over the enclave id, the incarnation, SHA-256(B), the payload's root hash, H, and the SHA-256 of step 5's evidence and of the installed SSH keys, which the incarnation keeps with that evidence and returns with every `EVIDENCE` answer; a member's device verifies the provider image's evidence and its binding to the statement, keys and B alike, and seats the incarnation on the sponsor's signed word, taking it for what the setup installed (11.10, Q-ENC-9).

The broker carries B's hash, the nonce, the evidence and the sealed bundle, and learns nothing it could use. A miner who rewrites B or the payload changes the report data, which step 6 refuses. A broker that starts a second VM with the genuine image gets a genuine enclave it cannot read; one that holds root in another VM of a provider's image can answer no step 5 the device takes, since under setup over SSH the evidence must bind the session's secret, and under the second and third forms the init lets in no key or boot input it does not refuse or measure (EPC-1). What remains is §2.6's physical attack on the machine: an incarnation is as safe as its machine.

**Unattended restarts** are off by default: a lost incarnation waits for a person's device. `ur enclave keeper <device>` names an always-on untagged device of the member (a desktop daemon, an indexer, never an enclave, which admits nothing, 11.4; for the network's indexer enclave, any Owner's or Admin's, whose admission makes them the incarnation's sponsor, DESIGN §7.7) that may start a new incarnation alone after a loss the provider's own status confirms or a suspension's top-up, never after a stop a person or a run made (11.11), but only on a machine whose chip identity (Intel PPID, AMD chip id) an earlier incarnation of this enclave already used, or on an A2 machine, or, for the network's indexer enclave, on any machine its Where row allows, telling its Owners and Admins each time and taking at most two new machines a week (11.10, Q-ENC-11); for any other machine, past that limit, and for any loss the provider's own status does not confirm, it pages the person instead. A keeper never holds a key the enclave uses: it only verifies and admits, as a person's device would.

### 11.8 Networking and default egress

The enclave's network is its sidecar's, set by `ur` (R-ENC-4):

| Part | Value |
|---|---|
| Address | a `BridgeAddress` /32 in the network's block, claimed by each incarnation (DESIGN §17.4) and shown by `ur enclave ls`; the private name `<name>.<net>` follows the running incarnation through the overlay resolver, so people and rules use the name |
| Routes | `ur tun` owns them: the block, granted prefixes and, with default egress on, the default routes, IPv6's too (DESIGN §17.11; owner decisions [479](DESIGN.md#od-479)-[482](DESIGN.md#od-482), [606](DESIGN.md#od-606)) |
| Default egress | on, to the egress destination of the enclave's mode: `auto` (URnetwork's network, the connect client's destination), `exits` (an exit of the network, a tag's or a named one) or `none` (no internet); the mode is the enclave subject's `BridgeEgress` statement, which its sponsor files with `ur enclave egress`, an `egress_change` action (DESIGN §5.4, kind 5), whose card says so when it moves an enclave off `none` after it took tainted input there (§7.10, §16.3's field 49); a network that requires default egress for `tag:enclave` holds it on ([owner decision 607](DESIGN.md#od-607)) |
| Default at create | the network's mode for `tag:enclave` if a policy sets one; else `auto` |
| Off (`direct`) | default egress off sends traffic out the provider's own network, from the miner's address, its connection metadata visible to the miner: allowed only by `enclave_egress_direct` (§16.3), an outward action each time, recorded |
| The host's interface | the enclave's init installs nftables rules: no inbound on the host interface but replies; outbound only the daemon's own marked transport (connect, api, evs, the broker) and, under `direct` alone, everything else; so a process cannot route around the tun, and the provider's public address or port mappings carry nothing; agents cannot change the rules: their `CAP_NET_ADMIN` holds only inside their container's own namespace (11.10) |
| SMTP | outbound TCP 25 refused in every mode, beside the providers' own rule; mail goes through DESIGN §14's edge |
| Ports under `auto` | URnetwork's providers carry a non-network source's traffic only to ports from 1024 up, less a few abused ones such as BitTorrent's, and below 1024 only to 80, 443, 853, the secure mail ports (465, 587 under STARTTLS, 993, 995), DNS over UDP and 123, 500 and 4500 (connect/ip_security_cfaa.go); so under `auto` an enclave's agents cannot reach SSH's port 22 or another low port outward, `git` over SSH, `scp` and `rsync` to port 22 failing while HTTPS remotes work, as the enclave's disclosure and the skill say (§2.8, §20.9); an exit of the network's own, whose provider allows its network's sources every destination (DESIGN §8.3), carries them under `exits` |
| Inbound | only over the overlay, by policy (§16.2); public exposure only through DESIGN §13's TLS edge or §17's forwards, as for any sidecar |

Traffic the enclave sends through URnetwork (overlay flows, `auto`, `exits`) counts toward the transfer balance as all traffic does ([owner decision 10](DESIGN.md#od-10)); `direct` traffic is the provider's bandwidth, charged as `enclave_host_egress` where the provider bills it (§9.6).

### 11.9 Storage

- **Scratch.** The VM's disk is a scratch volume the init formats at each incarnation with dm-crypt and dm-integrity under a key it makes in memory, not LUKS, since a host can alter LUKS metadata (Tinfoil's lesson, [Rpt:bb]); a host that changes a block makes reads fail, not lie, though dm-integrity authenticates each sector and not its age, so a host that puts back a sector's earlier contents from the same incarnation is not detected; the volume and its key last one incarnation, which bounds that replay. It is gone when the VM is.
- **What lasts.** Work lives in EVS: the Harness's workspaces are git-mode repos synced by the enclave's local tier (DESIGN §11.11, which has a system git here), records and summaries go to the member's vault and agents repo, and an agent's notes to its agent repo (§20). A restart re-syncs what the Harness needs, and the next incarnation reopens from the vault each run the last one held open (§24.7).
- **Persistent volumes** are Later: no provider in §4.4 offers one with keys the customer holds (Targon removed its volumes on 2026-11-11), and EVS covers the need.

### 11.10 What runs in it

| Process | User | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `ur daemon` (enclave mode) | root | the sidecar: transport, `ur tun`, the firewall, EVS, the record; holds the incarnation's keys in memory |
| `ur ssh-server` | root, dropping to the session's user | §12, on the overlay address only; it verifies each attach link's origin, joins `ur harness rpc` to the Harness and answers evidence requests itself, all outside the agents' container (§12.4-§12.6) |
| `ur harness serve` | root, in the daemon's namespaces, outside the agents' container | the Harness, enclave profile (§7.5), and the receiving end of every attach link (§7.10); its agents named `<enclave>-main` and up; it keeps each run's taint bit, starts the agents' tool processes in the container and opens their files beneath its root |
| the agents' container | root inside it: a systemd-nspawn Debian with its own user namespace (its root an unprivileged uid outside), PID, mount and network namespaces, its veth routed through `ur tun` and the daemon's rules, so it can neither read the daemon's memory, which no process in another user and PID namespace may trace, nor change the enclave's routes or rules; Yama's `ptrace_scope` stays at Debian's 1, since 3, a setting for the whole kernel, would refuse gdb and strace in the container too | the agents' tool processes (`bash`, `git` and the programs they start), and the external harnesses and PiG they run as programs |
| the gateway | inside the daemon | §8, on the enclave's loopback, and on a listener the daemon opens on the agents' container's own loopback, in its network namespace, with §8.7's token, Host and Origin checks, so PiG, Codex or Claude Code in the container reach the catalog at an ordinary base URL |
| `pig --mode rpc` | root in the agents' container, as a program | only when the person's session attach asks for it (§7.10) |
| the edit container | root inside it, in a user namespace of its own as the agents' container's | a person-only container for editors' remote servers (§12.9): its own PID, mount and network namespaces and root file system, which no agent process enters or writes, the agents' container's file system mounted at `/agents`, its veth routed as the agents' container's; an `edit` SSH session lands in it, and nothing runs in it otherwise |

"Full tools" (CO-5) means compilers, interpreters, the system git, build and network tools, and root to use them (CO-19): agents run as root inside their container, whose Debian root file system is an overlay on the image's on the scratch volume, so `apt`, services, low ports, gdb and strace all work there, and an `agent` SSH session (§12.5) lands in it, but for an exec of `ur harness rpc`, which the server joins to the Harness outside it (§7.10). The container is the boundary: its root is an unprivileged user outside, its network leaves only through the daemon's tun and rules (IC-8), and the daemon, its keys and the enclave's firewall sit in namespaces it cannot enter (Q-ENC-3). In an agents' enclave that daemon holds, since CO-43, everything its sponsor's devices hold (11.4), so the same boundary keeps the sponsor's data from agents with root and the internet: no key, token or link secret enters the container (IC-14), its agents reach the sponsor's data only through the Harness's tools, and in an enclave that reaches out no run holds both that data and the container (§7.8). The enclave's own root stays with the person: their SSH session, from their own untagged device alone (§12.5), may log in as it. What "full tools" leaves out is what the boundary takes away: kernel modules and kernel settings; the enclave's routes, firewall, clock and devices; and whatever needs a privilege outside the container's user namespace, such as a privileged nested container or a VM. Nothing the person or an agent installs is measured: the attestation speaks for the boot, and what happens after is recorded work.

**The container's boundary.** The Harness runs outside the agents' container, in the daemon's namespaces, and the container holds only what the agents run: their tool processes, which the Harness starts in it (`bash`, `git`, programs), and the external harnesses and PiG they run as programs. So the Harness and the daemon, not anything in the container, keep each enclave run's taint bit, and set it at any tool's result there, `bash`'s, `pig`'s and the file tools' alike, since all of it comes from a container that reaches the internet (§7.8). The container holds no credential but the hour-long gateway tokens IC-11 admits (I-7), and no API socket: the Harness opens the agents' files from outside, beneath the container's root (`openat2` with `RESOLVE_IN_ROOT`), so a link an agent planted resolves inside it, and hands `git` a pipe to the local tier for its pushes and fetches. `ur` inside it is a read-only bind mount from outside. One socket is mounted in, the container socket, for the harnesses that run there: it serves MCP's tools (§15.2), `ur gateway token` for the container's gateway grants, `ur install-harness`'s request for one (§8.7), and `ur hook` reports, and the daemon takes every call through it as a tainted run's, for kinds 23-25 and the inbox refusal (§20.4) alike. It binds a caller to its run by `SO_PEERCRED` and process ancestry where it can (a hook-bound harness's run), else to an unknown run, which is tainted, and marks taint itself on every result it serves, so a process that claims an untainted run is refused or bound to its real run. Nothing in the container can mint evidence: `/dev/tdx_guest`, `/dev/sev-guest`, configfs-tsm and any vTPM are absent from it, and `ur ssh-server` answers evidence requests itself (§12.6). Its veth takes only the container's own source address, and nothing in the enclave's own namespaces accepts input from it but the daemon's DNS port, where the container resolves through it: not the overlay SSH server, the local tier's git front or the mail receiver; the gateway's listener sits on the container's own loopback (§8.7). A seccomp filter, no nested user namespaces, `io_uring` and unprivileged BPF off, and the image's kernel kept current answer the kernel attack surface its namespaced `CAP_NET_ADMIN` opens; cgroup limits on CPU, memory and processes leave the daemon its share.

**The network's indexer enclave** (CO-19, CO-20). A network's mail and search services run on its indexer, an always-on sidecar an Owner or Admin designates (DESIGN §3.6's `IndexerSet`), and a network may make one enclave that indexer, so a person without an always-on desktop still has one. CO-19 asks whether that is supported: the design supports it whole, from the mail setup's offer through each member's grant to every restart, and it reaches users once an enclave provider passes its gate in a form the Where row allows; until then the setup offers an always-on device, as DESIGN does:

| | |
|---|---|
| Setup | at mail setup, where the network has no mail indexer, the app asks an Owner or Admin whether to run mail and search in a secure enclave (§15.4), showing the shape (`cpu-2`), the provider and label, the monthly price, what the enclave will hold, the reserve it sets aside and when it could still stop (the balance and its reserve spent, an unplanned restart's minutes, the provider's own outage); one approval on an Owner's or Admin's device creates it (`enclave_create`, §16.3), provisions it and signs the `IndexerSet`: the sdk's `Enclaves().Create` with `role: "indexer"`, or `ur enclave create <name> --role indexer` (§15), confirmed on a tty; the Harness's and MCP's `enclave_create` take no role, since DESIGN signs an `IndexerSet` only for the person, never through MCP. It is offered only where the Where row allows, the setup otherwise asking for an always-on device as DESIGN §15.6 does, and a balance that cannot fund its reserve is offered credit first (§9.5, §9.9) |
| One per network | at most one indexer enclave a network, at network scope (CO-20); members' own devices may still be member-scope indexers; readers refuse a second network-scope `IndexerSet` naming an enclave while one stands unretired, so a replacement retires the first |
| Its role | `indexer` in B (11.7), and so in the evidence each member's device checks before it grants or seats: EPC-1's first three forms bind it into what the VM measures, and under setup over SSH, which any network's indexer may use (CO-41), the sponsor's setup statement binds it with the incarnation's evidence, keys and payload (11.7), and a member's device, having checked the provider image's evidence and that binding itself, seats the incarnation on the sponsor's signed word, trusting the sponsor for what the setup installed (Q-ENC-9); in it the indexer runs only the daemon's mail and search services; no Harness, no agents' container, no gateway; its SSH server admits no one, root included, so neither its sponsor nor any agent can reach what a member's grant opens; a change is a new incarnation |
| No member's device | its incarnations are tagged sidecars its Owners and Admins sponsor, never consented for any member, so CO-43's access, an agents' enclave's, does not reach it: it holds the network's incoming mail and the mailboxes members grant it, nothing of one admin's vault, mail or accounts (Q-ENC-13) |
| The designation follows it | an `IndexerSet` names a sidecar, and each incarnation is a new sidecar (11.4), so for an enclave it names the enclave, and readers resolve it to the running incarnation: the incarnation whose `SidecarAdmit` its sponsor's or an admin's device filed after verifying its evidence, role included; each member's device verifies that evidence itself before it seats the incarnation as a mailbox reader, asking the running incarnation over the overlay, by an `EVIDENCE` call on the sidecar RPC that remote search uses (DESIGN §6.6; Appendix D), for a quote or report on its own nonce with the public keys and B, and, for an incarnation set up over SSH, its sponsor's setup statement, so it checks role, label, provider and keys itself, and the mail edge reaches it by the same resolution (Appendix D) |
| Mail, unread | it takes the network's mail: the mail edge reaches it over the overlay, TLS ends inside it, and it deposits each message into the recipient's mailbox as the mailbox's receiver (DESIGN §8.5), which needs no right to read the mailbox. It reads each member's new mail in plaintext as it receives it, whether or not that member granted it anything, before it seals the deposit; the setup and each member's mail settings say so, with the provider's disclosure line (§2.8), and a grant covers stored mail. This supersedes owner decision 12's "no hosted or TEE receiver" for the indexer enclave alone, on the argument and conditions below (CO-19; Q-ENC-10; Appendix D) |
| Team mail | under `team_mail: indexers`, the default, the indexer enclave carries `tag:mail` and receives the Team's network mail as DESIGN's `tag:mail` device does, from 24 hours after its `IndexerSet`, every member's devices telling them at once that it will read their incoming mail as it arrives, with the provider's disclosure line and who set it up and how (Q-ENC-10); under `member scopes`, members' own receivers take their mail and the enclave receives none, indexing only what members grant; a personal network's mail is network scope (DESIGN §3.6) |
| A member's grant | a mailbox is owner-bound, readable only by its member's consented devices (DESIGN §8.5), so the enclave indexes a member's mail, for the phone's "search more" (DESIGN §11.14), only once that member grants it (CO-20): `ur mail indexer grant`, confirmed on `/dev/tty` and refused to a caller with a harness process among its ancestors, or the app's switch (`GrantMailbox`, §15.4), on the member's own device, shown with the provider's disclosure (§2.8), which the member acknowledges before granting, since their mail goes there: at AP the provider company is inside the boundary, and a physical attack by the machine's holder could read what the enclave holds (§2.6). The grant is bound to the enclave's label and provider at the time, and, where an incarnation was set up over SSH, to the member who set it up, whom the grant sheet names with how; a move to another provider or label, or an incarnation another Owner or Admin set up over SSH, asks the member again. The grant names the indexer enclave and the mailbox alone (Q-ENC-6). It is the key `compute.indexer_grant` of the member's harness config, `{enclave_id, provider, label, setup_by}`, which only their own act writes, as `compute.disclosures` is (§2.8), so each of their devices reads it; `setup_by` names the member whose setup statement the grant accepted, and is empty under EPC-1's first three forms. It outlasts incarnations: the member's devices seat each new incarnation as a reader of the mailbox once its evidence verifies, so a member offline at a restart has their mail indexed again when a device of theirs next syncs. `ur mail indexer revoke`, or the switch, clears the key and unseats it at the mailbox's next generation |
| Always on | an Owner's or Admin's always-on device is its keeper (11.7), which restarts it alone on any machine the Where row allows, telling the Owners and Admins each time, at most two new machines a week, a third paging a person (Q-ENC-11); with no keeper, an approval-capable device of theirs admits a new incarnation, the apps prompting by notification. A planned restart, for an image or kernel fix, a profile's expiry (11.11) or a move, is make before break: the next incarnation starts, posts its mail-host key beside the running one's, takes the mail once its key is live, two TTLs (600 s) later (DESIGN §15.5), and only then is the old one stopped, so no mail waits. After an unplanned loss, mail waits on senders' retries (DESIGN §3.6) until the new incarnation runs and its key is live, about ten minutes more, and indexing waits; mail and indexes live in EVS (11.9). Silence alone never fails it, only the provider's report (11.11). Its `smtp/25/mx` listen, which every receiver needs (DESIGN §15.5), is requested for its tag, `tag:enclave-<id>`, and approved as any receiver's, for the lifetime the receiver's settings give (7 days by default, owner decision 687), so a new incarnation receives under it with no new approval, and its renewals reach the approvers as a desktop receiver's do (Appendix D); its reserve and grace keep it running past the balance (Cost), and after a suspension that outlasts them its keeper starts it again at the top-up (§9.9) |
| Its keys | each incarnation makes its own mail-host key in its VM and attests it with its identity key, as every receiver does (DESIGN §13.8's `TlsKeyAttestation`, §15.5), and posts its TLSA and its certificate order itself, so nothing of the mail role reaches it from a device and a keeper restarts it holding no key (11.7); the new key goes live two TTLs after it is posted, senders retrying meanwhile (DESIGN §15.5); for a custom domain, the network's ordering desktops, which keep its account key, order its certificate as they do a phone's (DESIGN §13.8) |
| Where | a Bittensor provider's enclave (CO-21) with a CPU shape, Hippius' or Cathedral's, after its gate (G-PROV-hippius, G-PROV-cathedral), by any of EPC-1's four forms in any network (CO-41, Q-ENC-9), and on a machine the broker did not choose, since a broker that could choose could aim a physical attack at the network's mail (§2.7): an A2 machine, or one the provider's own scheduler placed and signed for, which the device checks against the evidence's chip identity (Q-ENC-10); none passes the contract today (11.3), Hippius closest. Until one does, the mail setup offers no enclave and the network's indexer is a member's always-on device, as DESIGN has it (Q-ENC-5) |
| Cost | the shape's hourly price around the clock, from the network's compute balance (§9.6): tens of dollars a month at the 1.20 markup, by inference, depending on the provider; no budget stops it, only the balance (§9.7, §9.9). Its **reserve**: at setup, 7 days of its price move from the balance into a reserve that only its own `enclave_run` charges draw, and only once the rest of the balance cannot pay them; the reserve is refilled from the balance while the network is `active`. When the balance runs out, every other enclave stops as §9.9 says and the indexer runs on its reserve, then on 72 hours of grace, the notices counting down, so a lapsed card, or a store buyer with no threshold top-up, has about ten days before mail stops; the grace can add up to 72 hours of its price to what the network owes, beyond §9.9's floor. A chargeback's suspension (§9.11) likewise stops it only once what of its reserve no reversed lot funded, and its grace, are spent (Q-ENC-11) |

**Why it is the network's own receiver** (Q-ENC-10). The directive lets inbound TLS end only on a device or a customer-run sidecar (DESIGN's X6), and owner decision 12 ruled out hosted and TEE receivers; CO-19 and CO-20 ask for this one, and it meets the directive's test, which turns on who holds the keys and the plaintext, not on whose account pays for the machine. Every key it uses, its identity, client, reader, SSH host and mail-host keys, is made inside its VM and never leaves it (11.4); it joins the network only when a device of an Owner or Admin, having verified its evidence itself, files its admission, and it receives only by that person's signed `IndexerSet`; TLS ends inside it, under a key it attests with its own identity key, as every receiver's does (DESIGN §13.8); a mailbox opens to it only by its member's own grant, sealed by that member's device (IC-3); and nothing URnetwork runs holds a key, a login or a console into it. URnetwork's broker creates it, in URnetwork's account at the provider, pays for it and can destroy it. So the broker can deny service, refusing, delaying or ending an incarnation while mail waits on senders' retries; can choose the provider within the network's floor; and sees compute-4's and compute-5's metadata, which enclave is the indexer among it. It cannot read the sealed bundle, which goes to a key made in the VM; cannot have a device admit any VM but the one it checked, since the evidence binds B, the keys and, under setup over SSH, a secret the device sent only inside its verified session (11.7); cannot change what runs, which the measurement fixes, or under setup over SSH the sponsor's verified session; cannot log in, since the role's SSH server admits no one, the image starts no console login, and EPC-1 gives the provider's customer, the broker included, no key, console or command into a running guest; and cannot aim the machine, since the indexer runs only where the broker does not choose it (Where). What remains is the provider company at AP and the machine's holder by a physical attack (§2.6), and, under setup over SSH, the sponsor, whose word members take (CO-41): each is in the provider's disclosure (§2.8). In a Team no member's mail moves there unannounced: it receives only 24 hours after its `IndexerSet`, every member told at once (Team mail).

### 11.11 Stop, start, move, lose, remove

- **Stop** revokes the incarnation (11.4) and destroys its VM, every repo it read moving to keys it never holds (DESIGN §10.5) and the tokens and link secrets it held ending with its memory, so a stop asks no one to replace them (§25.7); the name, tags, grants, private name and agent names stay. Each stop's record entry and card name its cause: the person, a run (named, with its taint), the balance, or a loss; a keeper restarts only what the balance or a loss stopped (11.7), since a tainted run's stop waits for the person and an untainted run's carries the person's own instruction (§7.5). **Start** is a new incarnation through 11.7, the person's act, or a tool's under kind 19 (§7.5), on any machine and any provider meeting the network's floor. Only a person's act stops, starts or removes the network's indexer enclave; no tool reaches it (§7.5, §15.2, Q-ENC-12).
- **Lost.** A VM the provider reports gone or broken is `failed`. One silent to the orchestrator for 5 minutes is shown unreachable on its card, still running and charged, and is failed only on the provider's report, never for silence alone, so an outage of the broker or a relay fails no enclave; the person may stop it. A failed one's sidecar is revoked as 11.4 says; a keeper starts another only under 11.7's rule, else the person is told.
- **Age.** An incarnation runs no longer than its image's profile in the policy (`expires`, §5.4), set at most 90 days out when the profile is added and brought to 30 days after a fixed image ships (EPC-9); from 7 days before, its card says so, and its keeper, else the sponsor's next device online, replaces it, make before break for the indexer (11.10), so a kernel fix reaches every enclave within about six weeks of its release.
- **Provider leaves the catalog** (G-PROV-any): running enclaves are told, and keep running until the person moves them; a move is a stop and a start elsewhere.
- **Remove** is an outward action, `enclave_delete` (§16.3), whose effect runs on the approving device: it revokes a running incarnation, destroys its VM, erases the enclave's settings, retires its cards (§20.5), and leaves its incarnations' addresses to their 30-day tombstones (I-14).

### 11.12 The record

The enclave writes, into its sponsor's vault and, in a Team, the team record's reach entries: `enclave` entries for create, each incarnation's `AttestationResult`, start, stop, egress changes and removal; SSH sessions as reach receipts (§12.7); its Harness runs as runs (§7.7).

### 11.13 Limits

| Limit | Community / Pro / Team |
|---|---|
| Enclaves per network, running or on their way (`requested` to `joining`) | 2 / 5 / 50 |
| GPU enclaves per network | 0 / 1 / 10 |
| Incarnations started per enclave per day | 10 |
| Failed tries, creates and starts, per network per day | 5 / 10 / 50 |
| New machines the indexer enclave's keeper takes alone, per week | 2 |

Each also needs the balance for its next 10 minutes (§9.7) and the new-account gates of §9.11.

### 11.14 Alternatives considered

| Option | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accept a provider's image and unmeasured start-up data | enclaves now on Hippius or Lium | a miner rewrites the bootstrap and reads every key delivered; the TEE then protects nothing from the party it is for | rejected: EPC-1 |
| Keys made by the owner's device and given to every incarnation | one identity, address and host key for life | a key leaked once, from any machine it ran on, opens every later incarnation; agents with root could read it | rejected: keys per incarnation, made in its VM; a stable name and tags carry what must last |
| Keep a disk across incarnations, keyed by the owner | faster restarts | no provider offers customer-keyed volumes; EVS already keeps the work | Later |
| A container per enclave on a shared confidential VM | cheaper | other tenants in the VM (EPC-6) | rejected |
| gVisor (`runsc`) for the agents' container | a user-space kernel between the agents and the guest's, far less of it reachable from their root | slower system calls; some tools (debuggers, raw sockets, some `apt` post-install scripts) may fail; its own advisories | evaluated in M14 against the image's tool set, and adopted if `apt`, builds and the network tools pass (D-ENC-13) |
| An egress proxy in the enclave that swaps placeholder credentials for real ones on the way out, as Tinfoil's Bunkers do, so agents never hold a GitHub or cloud token | keeps third-party secrets out of agents' context, I-7's spirit | a TLS-intercepting proxy inside the enclave, with its own CA and host rules | Later |
| The agents' enclave as a tagged sidecar reached by grants, context packs and per-item shares (this design before CO-43) | a breach exposes only what was shared | the owner asked for full access (CO-43); a pack per continued run, a share per repo, link and connection, and settings sealed to each incarnation | superseded for the initial version; per-repo or per-connection shares are Later (11.4) |
| An agents' enclave admitted as an untagged device of its sponsor | DESIGN's consent with no new bit | drops `tag:enclave-<id>`, on which its claim, network reach, egress default and listeners rest, and hands a machine a miner holds the sponsor's authority to admit, consent and share | rejected: a tagged admission naming its sponsor, bit 3 (Q-ENC-14) |

### 11.15 Decisions proposed

**D-ENC-1 (proposed).** An enclave is a named line of incarnations; each is a tagged, sponsored sidecar whose keys are made in its VM and bound in its evidence, admitted by the verifying person's device, an agents' enclave's as one of its sponsor's devices (D-ENC-16), and revoked at its stop. *Why:* R-ENC-6; a leaked key ends with its incarnation; DESIGN §16.6 keeps enrollment off tools.

**D-ENC-2 (proposed).** The enclave platform contract, EPC-1 above all, gates every enclave provider; the reference provider serves development, CI and staging only, the production policy and catalog listing none of its profiles or shapes, and until a provider passes no user is offered an enclave. *Why:* 11.3; CO-21; CO-28.

**D-ENC-3 (proposed).** Default egress on, mode `auto` unless the network's policy for `tag:enclave` says otherwise; `direct` only by an outward action. *Why:* CO-7; the miner sees `direct` traffic.

**D-ENC-4 (proposed).** Scratch disk under dm-crypt and dm-integrity, work in EVS. *Why:* 11.9.

**D-ENC-5 (proposed).** A network may make one enclave its indexer, named by its enclave identity and followed across incarnations, in a role B and its evidence bind, set up by any of EPC-1's forms (CO-41), which runs no agents and admits no login; it takes the network's mail without reading mailboxes, and indexes a member's mailbox only by that member's grant, which its devices carry to each new incarnation. *Why:* CO-19, CO-20; DESIGN §8.5's owner-bound readers.

**D-ENC-6 (proposed).** The agents' container holds only the agents' tool processes and the harnesses they run, no credential but hour-long gateway tokens, `ur` read-only and no API socket; its one container socket's every call is a tainted run's, and nothing in the enclave's namespaces accepts input from its veth but DNS. *Why:* I-7, I-9; agents have root in their container, so anything kept beside them is theirs to rewrite.

**D-ENC-7 (proposed).** Each kind 19 shows its provider's disclosure line and waits for the sponsor's acknowledgment of that disclosure's current version, and step 6 accepts only the named provider's evidence; a member's mailbox grant waits for that member's own; a new version leaves running enclaves running. *Why:* CO-33; an enclave holds keys and data and may run root agents on the internet, and creating one is already the person's approved act; Q-ENC-8.

**D-ENC-8 (proposed).** Each incarnation of the indexer enclave makes its own mail-host key and receives under a listen grant its enclave's tag holds, and each member's grant is the key `compute.indexer_grant` of their harness config, so a keeper restarts it with no key to hand over and the member's devices seat each new incarnation; at most one indexer enclave stands at network scope. *Why:* CO-19's always-on indexer; CO-20; D-ENC-1's keys per incarnation; DESIGN §15.5's receivers.

**D-ENC-9 (proposed).** Any network's indexer enclave may be set up over SSH: its sponsor's device signs a setup statement binding the incarnation's setup evidence, its keys, B and the payload's hash, and a member's device seats the incarnation as a mailbox reader only on that statement, after checking the provider image's evidence and the binding itself, and only from the member its grant accepted. *Why:* CO-41's answer to Q-ENC-9; no evidence covers a payload installed over SSH, so members can rest only on the sponsor's word, which the statement makes explicit and checkable.

**D-ENC-10 (proposed).** Each create or start authorizes one VM, the device itself starting each retry under the same approval, at most 3; the states before `running` time out; their VMs count against the limits and their failures against a daily cap; the first 10 minutes are held at `requested`; any consented device of the sponsor resumes steps 2-9. *Why:* a broker that retries at will can aim placement (§2.7); free states before `running` invite create loops URnetwork pays for; a phone's OS suspends it mid-way.

**D-ENC-11 (proposed).** An enclave's tag is `tag:enclave-<id>`, its name a label; the first admission under the tag claims it for the enclave's sponsor, or for the indexer enclave its Owners and Admins, and readers refuse anyone else's admission under it. *Why:* names collide, and a tag bound by name lets one member's grants reach, or be taken by, another's sidecar.

**D-ENC-12 (proposed).** The network's indexer enclave keeps 7 days of its price in a reserve only its own charges draw, then 72 hours of grace; its keeper restarts it alone on any machine its Where row allows, telling the Owners and Admins, at most two new machines a week; planned restarts make before they break; silence alone fails no enclave. *Why:* CO-19's "always on"; Q-ENC-11.

**D-ENC-13 (proposed).** EPC-9 asks every provider for kernel fixes within 14 days, each a new profile, and no incarnation outlives its profile; gVisor is evaluated for the agents' container. *Why:* the agents' root holds `CAP_NET_ADMIN` in a user namespace, a known path into the kernel, and under EPC-1's other forms the kernel is the provider's.

**D-ENC-14 (proposed).** A start through a tool is a kind 19, a tainted run's `enclave_stop` waits for the person, and no tool stops, starts or removes the network's indexer enclave; each stop records its cause, and a keeper restarts only what the balance or a loss stopped. *Why:* a prompt-injected run could otherwise stop every enclave, the network's mail among them, or resume charges no budget bounds; Q-ENC-12.

**D-ENC-15 (proposed).** The indexer enclave is the network's own receiver on Q-ENC-10's conditions: every key made in it; no key, console, command or login into it for the provider's customer or URnetwork; the keys a device admits bound to the VM it checked, in every form; a machine the broker did not choose; and in a Team, reception only 24 hours after every member is told. *Why:* the directive lets inbound TLS end only on a customer's sidecar, and owner decision 12, which this supersedes for this enclave alone, excluded TEE receivers (CO-19, CO-20).

**D-ENC-16 (proposed).** For the initial version an agents' enclave's incarnation is one of its sponsor's devices: its admission, signed by an untagged consented device of the sponsor that verified its evidence, names the sponsor beside its tags with capability bit 3, so it is consented for the sponsor and reads and writes what their devices reach in EVS, their owner-bound repos, calendar links and connections included, while its network reach stays its tags'; it holds none of their authority (no admission, consent, share, suspension, revocation or key registration but its own, `IndexerSet`, config write or approval but its own runs' automatic decisions, and no version of their settings that another device takes); no `SponsorSet` moves it; its stop, loss or compromise revocation revokes it, every repo it read rotating away from it, as for any removed device; the network's indexer enclave stays a tagged sidecar outside this. *Why:* CO-42, CO-43; Q-ENC-4, Q-ENC-13, Q-ENC-14; a breach must not outlast its incarnation.

### 11.16 Questions

**Q-ENC-1.** Which providers do we support for enclaves? *Answer:* none today without a change on the provider's side: §11.3's table. The three CO-28 chose, each after its gate: Hippius first, for CPU, once it binds launch data, or adds setup over SSH's one feature (Q-ENC-7), and documents guest reports (G-PROV-hippius); Cathedral, for CPU, once it is generally available and passes the same (G-PROV-cathedral); Lium for GPU once it measures the renter's image (G-PROV-lium). Chutes' TDX VMs and Targon are not chosen (CO-28). Development runs on the reference provider, never a user (CO-21). *Decider:* owner.

**Q-ENC-2.** What is the default egress? *Options:* `auto`, `exits`, `none`, `direct`. *Answer:* `auto`, as for any sidecar whose network sets no egress mode (DESIGN §17.11: default egress on, mode `auto`): it keeps destinations from the miner and attributes traffic to URnetwork's network; a network that writes a policy sets `exits` or `none` for `tag:enclave`. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-ENC-3.** Root for agents? *Options:* (a) as `agent` without sudo, packages through the daemon; (b) the enclave's real root by default; (c) root by default inside the agents' own Debian container, its user and network namespaces apart from the daemon's. *Answer:* (c), as CO-19 asks: agents get root for everything Debian offers, `apt`, services and low ports included, while the incarnation's keys and the egress rules CO-7 has sidecar run stay outside their namespaces (11.10). The enclave's real root stays with the person's own SSH session; an agent with it could read the incarnation's keys from the daemon's memory or flush the firewall, making the enclave only as trusted as its least careful agent. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-ENC-4.** May a Team's enclaves be shared between members? *Answer:* not as devices. Since CO-43 an agents' enclave is one of its sponsor's devices, holding what their devices hold for the initial version (11.4), so sharing it would share the sponsor's vault, mail and accounts. Reach to it is shared through ordinary grants (§16.2: `ssh` and `dial` rules naming the enclave's tags), another member managing its agents only by a requested grant the sponsor approves, never as `root` and never launching one (§12.5, Q-HARN-9); its keys, its record and its access stay its sponsor's, and a member who wants an enclave makes their own. Handing an enclave to another member is Later, as a new enclave of theirs. *Decider:* owner, decided (CO-43).

**Q-ENC-5.** Until a Bittensor provider passes the enclave contract, may the indexer enclave run on a cloud's confidential VMs (the reference provider, 11.3), paid in USD? *Options:* (a) no; (b) yes, for the indexer role alone. *Answer:* (a), as the owner decided (CO-21): enclaves run only on Bittensor providers, so the indexer enclave, like every user-facing enclave, waits for G-PROV-hippius or the next provider to pass; until then a network's indexer is a member's always-on device, as DESIGN has it. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-ENC-6.** May a member's grant to the indexer enclave reach beyond the mailbox, to the vault or other repos? *Answer:* no. CO-20 grants the mailbox; the member's other repos are indexed by their own devices; and the indexer serves the whole network under its Owners' and Admins' sponsorship, so a member who wants an enclave to hold their vault and repos runs their own, which CO-43 makes one of their devices (11.4, Q-ENC-13). *Decider:* owner.

**Q-ENC-7.** Instead of the provider binding the bootstrap, can URnetwork set an enclave up by SSH into the provider's VM? *Options:* (a) no; (b) yes, always; (c) yes, where the provider's measured image takes nothing from the miner's host, installs keys only once and gives its customer no later way in, and has its SSH server bind the installed keys, the enclave id and its own session into a report. *Answer:* (c). Four dangers need these conditions. An image that reads start-up data or SSH keys from the host lets the miner plant its own key or a boot script, and a backdoor planted at boot leaves the attestation unchanged. A report proves only the image, so without the installed keys and enclave id bound into it a breached broker, or a miner who is also the provider's customer, could present a genuine VM of the same image on which it holds root. And without the server's own binding, a relay could splice a genuine guest's report into another session. And a key, console or command the provider's API adds after the report would let that broker, which drives URnetwork's account, or a miner with an impostor VM in its own account, take root after the check, so the provider offers none and the payload closes the provider's own access before it makes keys (11.7). With all of them, setup reaches only the VM made for this enclave, which only the device's key can enter; it is one small provider feature, a report the SSH server binds, not a new register, which SEV-SNP lacks without an SVSM vTPM. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-ENC-8.** Does a new version of an enclave provider's disclosure stop the sponsor's running enclaves there? *Options:* (a) no: the next kind 19 there, a creation or a move, asks, and each card shows the new line at once; (b) yes, until the sponsor acknowledges. *Answer:* (a). The enclave and what it holds are already there, and (b) would stop agents' work, and a network's indexer enclave its mail, for a change of text; the card marks the change until the sponsor opens it. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-ENC-9.** May the network's indexer enclave be set up over SSH (EPC-1's fourth form), which a provider may offer before it binds launch data? *Options:* (a) never: a member's device cannot check a payload only the sponsor's device vouches for (11.7); (b) in a personal network, whose one member is its sponsor: the device that set the incarnation up, a consented device of that member, verified its session and payload itself and seats it as the mailbox's reader, the person's other devices never seating an incarnation they cannot check; a Team's indexer enclave keeps EPC-1's first three forms; (c) always, members taking the sponsor's word. *Answer:* (c), decided by the owner (CO-41): any network's indexer enclave may be set up over SSH, its members taking the sponsor's word for what the setup installed, which the sponsor's device verified; members see who set it up before they grant. The sponsor's device signs a setup statement binding the incarnation's evidence, keys and payload, on which members' devices seat it (11.7, 11.10). *Decider:* owner, decided (CO-41).

**Q-ENC-10.** Does the network's indexer enclave satisfy the owner directive, and may it replace owner decision 12's "no hosted or TEE receiver"? *Options:* (a) no: keep owner decision 12, a network's indexer staying a member's always-on device; (b) yes in a personal network, and in a Team only on a provider that passes by EPC-1's first form or at A2, with a notice to every member before it receives; (c) yes in any network, on 11.10's argument and conditions. *Answer:* (c). CO-19 and CO-20 ask for the enclave, and it meets the directive's test, which is who holds the keys and the plaintext: every key is made in it, it joins and receives only by an Owner's or Admin's verified act, and nothing URnetwork runs can read its bundle, admit another VM, change its software or log in. The conditions: EPC-1 binds the keys a device admits to the VM it checked in every form (11.7's session secret; an init that refuses or measures every boot input); no form gives the provider's customer, the broker included, a key, console or command into the guest, and the image starts no console login; the broker does not choose its machine (A2, or the provider's signed placement); and in a Team it receives only 24 hours after every member is told. (b)'s limit to the first form or A2 yields to CO-41, which lets any network's indexer be set up over SSH, its members taking the sponsor's word; its notice is kept. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-42).

**Q-ENC-11.** Should the indexer enclave have its own reserve and a longer grace, and may its keeper restart it on a new machine with no person? *Options:* (a) no: it stops with the balance as any enclave does, and a keeper restarts it only on a machine an earlier incarnation used or an A2 one, paging a person otherwise; (b) yes: 7 days of its price reserved at setup, then 72 hours of grace, and unattended restarts on any machine its Where row allows, with a notice each time and at most two new machines a week. *Answer:* (b).
