### 24.8 External harnesses and the gateway

Codex, Claude Code and the Chat Completions harnesses keep their own sessions; of the first two the record already captures hooks, telemetry and transcripts (DESIGN §16.7). None of those shows what the model received: a transcript lacks the system prompt and tools, and once a harness rewrites its context the transcript no longer matches the request. The gateway sees each request and response whole, so it records them in the run §8.9 binds the call to:

```text
items      a request's instructions or system text and its tools, as a system node; its input messages and items
           in order; the response's output items as the router streamed them; each in its recorded form (24.9),
           without the hints whose place moves from call to call (Messages' cache_control)
binding    a call §8.9 binds by harness, agent and time alone records its entries with the OR of the taint bits
           of every live run of the grant, failing closed, and its nodes are untrusted to continue, fork and
           record_query (24.7)
match      chain_sha256 over the recorded input items; the longest prefix the run holds is the parent, so a
           harness's rewrite of its context (a cleared tool result) branches at its first changed item, and only
           the items after the prefix are written, one the run already holds as a same_as node; a request that
           shares no prefix starts a new tree: a side request, a sub-agent, or a compaction, its summary first
system     a change of instructions or tools writes a new system node, outside the chain, so a tool that appears
           mid-session does not break matching
resume     a request whose prefix an earlier run of the same grant holds takes that run's node as its parent,
           never its bytes, only when RECORD.md section 4.3 binds the session to that run or the harness reports a
           resume or fork; otherwise it starts a new tree, since sessions opened in one directory share their
           first items (Codex's environment context and AGENTS.md); the run's taint stays section 4.3's
index      chain hash to node, per run with a call in the last 24 h, in the daemon's sealed state; rebuilt from the
           run's nodes when an older run is continued
reasoning  the reasoning text the router streamed is recorded in the response's node; §8.5's sealed blob now also
           names that node, so a replayed blob, Codex's encrypted_content or Claude Code's thinking signature,
           matches it
order      new request items are journaled before the call goes upstream, and each response item before the
           event that completes it (`response.output_item.done`, `content_block_stop`, the chunk carrying
           `finish_reason`) reaches the harness, which may start a tool on it (IC-19); a retry answered from
           §8.5's ten-minute window records nothing new
search     the hosted search's results are stubs wherever they appear (24.9)
coverage   a run whose model calls the gateway recorded has source gateway; a hook's or telemetry's model_call whose
           request id the gateway never saw marks the gap context_partial, since that call's context is only what
           the transcript shows; a harness not set to the gateway is recorded as DESIGN §16.7 says, with that gap, and `ur status` names it with the command that sets it to the gateway (Q-CTXH-14)
```

What changes for D-GW-2, and what does not:

| | Before CO-25 | Since |
|---|---|---|
| What the gateway writes | a `model_call` per call (§8.9) | the same, with its `CallContext`, and the new items of each request and response as session entries |
| Responses served from storage | none, but D-GW-5's ten-minute retry window | unchanged |
| `store: true`, `previous_response_id` | refused with 400 | unchanged (Q-CTXH-9) |
| Reasoning across turns | a sealed blob the gateway alone opens | unchanged; the blob also names its node |
| Plaintext on disk | none | none: entries are sealed before they leave memory, and the index holds hashes and ids |
| Hooks, telemetry and transcripts | DESIGN §16.7 | unchanged (Q-CTXH-6); a hook's `model_call` merges with the gateway's by request id (§8.9) |

D-GW-2 is amended to say so (§8.11). For these harnesses CO-25 gives every call as the model received it, for review, export and cost by call, and a fork into the Harness: a gateway tree continues as a Harness run, its messages rendered as past turns and the harness's own tools shown as calls the Harness does not offer. Their own resume stays theirs (`claude --resume`, Codex's sessions), from their own files. In an enclave, PiG, Codex and Claude Code run in the agents' container against the enclave's own gateway (§8.7, §11.10), which records their calls the same way and writes the entries into the sponsor's vault as it writes its Harness runs' (24.5), so their history is kept too; every such call is a tainted run's (§11.10), so its nodes carry the tainted bit into any continuation, fork or `record_query`.

### 24.9 The exceptions

| Exception | What is kept instead | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Web search results | §21.6's stub: the call, the number of results, a hash of the answer, the payment and the charge. It holds in every form the daemon writes: the Harness's result and the MCP tool's (§15.2); and, since the gateway serves no search (§21.7), a harness's own copies of an MCP result: in its later requests through the gateway, which §24.8's session entries record, and in its transcript and hook payloads, which DESIGN §16.7's ingest takes; the gateway and the ingest replace each with the stub, matched first by the call that carried it, any result whose tool call names the MCP `web_search` tool in the harness's own form, which holds when a harness cuts a result short or saves it to a file, and then by hashes of what the MCP tool served, which the daemon keeps in its sealed state for the run's life | CO-26: results are not stored, so none answers a later query (Parallel's §2(c)(xi), §21.11). The model's own prose, citing what it used, is output and is kept (§21.6); a continued or forked run that needs the results searches again, a new charge (§21.8) |
| The person's redaction rules | DESIGN §16.7's secret rules (its gitleaks subset, PEM blocks, JWTs, URnetwork's key formats and high-entropy assignments) apply to every node, blob and transcript line before it is sealed, a marker standing where a match was. `record.redact.pii`'s hashing of email addresses and phone numbers does not apply to kinds 54 and 55, which stay in the author's vault, owner-bound and never indexed (24.5), so a resumed or continued run has the addresses the person typed and the attendees a calendar read returned (Q-CTXH-15); it applies where history leaves the member's devices otherwise: `ur harness export` and `ur record export --bodies` hash them in what they write, while a disclosure packet, whose bodies are checked against their commitments (RECORD.md section 11), carries them as sealed, its confirmation counting them | a secret in the record is on every device that opens the run and in every export (Q-CTXH-10); a rebuild marks it, and a continued agent reads it again where it lives; an address is the run's working data, which a marker would take from it |
| `keep: false` | details a built-in tool marks `keep: false` are not recorded, only its stub: today web search alone, whose text and details are both its provider's output; the recorder ignores `keep: false` from any other tool | a third party's terms; no tool can hide its output from the record |
| Mail (§23.11) | `mail_list` and `mail_read` results as references: the mailbox or group repo, each message's id, the call's `start` and `max_chars`, and the SHA-256 of the text the model read; a rebuild re-renders the text from the mailbox and checks that hash, so the call stays exact while the message stands, and after DESIGN §15.7's erasure the node reads as erased and the call inexact; the recorder takes this form from the mail tools alone, and a calendar tool's result is no exception and is kept whole | the mail stays in its mailbox, in EVS already, so erasing a message there leaves no copy in any run (D-MAILCAL-8) |
| A fetched page | no longer an exception: kept whole, every part the extractor made and not only the window the model read, up to the part cap (Q-CTXH-2) | CO-25; the page is the person's own visit |
| Parts past 64 MiB; the run-hour budget | the part's SHA-256 and size, with the gap `oversize` | storage; no context window took such a part whole (Q-CTXH-8) |
| What only a provider sees | nothing: the tokens its chat template made and its cache state are the provider's | out of reach; the record keeps the request as sent (24.6) |

### 24.10 Storage, retention and cost

Record bytes count toward the network's `storage` (DESIGN §16.7, §20.4). By inference, for planning, until §18 measures them, sealed and padded:

| Run | What it holds | Kept |
|---|---|---|
| A Harness task of 30 turns, local or remote | ~150 messages, a ~25 KiB system message, ~8 KiB of results a turn | 0.5-1 MiB |
| A research run with 20 fetches | the pages whole | 1.5-3 MiB |
| An enclave build of 50 turns | `bash` output up to 256 KiB a stream | 3-20 MiB |
| An hour of Codex or Claude Code through the gateway, ~80 calls | ~60 KiB of system and tools once, ~12 KiB of new items a call, side requests | 1.5-3 MiB beside the transcript DESIGN §16.7 already keeps; 25-50 MiB were each request kept whole |
| An enclave agent that works all day | ten to fifty runs like the build above | 30 MiB-1 GiB an enclave-day |

At RECORD.md section 13.2's 10 runs a member-day, five Harness tasks and five hours through the gateway, that is 10-20 MiB a member-day, 2.5-5 GiB a member-year of 260 working days. Against DESIGN §20.4's storage, below the 90% cap and before mail and files take their part: Community's 1 GiB, its one member's share being all of it (below), holds 2-4 months of it, or more than a year at a few light runs a day; Pro's 20 GiB, 3.5-7 years for one person; Team's 200 GiB, 36-72 member-years, so about 2-3.5 years for a Team of 20, whose members' default shares, a tenth each, hold 4-8 years apiece, before metered overage, which stops at 2 TiB. An enclave that works all day is outside that model: at 30 MiB-1 GiB an enclave-day it can fill Community's 1 GiB within a day to a month, which is why the caps below bind, and §18 measures each row. Each byte kept is uploaded once and read again by each device that opens its run, all of it counted toward the transfer balance ([owner decision 10](DESIGN.md#od-10)). Recording takes no compute charge.

**Pushes** bind DESIGN's storage before its bytes do ([owner decision 140](DESIGN.md#od-140)'s drive writes per push): a working member makes about 2,400 a day, DESIGN §19.6 putting the team directory's 36 at 1.5% of them. Session entries ride in the pushes a run's calls already make, each call's `model_call` push, and leave in one of their own only after a minute with no call (24.5), so at 10 runs a member-day, some 550-850 calls, they add by inference a few dozen pushes, 1-2%, where a push of their own at each call would add 550-1,700, 25-70%. An enclave that works all day pushes as a desktop does, its session entries riding its calls' pushes (24.5). §18 measures both.

```text
see       ur status, ur harness runs --size and the apps' run list: context bytes per agent, per enclave and per
          run, blobs apart; at 80% of the network's storage, or of a member's share below, a warning names the
          largest runs and offers one tap that expires the oldest blobs, class bulk, until history is under 70%
          of that cap, and a switch that does so again at each cap; each is the person's own act, confirmed in
          the app or on /dev/tty as retain is, and keeps every node, so runs stay readable and continuable,
          their oldest large parts pruned (after)
caps      two: 90% of the network's storage, and each member's share of it, the `compute` block's (§16.4)
          `"history": {"member_share": "auto"}`, which is all of it in a network of one member and 2/n of it
          in a network of n, and which a Team's Owner or Admin may set from 0.05 to 1 (Q-CTXH-16); a member's
          devices, their agents' enclaves among them (CO-43), enforce both from the vault's totals and the
          network's stored bytes as api reports them. At either cap every
          call is still journaled on the device before it is sent (IC-19); what stops is history leaving it: a
          part that would need a blob is kept by hash and size with an `oversize` gap, and nodes wait in the
          device's spool (DESIGN §16.7's 1 GiB, an enclave's lost with its incarnation, the oldest dropped first
          as spool_drop), pushing once there is room, so a run made past a cap continues only on its own device
          until then; the person is told, with the warning's offer. Mail, repos and the record's other kinds
          keep writing where DESIGN §20.7 would refuse every payload at the limit (Q-CTXH-13). So past a cap
          the newest history waits while the oldest stays whole, until the person frees room
prune     ur record erase --run <id> [--context | --blobs-only]: every entry of the run in the vault, its
          transcript, context, tool call and model call entries included; with --context its session entries and
          blobs; with --blobs-only its blobs alone; erasing a session_entry by id erases its blobs too; each listed
          first, with the run's same_as nodes and the calls whose context it cuts, and confirmed on /dev/tty or in
          an app, never through MCP, as RECORD.md section 8 has every erasure
retain    ur record retention set --log vault --class bulk --keep <days>: blobs expire after that many days and
          the messages stay; class capture likewise for the rest; the vault's default is 0, kept until erased
          (Q-CTXH-7); expiry keeps a node while a live run's path needs it, which the storage view shows
after     a pruned part reads as [pruned: <size>, sha256 <8 hex>] in a rebuild and in a continued run's context,
          and a rebuild counts it unverifiable, not a fault (24.6); an erased node reads as erased; erase lists
          the continued and forked runs whose paths it cuts
```

Compaction saves context, not storage: the messages it replaced stay in the tree.

### 24.11 Privacy

Every node, blob and call context is sealed on the device before it leaves (DESIGN §16.8; IC-2), so URnetwork's servers see what DESIGN §2.8's evs rows show for any record: per entry a token path, a padded size, a key slot and a push time. CO-25 makes the vault's pushes larger and adds writes where a call's context was not kept before, but it adds no field, so §14.6 gains no row. The timing those pushes show was visible before: a Harness run already pushed a `model_call` per call (§7.7), and compute-1 already shows a remote call's sizes and times, so an operator joining the two learns that a sidecar records its calls, which this section states. No server sees a context, an item, a chain hash or a request hash, and the gateway's index stays on the device. Session entries leave in their calls' pushes or at a turn's end (24.5), and the record's Padmé padding applies to them as to any. Two inferences are new, and the disclosures name them: a device fetches a run's entries only when the person opens, continues, forks or exports it (24.7), so its reads show evs which entries it opened and when, and by their push times which run; parts are kept whole and the fetch cap is lifted (24.9), so each large part's padded size shows at its push time, a fetched page's full extracted size among them, which an operator could match against pages whose size it knows (Q-CTXH-12). IC-19 states the rule.

### 24.12 Alternatives considered

| Option | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keep each call's whole request | the simplest rebuild | storage grows with the square of a session's length: 25-50 MiB an hour of Claude Code (24.10) | rejected: the tree and prefix matching |
| Deduplicate on the server across runs and people | the least storage | convergent encryption shows the server which items are equal; content-defined chunking leaks chunk sizes (DESIGN §11.7) | rejected |
| The agent repo as the store | an enclave reads its own agents' runs | readable by the member's other agents (§20.4); outside the record's chains, erasure and retention; a second copy | rejected; it holds no history |
| An `EvsShare` of the vault to an enclave | no packs | every run on a machine a miner holds (§2.6) | superseded by CO-43: the enclave reads the vault as its sponsor's device, which puts every run there, as its disclosure says (§2.8) |
| Context packs (this design before CO-43) | the enclave holds one run, not every run | a pack per run, sealed per incarnation, a confirmation per pack and a rebuild after each loss | removed by CO-43, the enclave reading the vault (24.7) |
| The enclave keeps its runs a second time where it can read them | restarts without a member's device | a second copy outside the record; an agents' enclave reads the vault (CO-43) | rejected |
| Hooks and transcripts alone for external harnesses | exists | no system prompt or tools, and no context after a harness's own edits | kept beside the gateway's entries (Q-CTXH-6) |
| Large parts as vault files | no 64 MiB limit | outside the record's erasure and retention; a part that large never reached a model whole | rejected |
| Serve `previous_response_id` from the record | Agents-SDK clients | the vault's sync a dependency of every call; no harness CO-4 names needs it | Later (§19.5) |

### 24.13 Decisions proposed

**D-CTXH-1 (proposed).** Every Harness run keeps its whole context history in the author's vault: one `session_entry` per message of its session tree, large parts as `session_blob` entries referenced by SHA-256, and each `model_call` naming the messages it read and wrote and its request's hash. *Why:* CO-25; §7.7; I-20.

**D-CTXH-2 (proposed).** Deduplication is the tree's, on the device and within a run: each message written once, calls naming it, the gateway matching requests by chain hash and repeated items by `same_as`; nothing is shared across runs or deduplicated on a server. *Why:* R-CTXH-6; a server that tests items for equality learns about them (DESIGN §11.7).

**D-CTXH-3 (proposed).** Parts are kept whole up to 64 MiB in 8 MiB blobs, §22.7's 64 KiB fetch cap lifted, under DESIGN §16.7's run-hour budget. *Why:* CO-25; Q-CTXH-2; Q-CTXH-8.

**D-CTXH-4 (proposed).** A call's context rebuilds from the record by the renderer it names and is checked against a request hash that covers each part by its own hash, so pruning leaves a call checkable; redactions and stubs mark where it differs from what was sent, and an erased node or pruned part reads as unverifiable, never as a fault. *Why:* R-CTXH-2; Q-CTXH-7's retention.

**D-CTXH-5 (proposed).** A run resumes on its own device and continues or forks on any of the member's devices from the vault, their agents' enclaves among them (CO-43); into an enclave only by the person's act, `ur harness continue`, the app, or `harness_continue` after the person's confirmation or kind 24's approval, and on a new incarnation for the runs a lost one held open; a continuation takes its nodes' taint and `private` mark. *Why:* R-CTXH-4; the vault stays owner-bound, the enclave reading it as its sponsor's device; Q-CTXH-4; Q-CTXH-11.

**D-CTXH-6 (proposed).** The gateway records every call's request and response whole, deduplicated against the run's earlier calls, and stays stateless to its callers (D-GW-2 as amended). *Why:* CO-25; R-GW-6.

**D-CTXH-7 (proposed).** Web search results, matches of DESIGN §16.7's secret rules and `keep: false` details stay out in every form the daemon writes, the gateway's entries and ingested transcripts included. *Why:* CO-26; DESIGN §16.7.

**D-CTXH-8 (proposed).** History is kept until the person erases it; at 90% of the network's storage, or at a member's share of it, by default all of it for one member and 2/n for n, it stops leaving the device, its nodes waiting in the spool and its blobs kept by hash and size, while every call is still journaled first, so mail and repos keep writing; blobs take a retention class of their own, `bulk`, and the person sees and prunes runs by size, the warning offering one tap that expires the oldest blobs. *Why:* CO-25; IC-19; DESIGN §20.4's quotas and §20.7's limit; Q-CTXH-13; Q-CTXH-16.

**D-CTXH-9 (proposed).** A node a tagged sidecar other than the member's own enclave wrote, or that the gateway recorded under a binding it inferred, is untrusted wherever a run takes it into its context or an agent reads it, and taints that run, since such a writer's taint bit is its own word. *Why:* IC-12; Q-HARN-8; I-9; CO-43, which makes the member's enclave one of their devices.

**D-CTXH-10 (proposed).** Session entries sit under their own stream prefix, which a reader may defer while still verifying its writers' chains, and from M11 phones lease per-request approval notices and the inbox prefixes rather than the whole vault. *Why:* RECORD.md section 5.5; DESIGN §16.8 and owner decision 573; I-8.

**D-CTXH-11 (proposed).** Kinds 54 and 55 keep DESIGN §16.7's secret rules but not `record.redact.pii`'s hashing, which applies where history leaves the member's devices otherwise: exports hash, and disclosure packets, which prove bodies by commitment, carry addresses and numbers as sealed, their confirmations counting them; a continued run searches again for results it needs. *Why:* CO-25; a resumed run needs the addresses the person typed; the vault is owner-bound and never indexed; Q-CTXH-15.

**D-CTXH-12 (proposed).** Session entries ride in the pushes their calls' `model_call` entries make, or leave at a turn's end or after 60 s, never in a push of their own at each call; an agents' enclave writes them as any of the member's devices does (CO-43). *Why:* IC-19 needs only the local journal; owner decision 140's drive writes per push.

### 24.14 Questions

**Q-CTXH-1.** Where is the history kept? *Options:* (a) the author's vault, as record entries; (b) each agent's repo; (c) a new repo kind per agent. *Answer:* (a). It is the record: the vault already holds Harness runs (§7.7) under the record's chains, erasure, retention, disclosure and I-20's line, and one copy is cheaper and simpler than two; the agent repo is readable by the member's other agents (§20.4), and a new kind would rebuild what the vault has. An agents' enclave reads the vault as its sponsor's device (24.7). *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-2.** Does CO-25 lift §22.7's 64 KiB cap on a fetched page's text? *Options:* (a) keep the cap; (b) keep the whole `FetchedPage` up to the part cap. *Answer:* (b). The record is the person's own and the page their own visit (§22.7), and the cap was a storage choice, not a term anyone set; an agent that continues a run, or a person reviewing it, gets the page that was read, not its first 64 KiB. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-3.** Does CO-25 override CO-26 on keeping search results? *Options:* (a) yes, keep results sealed in the person's vault; (b) no, stubs. *Answer:* (b). CO-26 answers Parallel's §2(c)(xi) by not storing results, and a sealed copy in the vault is storage that invites answering a later query from it (§21.11, Q-SRCH-9); the agent's prose, citing what it used, is kept, and if the owner ever allows storage, results become blobs like any part, with no format change. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-4.** How does an enclave read a run? *Options:* (a) an `EvsShare` of the vault; (b) a context pack sealed to the incarnation, built by a member's device; (c) the enclave's runs kept a second time in its agent repo; (d) from the vault, as one of its sponsor's devices. *Answer:* (d), since CO-43 makes an agents' enclave one of its sponsor's devices (§11.4): it reads every run from the vault as the member's other devices do. That puts every run on a machine a miner holds (§2.6), which the owner accepted for the initial version and the enclave's disclosure says (§2.8); (b)'s packs are gone with their builds, seals and confirmations (24.7), and (a) and (c) would add a share or a copy for what the enclave reads already. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-5.** Does deduplication reach across runs? *Options:* (a) within a run, with a parent link into an earlier run of the same grant when a harness resumes its own session; (b) across all of a member's runs, by content. *Answer:* (a). Bytes shared across runs would let one run's erasure take another's content, and a person could not erase one run without weighing every other; a parent link can only cut a path, which the rebuild names. The cost is a system prompt and tools stored once per run, about 60 KiB for Claude Code. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-CTXH-6.** With the gateway recording each call, should the transcript tail stop for runs it covers? *Options:* (a) keep both; (b) the gateway's entries replace the transcript. *Answer:* (a). DESIGN §16.7 keeps capture fixed, `record.capture` ignored until a person-only surface exists, and the two say different things: the transcript is the harness's own word, its local commands and its view after its own edits included, and the gateway's entries are what the model received; they differ exactly where the harness rewrote its context, which a reviewer wants to see. The overlap roughly doubles an external run's record (24.10). *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-7.** What retention does the history get by default? *Options:* (a) kept until the person erases it, as the vault keeps everything by default (RECORD.md section 8); (b) blobs expire after 90 days. *Answer:* (a). CO-25 says all, and the vault's owner sets its retention: the storage view warns at 80% of the network's storage and names the largest runs, and one command sets the `bulk` class's life. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-CTXH-8.** How large a part is kept whole? *Options:* (a) 8 MiB, one blob; (b) 64 MiB; (c) no cap. *Answer:* (b), in up to eight 8 MiB blobs, under DESIGN §16.7's 256 MiB a run-hour. No catalog model reads that much in one call, so a larger part never reached a model whole; past it, the hash and size stand, with the `oversize` gap. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-CTXH-9.** Should the gateway now serve `previous_response_id` from the record? *Options:* (a) no, it stays stateless to its callers; (b) yes. *Answer:* (a). Codex and Claude Code send full history and need no stored state; serving from the record would make the vault's sync a dependency of every call and the record a cache. It stays Later (§19.5), its data now kept. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-10.** Is redaction applied though it makes rebuilds inexact? *Options:* (a) yes, as for every entry; (b) keep context unredacted so that rebuilds are exact. *Answer:* (a). DESIGN §16.7 redacts before every seal, and a secret in the record is a secret on every device that opens the run and in every export; a rebuild marks each redaction, and a continued agent that needs the secret reads it again where it lives. Email addresses and phone numbers are not secrets of that kind, and `record.redact.pii`'s hashing spares kinds 54 and 55 (Q-CTXH-15). *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-11.** Who may move a run into an enclave? *Options:* (a) any of the member's sidecars, agents included, with no gate; (b) only the person's act, on an untagged consented device: `ur harness continue --enclave` or the app, each confirmed on /dev/tty or in the app's UI, or an agent's `harness_continue`, which sends only after that confirmation, or after kind 24's approval when the run is tainted or a continued node is flagged or untrusted and the enclave reaches out; and, after a loss, the next incarnation for the runs the last one held open; (c) the person alone, with no agent path. *Answer:* (b). Since CO-43 the enclave reads every run from the vault, so a move carries no data there that it lacks; but it starts work the person pays for, in an enclave whose agents may reach the internet, and a prompt-injected agent that could move any run would do both unasked, so every move waits for the person: a confirmation in the app or on /dev/tty, never an RPC `ui_response`, which a process could answer, and, from a tainted run or with untrusted nodes into an enclave that reaches out, kind 24's approval on another device, which shows the taint, the egress and `ContextFields` (D-HARN-7, §16.3), since the enclave's daemon would otherwise hold those nodes from its container (§7.8). (c) would cost the person who asks their own bot to move a run the same confirmation with an extra step. A shell is no way around it: `ur harness continue --enclave` refuses a caller with a harness ancestor (24.7). *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-12.** Should session blobs be padded past Padmé, so a part's size says less? *Options:* (a) Padmé alone, as every EVS file; (b) pad each blob's content to the next power of two above 64 KiB. *Answer:* (a). Padmé already bounds what a size says to a few percent, and evs sees no URL, so matching a fetched page by its size needs a candidate list and the push time; (b) costs up to twice the bytes of every blob, against the storage that D-CTXH-8's caps ration. 24.11 discloses the inference, and §18's measurements can reopen this. *Decider:* peer review.

**Q-CTXH-13.** CO-25 asks for all history; may it be capped below the network's storage? *Options:* (a) no cap: history may fill the network's storage, where evs refuses every payload, mail included (DESIGN §20.7); (b) history stops at 90% of the network's storage and at each member's share (by default all of it for one member and 2/n for n, Q-CTXH-16), a part past either kept by hash and size with an `oversize` gap and the person told. *Answer:* (b). Under (a) one enclave that works all day fills Community's 1 GiB within days, and in a Team one member's runs stop every member's mail, which no admin can prune, since a vault is its owner's alone (RECORD.md section 8); (b) keeps everything up to the caps, names what it drops, and leaves the person the storage view, pruning and the `bulk` class to make room. *Decider:* owner, confirmed (CO-35).

**Q-CTXH-14.** Does CO-25 reach a harness that calls its own provider rather than the gateway, such as Claude Code on the person's own Anthropic account? *Options:* (a) as far as DESIGN §16.7's capture reaches: its transcript and hooks, the run marked `context_partial`, and `ur status` naming the harness with the command that sets it to the gateway; (b) the gateway forwards to the person's own provider keys, so every call is kept whole; (c) a local TLS-intercepting proxy for the harness's own provider traffic. *Answer:* (a). Only a call that passes through sidecar can be kept as the model received it. (b) reverses Q-GW-4, putting providers outside the catalog's labels, disclosures and budgets behind the gateway and another company's API keys in the daemon; (c) puts a certificate authority into the person's trust store to read their traffic to another company. The Harness's runs, and every call of a harness set to the gateway, which one command does, are kept whole; a harness that keeps its own provider keeps what its transcript shows, and its record says so. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-15.** Should session history be exempt from `record.redact.pii`'s default hashing, so a run resumes with the addresses the person typed? *Options:* (a) no: kinds 54 and 55 hashed as every entry is; (b) yes for kinds 54 and 55, DESIGN §16.7's secret rules kept, the hashing applied where history leaves the member's devices. *Answer:* (b). Hashing before seal makes every resumed or continued run lose each address and number the person typed or a tool read ("invite bob@example.com" becomes a marker, and so does every attendee a calendar read returned), which a phone meets at every app death, while the vault already keeps them owner-bound, sealed and out of every index; secrets stay redacted, since a secret in the record is on every device that opens the run. `ur harness export` and `ur record export --bodies` hash them in what they write. A disclosure packet proves each body by its commitment, so it cannot hash without breaking the proof: it carries them as sealed, and its confirmation counts them, so the person chooses. This narrows [owner decision 452](DESIGN.md#od-452)'s default for two new kinds. *Decider:* owner.

**Q-CTXH-16.** What is a member's default share of the network's storage for history? *Options:* (a) half, whatever the network's size; (b) all of it in a network of one member and 2/n of it in a network of n, which a Team's Owner or Admin may set from 0.05 to 1. *Answer:* (b). Half keeps a one-person network's history to 512 MiB of Community's 1 GiB, one to two and a half months at 24.10's rates, though the 90% cap already keeps room for its mail, and lets one member of a Team of 20 take 100 GiB of its 200; 2/n lets each member use twice an even split, the 90% cap still keeping mail and repos writing. Q-CTXH-13's caps stand as confirmed (CO-35); only the share's default changes. *Decider:* owner.

### 24.15 Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| History fills a network's storage, Community's above all | high | without the caps, every EVS write of the network refused, mail included (DESIGN §20.7) | the caps at 90% and each member's share; the storage view and its warning, whose one tap expires the oldest blobs; pruning and the `bulk` class (24.10); deduplication; the run-hour budget |
| An enclave, compromised, writes nodes that look untainted | low | injected text in a run continued elsewhere | its Harness keeps taint outside the agents' container, and every tool that touches the container taints its run (§7.8); a compromised enclave is a compromised device of the member, revoked as one (§11.4); another member's enclave's nodes stay untrusted (IC-12) |
| A `ur_continue` replayed | low | a run continued twice, unasked | each carries its confirmation's or approval's id, which the enclave refuses a second time (24.7) |
| A renderer change breaks the rebuild of older calls | medium | old calls read as differing | renderers kept by id; §18's goldens on every release |
| A harness changes its request shape between releases, breaking prefix matches | high | more storage, never less history | `same_as` bounds the cost to node headers; §18's conformance per harness release |
| Search result text slips into an entry by a form the matcher misses | medium | a result stored, against CO-26's footing | stubs matched by hashes of what the MCP tool and the Harness served; §18's corpus of synthetic results with marker strings |
| Secrets in context that the redaction rules miss | medium | a secret on every device that opens the run | DESIGN §16.7's rules and the person's `pii` setting; erasure; the person's own enclaves hold what their devices hold (CO-43) |
| Addresses and phone numbers kept as typed (Q-CTXH-15) | high | on every device of the member that opens the run, their enclaves among them, and in a disclosure | the vault, owner-bound, sealed and never indexed; hashed at export; counted on a disclosure's confirmation (24.9) |
| A phone opening a large run | medium | transfer and storage | fetched on demand; blobs only when a node is shown or rebuilt |
| Journal first adds latency to each call | low | an fsync before each call | batched with the call's other entries |

### 24.16 Tests

- **Rebuild.** Every call of a corpus of Harness runs, on local and remote models, with compactions, branches, model and effort changes, sub-agents and retries, rebuilds from the vault to its `request_sha256`; calls with redactions or stubs differ exactly at their marked nodes, and calls with pruned parts or erased nodes read as unverifiable there, without an alarm.
- **Deduplication.** A 200-call Codex session and a Claude Code session through the gateway store each item once, their recorded bytes within 1.2 times the distinct items'; a compaction and a cleared tool result branch at the first changed item; replayed reasoning blobs match their nodes; side requests and sub-agents land as their own trees; a second Codex session in the same directory starts its own tree, not a resume; a call bound by time alone records its entries flagged while any live run of its grant is tainted.
- **Completeness.** The daemon killed between journal and call and between response and tool, and an enclave's VM destroyed mid-turn: every call made has its context in the record, and a lost response is a coverage gap; a tool Codex starts from `response.output_item.done` finds that item already journaled; an enclave's session entries written to the vault in its calls' pushes, as a desktop's are; session entries leave in their calls' `model_call` pushes, at a turn's end or after a minute, never in a push of their own at each call.
- **Continue and fork.** On a second desktop, a phone test app and the member's enclave, from the vault; a phone continuing a desktop's run on a smaller model, its `model_change` recorded; flagged nodes carry taint, and so do nodes another member's enclave wrote with its bit cleared, and marked nodes the `private` mark; erasing a source run shows erased nodes in its forks' rebuilds; a phone that syncs the vault fetches no session entry until a run opens, verifies each deferred entry when it fetches it, and wakes for approval notices, not for session pushes.
- **Into an enclave.** `ur harness continue --enclave` under a harness ancestor is refused; `harness_continue` sends nothing before the person's confirmation, an RPC `ui_response` never counting, and from a tainted run or with untrusted nodes into an enclave with egress waits for kind 24, whose `ContextFields` match the run sent; a replayed `ur_continue` is refused; a continued run that holds the member's mail starts with the `private` mark.
- **Web search.** Synthetic results carrying marker strings, built from Parallel's documented schema (§21.11), appear in no node, blob or transcript entry, through the Harness and through the MCP tool, whose results Codex and Claude Code carry into their requests through the gateway and into their transcripts.
- **Caps and settings.** A 9 MiB result is two blobs; a 65 MiB part is kept by hash and size with `oversize`; the run-hour budget holds; `keep: false` from a non-built-in tool is ignored; history stops leaving the device at 90% of the network's storage and at a member's share, every call still journaled, its nodes pushing from the spool once the one-tap expiry frees room, while mail keeps landing; `member_share` all of the storage for one member and 2/n for n.
- **Privacy.** DESIGN §22.7's metadata guard finds no new server field.
- **Erasure and export.** `ur record erase --run` leaves no entry of the run; erasing a node erases its blobs and lists its `same_as` dependents; expiry keeps a node a live run's path needs; `ur harness export` needs RECORD.md section 9's confirmation and writes its `disclosure` entry first; `ur harness show` prints stubs off a terminal; a run resumed after its daemon is killed, and on a phone after the app is closed, keeps the address the person typed and a calendar read's attendees, while `ur harness export` hashes them under `record.redact.pii` and a pack's confirmation counts them.
- **Sizes.** Each row of 24.10's table measured on its corpus, its bytes per run set against the estimate.

### 24.17 Phasing

M11: the two kinds, the Harness's recording, call contexts and rebuilds, resume, continue and fork across the member's devices, `ur harness runs`, `show` and `continue`, the storage view, its caps and pruning, the `s/` prefix and deferred reading, and per-request approval notices for phones (D-CTXH-10). M12: the gateway's recording for Responses and Chat Completions, with Codex. M13: Messages, with Claude Code, and search stubs in the gateway's entries and ingested transcripts, with web search. M14: continuing runs in enclaves, which read them from the vault as their sponsors' devices (CO-43). §19.

## 25. Connected services

### 25.1 Purpose and scope

This section designs CO-36 and CO-37: the Harness knows how to connect a person's account at an OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect (OIDC) service, such as Google Calendar, and every OAuth credential a connection holds is stored in EVS. It generalizes §23.6's OAuth forms into one mechanism: a signed list of service definitions (25.4); a connection that only the person makes, on their own device, where its redirect lands (25.5); one owner-bound `secret` repo per connection, holding its record and every credential it has (25.6); typed tools, the calendar's first, beside a generic `service_call` to which the daemon attaches the token (25.9); and outward action 26 for a tainted run's writes and sends, a write decided first by the device's safety classifier in auto mode (§27), while a run that has read nothing untrusted needs no approval (CO-40; 25.10). Google and Microsoft come first, and the calendar's `google` and `microsoft` forms become connections (25.13). No URnetwork server sees a redirect, a code, a token or a result, and no agent sees a credential (I-7). Enclaves and tagged sidecars get no connection (Q-CONN-5).

The owner's words, 2026-11-23:

> CO-36: "Generally the harness should know how to auth OIDC connect services like Google Calendar"
>
> CO-37: "oauth credentials should be stored in evs"

### 25.2 Requirements

| Id | Requirement | Source |
|---|---|---|
| R-CONN-1 | The Harness and the apps connect a person's account at OAuth 2.0 and OIDC services from a signed list of definitions, Google's and Microsoft's first; a new service takes a policy update, never a release | CO-36 |
| R-CONN-2 | Only a person starts and completes a connection, on their own approval-capable device, in the system browser, with PKCE, `state` and, for OIDC, `nonce` and the ID token's checks; an agent may ask for one and never answers | CO-36; I-8; RFC 8252; RFC 9700 |
| R-CONN-3 | The redirect lands on the device; no URnetwork server sees an OAuth redirect, code or token | the directive |
| R-CONN-4 | Every OAuth credential a connection holds, with its record, is stored in EVS in an owner-bound `secret` repo, a rotated token written back at once, so every consented device of the member uses the same connection and losing a device loses none | CO-37 |
| R-CONN-5 | No credential enters an agent's context, a tool result, a record entry, an approval, an error or a log | I-7 |
| R-CONN-6 | A connection asks for the narrowest scopes of the features the person picks, and for more only when the person adds a feature | Google's OAuth policies; derived |
| R-CONN-7 | What a service returns is untrusted and taints the run | I-9 |
| R-CONN-8 | A write or send from a tainted run waits for approval: the device's safety classifier decides a write first in auto mode, and a person every send and every call the definition does not classify; a run that has read nothing untrusted calls without approval once the person has connected the service | I-8, I-9; CO-40 |
| R-CONN-9 | Calls leave through URnetwork's network, so the provider sees an exit's address, one exit per connection, unless `direct` was chosen for it (Q-CONN-16) | the directive; IC-7 |
| R-CONN-10 | A person can disconnect a service, revoking it at the provider where the provider allows, and is asked to replace a connection after any revocation of a device that could read it | derived from §23.6 |
| R-CONN-11 | The calendar's `google` and `microsoft` forms are connections | CO-36 |
| R-CONN-12 | A connection's tokens, and a calendar link's secret, open only on the member's own devices that use them, never on a Team's audit reader or a device of another platform, and a member who leaves has them revoked at the provider | CO-37; I-7; derived (Q-CONN-15) |

### 25.3 What the protocols and providers require (2026-11-23)

| Source | What it says |
|---|---|
| RFC 8252, OAuth for native apps | apps "MUST use an external user-agent", never an embedded one; three redirects: a private-use scheme on a reversed domain the app controls, a claimed `https` URI, which apps "SHOULD use … over the other options where possible", and the loopback `http://127.0.0.1:{port}/{path}`, where the server "MUST allow any port" and `localhost` is "NOT RECOMMENDED"; PKCE required; a secret built into a distributed app is not confidential [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252] |
| RFC 9700, OAuth security BCP (January 2025) | public clients "MUST use PKCE"; their refresh tokens "MUST be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation", and under rotation a reused old token makes the server "revoke the active refresh token"; a client of several servers defends against mix-up with RFC 9207's `iss` or a redirect per issuer; exact redirect matching, loopback ports aside; `state` spent at first use [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700] |
| RFC 9207, issuer identification | the authorization response carries `iss`, and a client "MUST reject" one that differs from the issuer it expects [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9207]; Google's discovery says it sends it, Microsoft's does not [https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration] [https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration] |
| RFC 7009, revocation | revoking a refresh token "SHOULD also invalidate all access tokens based on the same authorization grant"; an unknown token answers 200 [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009] |
| OIDC Core 1.0 and Discovery 1.0 | the ID token's `iss` "MUST exactly match" the issuer, `aud` holds the client id, `nonce` is checked, and one taken straight from the token endpoint over TLS may be checked by TLS in place of its signature; `sub` and `iss` together are "the only Claims that an RP can rely upon" as a stable identifier, `email` not [https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html]; discovery lives at `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`, whose `issuer` "MUST be identical" to the URL used [https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html] |
| Google, desktops | loopback on "a random available port"; custom schemes "no longer supported on Android and Chrome apps"; loopback "DEPRECATED for Android, Chrome app and iOS" clients; "Always use PKCE"; "refresh tokens are always returned for installed applications"; "Incremental authorization is not supported for installed apps"; desktop apps "cannot keep secrets"; revocation at `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/revoke`, of an access or a refresh token [https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/native-app] |
| Google, iOS and Android | iOS takes the redirect on the client's reversed-client-id URL scheme [https://developers.google.com/identity/sign-in/ios/api-access]; Android's `AuthorizationClient` returns access tokens with "a lifespan of one hour", fetched again "without any user interaction", a refresh token only through a server's exchange, and "Don't store refresh tokens on the device"; its result names no account; `revokeAccess()` "revokes all scopes previously granted" [https://developer.android.com/identity/authorization] |
| Google, policies | "a separate OAuth client for each platform"; no embedded user-agent; "the smallest set of scopes"; scopes "in context"; "always store encrypted tokens at rest" [https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/policies]; a person may grant some of the scopes asked and not others, so an app checks what was granted [https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/resources/granular-permissions]; 100 refresh tokens per account per client, a new one invalidating the oldest "without warning", and a token unused for six months lapses [https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2]; Workspace API data may not be used "to create, train, or improve a machine learning or artificial intelligence model beyond that specific user's personalized model" [https://developers.google.com/workspace/workspace-api-user-data-developer-policy]; restricted scopes take a CASA assessment "at least every 12 months" where their data is stored or sent on servers [https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification] |
| Google, Limited Use | data from its scopes may serve only "user-facing features that are prominent in the requesting application's user interface"; "Transfers of data are not allowed, except" to provide such features "and only with the user's consent", for security, to comply with law, or in a merger; "Don't allow humans to read the data" without the user's "affirmative agreement", security, law or aggregated internal use; and these rules "apply to the raw data obtained from the scopes and data aggregated, anonymized, or derived from them" [https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy] |
| Google, clients and quota | a Desktop client's `client_secret` is listed as optional at the token exchange and at refresh, and "Desktop apps are public clients and cannot keep secrets confidential"; a deleted client answers `deleted_client`, and a Workspace administrator's restriction `admin_policy_enforced` [https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/native-app]; "You must never commit client credentials into publicly available code repositories", and a developer "must create separate projects in the Google Cloud Console for each deployment tier, such as development, staging, and production" [https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/policies]; the Calendar API allows 10,000 requests a minute a project and 600 a minute per user in a project, answering `403` or `429` `usageLimits` past either, and an increase may be asked for and refused [https://developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/guides/quota] |
| Microsoft | the auth code flow with PKCE for desktop and mobile apps; a refresh token "Only provided if `offline_access` scope was requested"; tenants `common`, `organizations`, `consumers` or an id; `response_mode` `query`, `fragment` or `form_post` [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-auth-code-flow]; loopback ports ignored in matching, `127.0.0.1` preferred to `localhost`, `[::1]` unsupported [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/reply-url]; refresh tokens "bound to a combination of user and client", 90 days, replaced at every use, old ones not revoked: "Securely delete the old refresh token after acquiring a new one" [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/refresh-tokens]; discovery's issuer is the template `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantid}/v2.0`, with no revocation endpoint [https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration]; a work or school user revokes in My Apps what they consented to, never what an administrator did [https://support.microsoft.com/en-US/accounts-billing/work-school/edit-or-revoke-application-permissions-in-the-my-apps-portal]; ID Protection flags a refresh token "played from an unfamiliar location", and scores unfamiliar sign-in properties on non-interactive sign-ins [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks] |
| Microsoft, refusals | Entra answers with AADSTS codes: 65001 `DelegationDoesNotExist`, 90094 `AdminConsentRequired` and 90095 (the admin consent workflow), 65004 `UserDeclinedConsent`, 50105 `EntitlementGrantsNotFound` (the user is not assigned the app), 53000 `DeviceNotCompliant`, 53001 `DeviceNotDomainJoined`, 53003 `BlockedByConditionalAccess`, 50131 `ConditionalAccessFailed`, 50076 and 50079 (multifactor authentication required), 7000112 `UnauthorizedClientApplicationDisabled`, and at a refresh 700082 (expired by inactivity), 70043 (sign-in frequency) and 50173 (the grant revoked, as by a password change) [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes] |
| The platforms' browsers | `ASWebAuthenticationSession.Callback` (iOS 17.4, macOS 14.4) matches a custom scheme or an `https` host and path and passes the URL to the session's handler [https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/aswebauthenticationsession/callback]; Chrome's Auth Tab (Chrome 137 and later) captures the redirect and returns it to the app, an `https` callback needing Digital Asset Links verification, and other browsers fall back to a Custom Tab [https://developer.chrome.com/docs/android/custom-tabs/guide-auth-tab]; `DomainVerificationManager` tells an app whether its App Links hosts are verified [https://developer.android.com/training/app-links/verify-android-applinks] |

So a redirect can always land on the device; Google binds tokens to a client per platform and keeps refresh tokens off Android devices, while Microsoft's one client serves every platform with a rotating token; neither should need a client secret from a native app, though Google issues its Desktop clients one (25.4); a provider that scores sign-ins can read a changing address as a stolen token; and a work tenant may refuse URnetwork's app whatever its publisher's status, for want of an administrator's consent, a managed device or a trusted address (25.5).

### 25.4 Service definitions

```text
ServiceDefinition, one per id in the signed policy's services (§5.4); a person's own in its connection's record
  id, name        [a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,23} (google, microsoft), and the name the apps show
  issuer          the OIDC issuer, its endpoints read from <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration; for a provider
                  without OIDC, RFC 8414's metadata or explicit authorization, token, revocation and userinfo
                  endpoints; iss_template where the issuer names a tenant (Microsoft's {tenantid}, from tid)
  hosts           the hosts an endpoint may be on; discovery that names another is refused
  clients         per platform (desktop, ios, android): URnetwork's public client id and its redirect: loopback;
                  an ios callback (a scheme, or an https host and path); android_authorization (Google's
                  AuthorizationClient); or an android App Link with an optional private-use scheme. A client
                  secret only where a provider requires one of a native client, which RFC 8252 section 8.5
                  treats as public: Google's Desktop client's, should G-CONN-google find its token endpoint
                  needs the secret Google issues it, kept in URnetwork's vault and written into the policy at
                  signing, never into a repository (25.3)
  binding         per_platform: a refresh token serves only devices of the platform whose client minted it;
                  per_client: one serves every device
  offline         how a refresh token is asked for: a scope (offline_access) or nothing (Google's installed apps)
  identity        the scopes that name the account (openid, email), and the claim the apps show
  features        per feature: its name, its scopes, the typed tools that use it, its words for the consent
                  screen; no scope that no feature names is ever asked for
  api_hosts       the hosts the tools may call, https on 443, and the default one
  rules           service_call's classes by method and path pattern (25.10): read, write, send, typed (naming its
                  tool, for every method on its paths, reads included) or refused, each naming the feature it
                  needs; a refused rule wins over every other; patterns match the canonical path (25.9),
                  case-folded for an API whose paths are case-insensitive (Graph's); a GET or HEAD no rule
                  names is read, and any other method no rule names is send
  mask            response fields that carry a credential, such as a pre-authenticated download URL
  rotation        none; rotating (a new refresh token at each refresh, old ones still valid); or strict (a
                  reused old token revokes the grant)
  revocation      rfc7009 with its endpoint; android_revoke_access; or none, with the page where a person
                  removes the app
  model_rule      any, or limited_use (25.10)
  egress          the default route of its calls: auto, unless its gate's 30-day exit test made it direct
                  (§19.2, Q-CONN-16)
  gate            G-CONN-<id> (§19.2); the disclosure is connect:<id> (25.12)
```

The first two:

| | `google` | `microsoft` |
|---|---|---|
| Issuer | `https://accounts.google.com`, by discovery; `iss` may also be `accounts.google.com`, as Google allows | `https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/v2.0`, by discovery; `iss` the template with the token's `tid` |
| Endpoint hosts | `accounts.google.com`, `oauth2.googleapis.com`, `openidconnect.googleapis.com` | `login.microsoftonline.com`; `graph.microsoft.com` for userinfo |
| Clients | three in one Google Cloud project: Desktop, iOS and Android | one app registration, a public client for work, school and personal accounts |
| Desktops | loopback, `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/cb/google` | loopback, `http://127.0.0.1/cb/microsoft`, its port ignored in matching |
| iOS | the reversed-client-id scheme, in `ASWebAuthenticationSession` | a private-use scheme on the app's bundle id, in `ASWebAuthenticationSession` |
| Android | `AuthorizationClient`: no redirect, no refresh token | the App Link in Chrome's Auth Tab, else the private-use scheme (Q-CONN-6) |
| Binding | `per_platform`: a Desktop token and an iOS token | `per_client`: one token |
| Offline | always, for installed apps | `offline_access` |
| Identity | `openid email` | `openid profile` |
| Feature `calendar` | `calendar.events.owned`, `calendar.calendarlist.readonly` (§23.6) | `Calendars.ReadWrite` |
| API hosts | `www.googleapis.com` | `graph.microsoft.com` |
| Typed rules | every method on `/calendar/v3/` and below: the calendar tools | every method on any `…/events`, `…/calendarView`, `…/calendars` and `…/calendarGroups` path and below, under `/me` or `/users/{id}`, the invitation actions included: the calendar tools |
| Refused | every `watch` path, `/calendar/v3/channels/stop` and every `acl` path (sharing) | `/subscriptions` and below, any `…/calendarPermissions` path and any `…/permissions` path (sharing) |
| Rotation | `none` | `rotating` |
| Revocation | `rfc7009`; on Android, `revokeAccess()` | `none`: My Apps for work and school accounts, the account's own settings for personal ones |
| Model rule | `limited_use`, by Google's Limited Use rules and its Workspace API policy (25.3, Q-CONN-9) | `any` |
| Default egress | `auto` until G-CONN-google's exit test says otherwise (Q-CONN-16) | `auto` until G-CONN-microsoft's exit test says otherwise (Q-CONN-16) |
| Gate | G-CONN-google | G-CONN-microsoft |

**Adding a service** (Q-CONN-1). A policy update, never a release: URnetwork registers its public clients with the provider, passes the provider's own review where it has one (the gate, §19.2), writes the definition, its rules and its disclosure text, and the two policy signers sign a new policy, which devices take as they take any (§5.4). Staging's definitions name clients in projects of their own, with their own test users, as Google requires of each deployment tier (25.3), so tests never spend production's quota or touch its verification. A definition only narrows a connection made under an older one: a token goes only to API hosts that both the current definition and the connection's record list (25.6). Typed tools ship in releases; until a service has them, `service_call` serves it (Q-CONN-3). A policy past its `not_after` stops remote inference (§5.4), not connections, since a definition names only the person's own provider's hosts. A network's policy chooses which services its members may connect for agents (§16.4).

**A person's own definition** (Q-CONN-2). On a desktop, `ur connect --issuer <url> --client-id <id> --api-host <host>… --scope <s>…` connects a provider no policy lists, such as a self-hosted Keycloak, Authentik, Forgejo or Nextcloud. The device reads the issuer's OIDC discovery, else RFC 8414's `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`; refuses an issuer that is not `https` or does not offer S256 PKCE; shows the issuer, the endpoints' hosts, the scopes and the API hosts on `/dev/tty`; and, once the person confirms, runs 25.5's flow with the loopback redirect the person registered for their own client. The definition lives in the connection's record, which no one else reads; its rules are the defaults alone, so every call that is not a `GET` or `HEAD` is a send, W in an untainted run (CO-40) and kind 26 in a tainted one, where it always goes to the person (25.10, §27.7); its model rule is `any`, and its disclosure `connect:custom` (25.12); a client secret the person's provider issued for that client lives only in the record too (25.6). An issuer at a private name of the network is reached over the overlay with its certificate pinned at save, as §23.7 reaches a calendar at home.

### 25.5 Connecting

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| Who | a person, on their own device that is approval-capable and not read_only: the apps' Connected services screen (§15.4), or `ur connect <service>` confirmed on `/dev/tty` (DESIGN §16.6's control mode); never an agent, a tagged sidecar, an enclave, an MCP session or an RPC client |
| An agent's request | `connection_request` (25.9) shows the person a card, a `ui_request` of kind `connect` (§7.6) naming the service, the features with their scopes in words, and the agent's reason as its claim; only the person's own input, a tap in the app or an answer on `/dev/tty`, answers it, never a `ui_response` from a run or over an attach link (§7.10); the agent learns `connected` with the label, `declined` or `pending` |
| Before | the device holds the newest policy's definition; the disclosure `connect:<service>` is acknowledged at its current version, the connect sheet or `ur connect` showing its whole text and taking the person's acknowledgment first where it is not (25.12); the person picks features, and the request asks for their scopes and the identity scopes, nothing else |
| The request | made in memory: a PKCE verifier of 32 random bytes and its S256 challenge (RFC 7636), a `state` and a `nonce` of 16 random bytes each, single use, kept at most 10 minutes; `login_hint` with the account when adding a feature or replacing a connection; Microsoft's `prompt=select_account` for a second account |
| Desktops | the daemon, or a desktop app's sdk, binds `127.0.0.1` on a random port, opens the system browser at the authorization URL, takes one request on `/cb/<service>`, answers a static page with no script, and closes the port; a machine with no browser cannot connect, and uses a connection another device made, from EVS |
| iOS | `ASWebAuthenticationSession` with the definition's callback, which the session matches itself and hands only to the app |
| Android | Google: `AuthorizationClient` for the account the person picks, no redirect and no refresh token (CO-35). Other services: the App Link in Chrome's Auth Tab, which captures the redirect without loading it, used only while `DomainVerificationManager` reports the host verified for the app; with no Auth Tab, the definition's private-use scheme in a Custom Tab, PKCE making a code another app catches useless; with neither, the person connects on another device and the phone uses that connection from EVS (Q-CONN-6) |
| The redirect | lands on the device: the loopback port, the session's callback, the Auth Tab's capture or the app's scheme, never a URnetwork host. The App Links host, `oauth.ur.io`, serves only `/.well-known/assetlinks.json` and answers everything else `404`, logging no path or query, so nothing but that file is ever asked of it |
| Checks | `state` equal to the flow's, then spent; RFC 9207's `iss` equal to the issuer where the provider sends it (Google); the redirect path names the service, so a code from one issuer is never redeemed at another (RFC 9700's mix-up defense); an `error` ends the flow, showing its code but not its description, which the provider's page wrote |
| Organizations' refusals | an organization can refuse URnetwork's app whatever its publisher's status, so the flow's error maps to a text that names the fix, never the provider's description: Entra's 65001, 90094 or 90095, "your organization lets only an administrator approve URnetwork's app: ask your IT administrator", with the admin-consent link; 50105, "your administrator has not assigned you URnetwork's app"; 53000 or 53001, "your organization allows this account only on its managed devices"; 53003 or 50131, "your organization's sign-in policy refused this connection", naming `direct` where the person's own address may pass (Q-CONN-16), else the administrator; 7000112, "your organization has turned URnetwork's app off"; 50076 or 50079, a sign-in again with multifactor authentication; 65004 and Google's `access_denied`, declined; Google's `admin_policy_enforced`, "your Workspace administrator must allow URnetwork's app" (25.3). Expected Microsoft coverage: personal accounts, and work or school tenants that let a user consent to a verified publisher's app for `Calendars.ReadWrite` and set no Conditional Access policy that the device or its address fails |
| The exchange | the code, the verifier and the redirect to the definition's token endpoint, through the egress, from the exit the connection will keep (25.8); for URnetwork's clients no client secret, but the Desktop client's where the definition carries one (25.4) |
| The ID token | taken from the token endpoint over TLS, which stands in for its signature (OIDC Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7, step 6): `iss` exactly the issuer, or the template filled with the token's `tid`; `aud` the client id; `azp`, where present, the client id; `exp` ahead; `iat` within 10 minutes; `nonce` the flow's. Android's Google path has none: the device asks `openid email` with the feature's scopes and reads `sub` and `email` from the userinfo endpoint |
| Scopes granted | the token response's `scope`, which may be fewer than asked; a feature missing any of its scopes stays off, and the screen says which |
| Saved | 25.6's record and tokens, written to the connection's new `secret` repo before any token is used; then the `connection` event (25.11), and the asking agent learns the label |
| Adding a feature | the same flow for the union of the connection's scopes and the feature's, with `login_hint`, since Google's installed apps have no incremental authorization; the new ID token's `sub` must equal the record's, else the grant is refused as another account's; the new refresh token replaces the old, which is dropped rather than revoked, so no revocation reaches the grant the new one carries |
| Another account | a second connection to the same service, with its own label and repo |

CF-19 (§3.4), "connect my Google Calendar":

```text
person    the apps' Connected services screen, or ur connect google confirmed on /dev/tty; or an agent's
          connection_request card, which only the person's own tap or terminal answers
device    the newest definition; disclosure connect:google at its version; features → scopes
          PKCE verifier and S256 challenge, state, nonce, in memory for at most 10 minutes
browser   the system browser, outside the egress: the provider's sign-in and consent, from the person's address
          (desktop: the loopback port; iOS: ASWebAuthenticationSession; Android: AuthorizationClient or Auth Tab)
device    ◀─ the redirect, on the device: state spent, iss checked where sent, the path naming the issuer
          DoH and connect through the egress, from the exit the connection will keep ─▶ the token endpoint:
          code + verifier ◀─ refresh and access tokens, ID token, granted scopes
          the ID token's iss, aud, azp, exp, iat, nonce; features on by the scopes granted
          connection.json, the record and the refresh token, into a new secret repo with no label
Harness   the connection event; the asking agent learns the label; from here tools attach tokens in the daemon
```

### 25.6 Where a connection is kept

```text
Connection v1, JSON, the one file (connection.json, versionless) of a secret repo with no label in the config
  label         [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,31}: the person's name for it ("personal", "work"), kept only here
  service       the definition's id and the policy version it was made under; for a person's own definition
                (25.4), the definition itself
  issuer        the issuer the ID token named (Microsoft's with its tenant), and the endpoints used
  account       the account's display name (an email or user principal name) and, where the issuer names one,
                its tenant
  subject       the ID token's or userinfo's sub: with issuer, the connection's identity (OIDC Core section 5.7)
  features      the features the person chose, each on or off by the scopes granted
  scopes        the scopes the provider reported granted, and for each token entry below the scopes granted
                to it: a feature is on for a platform only where that platform's token holds its scopes, the
                screen offering Add feature there
  api_hosts     the API hosts shown at connect; calls go only to hosts here and in the current definition
  tokens        per client: {platform (desktop, ios or any), client_id, refresh_token, issued}: Google's desktop
                and ios entries, Microsoft's one any entry, none for a Google account only Android connected
  client_secret any secret the connection's client needs: a person's own client's, where their provider
                issued one; for URnetwork's clients none today, and a copy of the definition's should a
                provider ever require one
  egress        auto, or direct where the person or the policy chose it (25.8, Q-CONN-16)
  exit          under auto, the exit the connection keeps (25.8): its provider's client id, its country and
                when it was chosen, and the changes in the last 30 days
  generic       whether service_call may use it (25.9)
  state         active, rejected (a refresh answered invalid_grant), suspended (the provider refused
                URnetwork's client itself, 25.7) or removed
  refreshing    for a strict definition: the device refreshing and until when (25.7)
  saved         the device that connected it and when; the device and time of the last write
```

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| What EVS holds (CO-37) | every OAuth credential the connection holds: its refresh tokens, its per-platform tokens, any client secret that applies, and the record above; no credential lives only on one device's disk, so every consented device of the member uses the same connection, and losing a device loses none |
| Where | one `secret` repo per connection, since a `secret` holds one secret (DESIGN §8.5): owner-bound, created by the connecting device, with no label or display name in the config repo, which every admitted sidecar reads (DESIGN §7.9, §11.12), so other members' devices, tagged sidecars and other members' enclaves see one more `secret` repo id and nothing of the connection; at most 16 a member; `connection.json` versionless (DESIGN §11.7), so a rotated token leaves no history |
| Write-back | a refresh that returns a new refresh token writes it to `connection.json` before the new access token is used, so a crash loses no grant: at every refresh for a `strict` definition, under 25.7's lease, and for a `rotating` one, whose old tokens stay valid (Microsoft), only once the stored token is 7 days old, so an hour of agents' refreshes shows storage no write; every write is conditional on the content it read, and one that loses rereads and keeps the newer token |
| Access tokens | derived from the refresh token and short-lived (an hour at Google and Microsoft), they live only in the memory of the daemon or app process that refreshed them, never written to disk or EVS (Q-CONN-4); a device that restarts refreshes from EVS |
| Google on Android | `AuthorizationClient` gives the phone access tokens for its Google account, and Google issues it no refresh token (CO-35, Q-MAILCAL-13). EVS holds that connection's record, with the account, the subject and the scopes (and, for the calendar, the link's calendar id, §23.6), and no long-lived credential exists to hold: CO-37's rule holds here as for every connection, every credential that exists being in EVS and the access token derived and short-lived |
| Never shared; read by the person's enclaves | `ur` and the apps file no `EvsShare` of a connection's repo, so no other tagged sidecar, a cloud agent or the network's indexer enclave, reads one; MCP's evs, search and `ur://evs` surfaces refuse the kind (DESIGN §16.6); the member's agents' enclaves read it as their other devices do, being among them (CO-42, CO-43, §11.4), their daemons attaching its tokens outside the agents' container (25.8), so no token enters a container or an agent's context: an enclave's creation, after its disclosure says it holds what the person's devices hold (§2.8), is the share, and nothing more is filed; in a Team whose `audit` block names `kind:secret`, the audit reader holds the repo and reads the record, its service, account, features and scopes, but opens no token (below), which the connect screen says |
| Readers | the member's consented devices, desktops' daemons, phones' apps and the member's agents' enclaves alike, each reading its synced copy at each call, opening the token sealed to it and holding it in memory for that call and its refresh |
| Sealed to the devices that use them (Q-CONN-15) | inside the repo, each token, and any `client_secret` of a person's own client, is sealed again with HPKE-XWing (DESIGN §10.5), its info naming the repo and the client, once for each of the member's consented devices that uses it, their agents' enclaves' incarnations among them, to that device's ReaderKey under DESIGN §10.5's delivery rule: a Google Desktop token for each desktop and each enclave, an iOS token for each iPhone and iPad, Microsoft's one token and a person's own client's for each device; so a Team's audit reader, another tagged sidecar and a device of another platform open none. The device that writes a token seals it for itself and for every device that has an entry; a device that has none, a new one or one whose ReaderKey lapsed, asks by writing a file into the repo that names itself and its platform, and any device that holds the token seals it one at its next sync, the asker meanwhile answering as Use on this device does (25.7); a device re-seals its own entry to its newest ReaderKey as it opens it, and keeps a ReaderKey's private half while an entry is sealed to it; every write is an `EXACT_HEAD` push on the version read (DESIGN §11.7, §11.8), so none drops another's entry. A lost device holds only its own entries, so Replace (25.7) revokes at Google only its platform's token; a calendar link's secret is sealed the same way (§23.6) |
| At rest | EVS keeps the repo only as ciphertext, on every device and server, as Google asks ("always store encrypted tokens at rest") |

### 25.7 Tokens in use, rotation, revocation and loss

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| Refresh | when a device has no access token, holds one within 2 minutes of its expiry, or gets a `401`: it refreshes through the connection's exit (25.8); a refresh answering `invalid_grant`, or a `401` with a fresh token, marks the connection `rejected`, and the apps ask the person to reconnect |
| Per platform | a `per_platform` definition's token is used by, and sealed to (25.6), only devices of the platform whose client minted it (Google: a desktop token serves every desktop and an iOS token every iPhone and iPad; Android devices keep none); a `per_client` definition's one token serves every device, since Microsoft binds its tokens to the user and the client, not the platform. **Use on this device** (Q-CONN-13): on a desktop or an iPhone whose platform the record holds no token for, the person makes the connection usable there, in the Connected services screen or with `ur connect <label> --here` on `/dev/tty`, by 25.5's flow with `login_hint` set to the record's account, its token written into the same record as its platform's entry only once the new ID token's `iss` and `sub` equal the record's, else refused as `account_mismatch`; an Android phone asks `AuthorizationClient` for the record's account and the features' scopes at its first use, taking a token without the person where Google grants one, showing Google's consent where Google asks for it, and reading `sub` from the userinfo endpoint at each app process's first token, refusing one for another account as `account_mismatch`; a phone that holds no such Google account offers to add it in Android's settings. Until then the connection's tools on that device raise a `ui_request` of kind `connect` naming the connection in a run the person is attached to, waiting up to 10 minutes as `connection_request` does (25.9), and answer `connect_on_device` to any other caller |
| Strict rotation | a device first writes `refreshing` (itself, now + 30 s) by an `EXACT_HEAD` push (DESIGN §11.7, §11.8) on the version it read; the winner refreshes, writes the new token and clears the mark; a loser waits for that write, up to 30 seconds, and uses the new token; so no two devices present one token, which a strict provider reads as theft and answers by revoking the grant (RFC 9700 section 4.14). No launch definition is strict |
| Idle | no device refreshes a connection no tool is using: an unused grant should lapse (Q-CONN-11); the screen shows when one will, 90 days after its last refresh at Microsoft and after six months unused at Google |
| Disconnect | `ur disconnect <label>` or the screen's Disconnect, confirmed on `/dev/tty` or in the app: revoke each token the record holds at the definition's revocation endpoint (RFC 7009 at Google), or by `revokeAccess()` on Android; with none (Microsoft), open the page where the person removes the app, saying that the token stays valid at Microsoft until it is removed there or lapses; then delete the repo (DESIGN §11.12) and the calendar links that name it, which the confirmation lists |
| A lost device | a revocation (DESIGN §7.10) moves the repo to a generation the device cannot read, but the tokens it held still work at the provider; so after any revocation of a device that could read a connection, for compromise or not, but an enclave incarnation's stop or loss (below), the member's devices list it and offer Replace: revoke at the provider (at Microsoft, remove the app's access there, since rotation leaves old tokens valid), connect again, and write the new tokens under the new generation, as §23.6 does for calendar links |
| An enclave's incarnation | it reads and refreshes a connection as any device of the member does (25.6), its daemon holding access tokens in memory and attaching them outside the agents' container (CO-42, CO-43); its stop and its loss each revoke it (§11.4), and the repo's next generation is sealed without it, the copies sealed to its ReaderKey opening for no one once that key ends with the VM and dropped at the repo's next write, and the tokens it held lived only in that VM's memory, so neither asks anyone to replace anything; a compromise revocation lists every connection and link it could read and offers Replace, as for any device; a grant of its own per enclave, revoked at the provider apart from the person's devices, is Later (Q-CONN-17) |
