The accepted TAO/USD price fell 12.3% in under two weeks this month (10.6), which would turn the 1.20 markup into about 1.05 on a week's spend; (b) cuts the exposure to a day or two, at the cost of more and smaller trades. It changes what CO-35 confirmed, so the treasury buys TAO weekly until the owner takes it. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-ENC-1 | §11 | Which providers do we support for enclaves? | none today without a change on the provider's side: §11.3's table. The three CO-28 chose, each after its gate: Hippius first, for CPU, once it binds launch data, or adds setup over SSH's one feature (Q-ENC-7), and documents guest reports (G-PROV-hippius); Cathedral, for CPU, once it is generally available and passes the same (G-PROV-cathedral); Lium for GPU once it measures the renter's image (G-PROV-lium). Chutes' TDX VMs and Targon are not chosen (CO-28). Development runs on the reference provider, never a user (CO-21). | owner |
| Q-ENC-2 | §11 | What is the default egress? | `auto`, as for any sidecar whose network sets no egress mode (DESIGN §17.11: default egress on, mode `auto`): it keeps destinations from the miner and attributes traffic to URnetwork's network; a network that writes a policy sets `exits` or `none` for `tag:enclave`. | owner |
| Q-ENC-3 | §11 | Root for agents? | (c), as CO-19 asks: agents get root for everything Debian offers, `apt`, services and low ports included, while the incarnation's keys and the egress rules CO-7 has sidecar run stay outside their namespaces (11.10). The enclave's real root stays with the person's own SSH session; an agent with it could read the incarnation's keys from the daemon's memory or flush the firewall, making the enclave only as trusted as its least careful agent. | owner |
| Q-ENC-4 | §11 | May a Team's enclaves be shared between members? | not as devices. Since CO-43 an agents' enclave is one of its sponsor's devices, holding what their devices hold for the initial version (11.4), so sharing it would share the sponsor's vault, mail and accounts. Reach to it is shared through ordinary grants (§16.2: `ssh` and `dial` rules naming the enclave's tags), another member managing its agents only by a requested grant the sponsor approves, never as `root` and never launching one (§12.5, Q-HARN-9); its keys, its record and its access stay its sponsor's, and a member who wants an enclave makes their own. Handing an enclave to another member is Later, as a new enclave of theirs. | owner, decided (CO-43) |
| Q-ENC-5 | §11 | Until a Bittensor provider passes the enclave contract, may the indexer enclave run on a cloud's confidential VMs (the reference provider, 11.3), paid in USD? | (a), as the owner decided (CO-21): enclaves run only on Bittensor providers, so the indexer enclave, like every user-facing enclave, waits for G-PROV-hippius or the next provider to pass; until then a network's indexer is a member's always-on device, as DESIGN has it. | owner |
| Q-ENC-6 | §11 | May a member's grant to the indexer enclave reach beyond the mailbox, to the vault or other repos? | no. CO-20 grants the mailbox; the member's other repos are indexed by their own devices; and the indexer serves the whole network under its Owners' and Admins' sponsorship, so a member who wants an enclave to hold their vault and repos runs their own, which CO-43 makes one of their devices (11.4, Q-ENC-13). | owner |
| Q-ENC-7 | §11 | Instead of the provider binding the bootstrap, can URnetwork set an enclave up by SSH into the provider's VM? | (c). Four dangers need these conditions. An image that reads start-up data or SSH keys from the host lets the miner plant its own key or a boot script, and a backdoor planted at boot leaves the attestation unchanged. A report proves only the image, so without the installed keys and enclave id bound into it a breached broker, or a miner who is also the provider's customer, could present a genuine VM of the same image on which it holds root. And without the server's own binding, a relay could splice a genuine guest's report into another session. And a key, console or command the provider's API adds after the report would let that broker, which drives URnetwork's account, or a miner with an impostor VM in its own account, take root after the check, so the provider offers none and the payload closes the provider's own access before it makes keys (11.7). With all of them, setup reaches only the VM made for this enclave, which only the device's key can enter; it is one small provider feature, a report the SSH server binds, not a new register, which SEV-SNP lacks without an SVSM vTPM. | peer review |
| Q-ENC-8 | §11 | Does a new version of an enclave provider's disclosure stop the sponsor's running enclaves there? | (a). The enclave and what it holds are already there, and (b) would stop agents' work, and a network's indexer enclave its mail, for a change of text; the card marks the change until the sponsor opens it. | owner |
| Q-ENC-9 | §11 | May the network's indexer enclave be set up over SSH (EPC-1's fourth form), which a provider may offer before it binds launch data? | (c), decided by the owner (CO-41): any network's indexer enclave may be set up over SSH, its members taking the sponsor's word for what the setup installed, which the sponsor's device verified; members see who set it up before they grant. The sponsor's device signs a setup statement binding the incarnation's evidence, keys and payload, on which members' devices seat it (11.7, 11.10). | owner, decided (CO-41) |
| Q-ENC-10 | §11 | Does the network's indexer enclave satisfy the owner directive, and may it replace owner decision 12's "no hosted or TEE receiver"? | (c). CO-19 and CO-20 ask for the enclave, and it meets the directive's test, which is who holds the keys and the plaintext: every key is made in it, it joins and receives only by an Owner's or Admin's verified act, and nothing URnetwork runs can read its bundle, admit another VM, change its software or log in. The conditions: EPC-1 binds the keys a device admits to the VM it checked in every form (11.7's session secret; an init that refuses or measures every boot input); no form gives the provider's customer, the broker included, a key, console or command into the guest, and the image starts no console login; the broker does not choose its machine (A2, or the provider's signed placement); and in a Team it receives only 24 hours after every member is told. (b)'s limit to the first form or A2 yields to CO-41, which lets any network's indexer be set up over SSH, its members taking the sponsor's word; its notice is kept. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-ENC-11 | §11 | Should the indexer enclave have its own reserve and a longer grace, and may its keeper restart it on a new machine with no person? | (b). CO-19 asks for it always on, and under (a) it stops an hour after the balance reaches zero, which a store buyer with no threshold top-up reaches unawares, and most restarts page a person, since no provider pins machines; the reserve costs a network a week of its price up front, the grace at most 72 hours more owed, and the weekly limit keeps a breached broker from drawing machines at will. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-ENC-12 | §11 | Should an agent's `enclave_stop` and `enclave_start` need the person in a tainted run, with the network's indexer enclave outside agent tools? | (b). A stop destroys the VM and its scratch disk, so under (a) a prompt-injected run, local or through MCP, could stop every enclave the person sponsors, the network's mail with them, and a start would resume per-second charges no budget stops and admit an incarnation by a tool, which 11.4 forbids; a tainted run's `agent_stop` already waits for the person (§7.10). | owner |
| Q-ENC-13 | §11 | Does CO-43's full access extend to the network's indexer enclave? | (a). The indexer serves the whole network: it holds every member's incoming mail and the mailboxes members grant it, and its sponsors are the network's Owners and Admins, any of whom may admit its incarnations (11.4), so its access is not one member's; under (b) every member's mail would sit beside one admin's vault, mail and accounts on one machine, a breach exposing them together, and members' grants (CO-20) already give it what it needs. It keeps its measured role, with no Harness, no agents and no login (11.10). | owner |
| Q-ENC-14 | §11 | How is an agents' enclave given its sponsor's access (CO-43)? | (b), for the initial version. It rests on DESIGN's own consent (§8.5's `scoped` clause) and key delivery, so the enclave reads what the sponsor's devices read with no share to keep current, and it keeps `tag:enclave-<id>`, on which its claim, its network reach, its egress default and its listeners rest (§11.8, §16.5, §26); (a) would drop the tag and give a machine a miner holds the sponsor's authority to admit devices, consent and share, which would outlast the incarnation's revocation; (c) is what CO-43 replaced: a share per item, which reaches no new repo by itself. The bit also keeps the enclave from the sponsor's authority and from writing their settings (11.4). | peer review |
| Q-SSH-1 | §12 | Should desktops and other sidecars run the SSH server too? | not at launch; CO-5 is about enclaves. `ur ssh serve` for a person's own machines is Later, behind the same rule. | owner |
| Q-SSH-2 | §12 | Should person sessions be recorded? | receipts only (12.7); full recordings Later, to the person's vault, by a Team policy. | owner |
| Q-GIT-1 | §13 | Rebase? | (a) at launch; merge covers the agent's need to integrate, and coding agents' own instructions avoid rewriting history. A linear `rebase` of unpushed commits is the first addition if agents trip over its absence. | peer review |
| Q-GIT-2 | §13 | Other remotes (GitHub) from the local Harness? | no: CO-6 gives the local Harness EVS for storage, and a GitHub remote would be network access by another name; enclaves use the system git for GitHub, through their egress. | owner |
| Q-CACL-1 | §16 | Is each remote inference call an outward action? | (b). A call per approval would make agents unusable; budgets, model rules and taint bound the risk, and the record holds every call. | owner |
| Q-CACL-2 | §16 | Default budgets? | $5 a day and $50 a month per agent and per tagged subject, $20 a day and $200 a month per untagged device for calls naming no agent, enforced by the broker and raised by policy or by `compute_budget_raise`. | owner, confirmed (CO-35) |
| Q-CACL-3 | §16 | What may a new network use? | (a), as CO-18 says. Every model carries its label in the catalog and on every message, and the apps put the TEE-only switch beside the model picker. | owner |
| Q-CACL-4 | §16 | Should an untagged device's spending have a daily ceiling across all its agents? Q-CACL-2's budgets bind each agent id, and its $20 a day only the calls that name no agent, so a same-user process that mints new agent ids can spend past $5 a day each, bounded only by the balance and auto-renew's limits. | (b). It keeps CO-35's per-agent figures and bounds what a prompt-injected or modified local process can spend in a day, which per-agent figures cannot, since an agent id is the device's own word. | owner, confirmed (CO-41) |
| Q-CPHASE-1 | §19 | If no inference provider has passed its gate when M12 would start, what gets built? | (b). What a person can use ships first, and nothing is stranded if a provider declines; CO-28's choice of providers stands, revisited only if one declines in writing. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-CPHASE-2 | §19 | Should Chutes' TEE path stay in M12, though CO-32 drops Chutes from launch? | (b). Until then no user can reach the path, and M12's exits then need no TEE call. | owner |
| Q-CPHASE-3 | §19 | Does M14 start before a provider commits to EPC-1? | (c). The platform is most of M14 and no provider's choice changes it, while an adapter, the indexer enclave or the management link built before a commitment is work no user reaches if the provider declines. | owner |
| Q-CPHASE-4 | §19 | Which of 19.7's deferrals do you take? | (b), decided by the owner (CO-42): none of §19.7's deferrals is taken; everything in its first table stays in scope, placed in the milestones §19.1 gives, and §19.4's effort includes it. | owner, decided (CO-42) |
| Q-CPHASE-5 | §19 | How many engineers build M11 to M16? | (a). The work is about 74 to 100 engineer-months, 19.7's items included (CO-42): with (a) the first release comes about 6 to 8 months after M10's exit and web search about 8 to 10, and with (b) about 10 to 13 and 14 to 18. With fewer engineers 19.3's order holds and every date moves. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-SKILL-1 | §20 | Are names unique per member or per network? | (a). A personal network has one member, so the two agree there; in a Team, other members address an agent as `<name>` with its member shown, which `agent_find` and the directory resolve, and no member's agents can squat another's names. | owner |
| Q-SKILL-2 | §20 | Is there one shared repo for a whole Team's agents? | (b). CO-15 asks for "a general repo and inbox shared by all agents", and in a Team "all agents" includes other members'; the Team inbox gives every agent one place to be reached, while summaries, which say more than owner decision 170's titles, projects and branches, stay in each member's agents repo. Every Team inbox message taints its readers. | owner |
| Q-SKILL-3 | §20 | How often are summaries written? | every 15 minutes of active work, with 5-60 settable, plus at task end and session end. Fifteen minutes keeps "what is it doing" current enough without spending many model turns. | owner |
| Q-SKILL-4 | §20 | Can agents in different networks message each other? | (a); cross-network shares (DESIGN §17.9, v1) carry ports and subnets, not EVS deposits, so it waits for a design of its own (Later). | owner |
| Q-SKILL-5 | §20 | Does the skill write to the team directory too? | (a). The directory already announces title, project and branch (owner decision 170); summaries hold more and stay with the member. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-1 | §21 | Is one public payment per search acceptable? | (a). It is the only path that keeps every URnetwork server out of the query while URnetwork pays (21.4), and the counts it reveals are URnetwork's, not a person's. | owner, confirmed (CO-35) |
| Q-SRCH-2 | §21 | How is Parallel paid, given CO-10? | per search in USDC on Base, from URnetwork's payer address to the payee each challenge names, which the treasury funds in USD. CO-10 sets how Bittensor providers are paid; Parallel is not one and takes no gamma, and CO-28 names it. Users still pay only fiat, into the compute balance; the apps give no user USDC to hold or move, though a modified client can direct an authorization to itself (CO-29, Q-SRCH-13). | owner |
| Q-SRCH-3 | §21 | Which of Parallel's paths? | (a). It needs no agreement (CO-27) and puts no key on a device or a server; (b) would bring zero data retention on Scale and no public payments, but its tokens can only be scoped `*` and spend until they expire, so it waits for narrower scopes (21.12); (c) is no basis for a metered product. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-4 | §21 | Is search on by default? | (a), under the web search clause the network accepted with its compute terms (21.9). CO-16 makes search built in; each person still acknowledges the disclosure before their first search (21.6), each search's card names Parallel and its price, and a network's policy can turn search off. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-5 | §21 | Any free searches? | none. CO-16 puts the cost on the compute balance; a network with no balance, or in grace, gets `insufficient_quota` from the tool, and its agents carry on without search. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-SRCH-6 | §21 | Should the local Harness also fetch the pages it finds? | yes: CO-17 asks for it, and §22 designs `web_fetch` on every leg. Parallel's excerpts already carry the relevant text of each result, so an agent fetches when it needs a whole page, its links or its tables. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-7 | §21 | May external harnesses keep `web_search` as an MCP tool, now that the gateway serves no hosted search? | (a). The MCP tool is URnetwork's own tool and result format, used by the network's own harness on its member's device: an integration of the Services into URnetwork's application, which Parallel's §2(b) allows. The gateway's case differs: there the gateway would answer the harness's own built-in tool, in the harness vendor's shape, inside the vendor's product, which is why CO-26 turns it off. DESIGN §16.5 already gives external harnesses the Harness's tools by the same names. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-8 | §21 | Who holds the payer key? | `searchsigner`, a rate-limited signer on hosts of its own, apart from the broker's (21.5): it signs only Base USDC within the policy's ceiling and the amount of a ticket the broker admitted, after screening the payee, under a daily cap, from a float of at most two days of searches; it never learns a network, and the broker never a payee or nonce; the treasury's USDC refills it. | peer review |
| Q-SRCH-9 | §21 | Are results kept in the record? | (a). CO-26 rests the reading of Parallel's §2(c)(xi) on not storing results; a sealed copy in the person's own record would fit §2(b)'s one End Customer, but a kept result invites answering a later query from it, which §2(c)(xi) bars, and the agent's own prose, which cites what it used, is kept. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-10 | §21 | Which mode is the default? | `fast`: the gateway's own default and Parallel's recommendation for agents, about 700 ms. All four modes cost $0.01 on the gateway, so an agent asks for `advanced` when it needs depth, and for `turbo` only in English or Japanese. | peer review |
| Q-SRCH-11 | §21 | Should URnetwork keep which network each payment belonged to, so that Parallel's complaints can be traced? | (a). The escrow would be the one record joining Parallel's log to a network, against R-SRCH-4; per-network budgets, caps and rates and time-based tracing carry the duty instead, at the risk that one network's abuse stops search for all until it is found. The sanctions records of 21.5 join no search: they keep a network only for a payee the screen refused, never paid, or an authorization settled outside the gateway, which bought none. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-12 | §21 | Which search provider? | (a), as CO-28 decides: Parallel needs no enterprise agreement and lets each device call it directly, unintercepted (CO-27); Brave is dropped (21.12). The client is one adapter, so the owner's review of alternatives under CO-30 can switch it with a release. | owner |
| Q-SRCH-13 | §21 | Does a device naming the payee keep the compute balance a closed loop? | (a). CO-29 accepts that a member's modified client may direct each authorization, at most the policy's ceiling, to an address of its own, "as long as we take a percentage of each call", which every settled authorization pays. The ceiling, the network's budgets, daily cap and rate, §9.11's purchase limits and §17's monitoring of search volume by network bound it, and counsel reads §10.8 under CO-29 before launch (G-SRCH-parallel). If counsel finds the exclusion lost, (c) is the path, and URnetwork asks Parallel for it now. | owner, confirmed (CO-41) |
| Q-SRCH-14 | §21 | May search launch without zero data retention? | (a), decided (CO-31): search launches on Parallel's terms, under which it may train on queries and results, not linked to the person, with the disclosure before each person's first search (21.6). Queries carry no identity of the person, only an exit's address and URnetwork's payer address, and the query check (D-SRCH-4) keeps secrets and personal data out. Asking Parallel for zero retention on the keyless path is a later improvement, which would change the disclosure's text. | owner, decided (CO-31) |
| Q-SRCH-15 | §21 | Should the signer screen each search payee before signing, and should the broker cap a network's searches by a limit its policy cannot raise? | (b). CO-29 accepted cash-out "as long as we take a percentage of each call"; it did not accept URnetwork's payer paying a sanctioned address, which a client submitting to Base itself would put past the facilitator's screening, nor a path from a stolen card to USDC bounded only by limits the fraudster sets, where a chargeback takes back the USDC and the percentage both. The screen costs one read of Base per search; the cap, 200 searches a day in a network's first paid week and 2,000 after, binds few honest networks, and URnetwork's review raises it. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-FETCH-1 | §22 | Is a fetch a compute charge? | (a). A fetch pays no third party, and owner decision 10 already counts its traffic; a charge would bill the person twice for the same bytes. | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-FETCH-2 | §22 | Through which egress? | `auto` by default, so sites see an exit's address; `exits` by the network's policy; never `direct` from a device, which would expose its address and bypass the sidecar's own transports (IC-7). | owner |
| Q-FETCH-3 | §22 | Does it obey `robots.txt`? | (a). It fetches a page when a person's agent asks, as a browser does, so crawler rules for `*` do not describe it, but a site can still refuse it by name; the `User-Agent` names it and links a page saying so. | owner |
| Q-FETCH-4 | §22 | May an agent fetch a URL it composed? | yes while its run is untainted; once tainted, only with an approval, the device's safety classifier's in auto mode on a site the member has used (§27.4), else a person's, and even listed URLs are narrowed (22.5). Agents compose URLs often, from documentation patterns, so a blanket refusal would hobble them, and an untainted run has read nothing that could compose one for an attacker. | owner |
| Q-FETCH-5 | §22 | An MCP `web_fetch` for external harnesses? | no. They have their own fetch tools, and 22.5's rule needs the run's context, which an MCP call does not carry. The gateway fetches nothing either, since it serves no hosted search (§21.7). | owner |
| Q-FETCH-6 | §22 | PDFs? | Later. A PDF parser is a second attack surface and a size cost on phones; papers and manuals are the common case, so it comes after the HTML path proves out, likely in enclaves first. | peer review |
| Q-FETCH-7 | §22 | A page that builds its content with script comes back nearly empty on devices (22.6): should `web_fetch` render script at launch? | (a). A browser on devices is tens of MB and a large attack surface, against DESIGN §18.10's size budgets; (c) shows a third party every URL and page (22.9); in an enclave, `apt` already brings a browser under the enclave's egress, so bundling one adds image size for what an agent can do itself; and static fetch covers the documentation, articles and references agents read most. | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-1 | §23 | What is the "calendar edit link" CO-24 names? | (b). None of the six providers read offers (a): Google's, iCloud's, Fastmail's, Proton's, Outlook's and Nextcloud's links all only read, and writing takes a CalDAV app password or an OAuth grant (23.3); the app's calendar settings say so in one line and ask each provider for the right thing. | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-2 | §23 | How do Google and Microsoft calendars, which write only through OAuth, get in? | (b), built in M13 and offered as each provider passes its gate (G-CONN-google, G-CONN-microsoft), with (a) until then. Most people's calendars are Google's or Microsoft's, and OAuth with PKCE runs on the device, its code never reaching a URnetwork server, with one Google client per platform and none of Google's refresh tokens on Android devices (Q-MAILCAL-13); (c) is a server reading calendars, which the directive rules out. | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-3 | §23 | Does an agent's read mark mail read? | (a). A summary the person has not read would otherwise empty their unread list, and a tainted run could hide mail from them by reading it. | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-4 | §23 | May an agent flag, file or delete mail? | (a). CO-24 asks for summaries; a `mail_flag` tool, W for flags and labels in an untainted run, is a small later step; deletion stays the person's, since an erasure cannot be undone (DESIGN §15.7). | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-5 | §23 | May a model without a TEE read mail? | decided by the owner (CO-34): "The first usage of a non-tee model should be prompted just like the parallel search prompt." So (d): the disclosure says that everything in the conversation, the mail and calendar items an agent reads included, goes to the provider in plaintext; once the person has acknowledged it, the model reads mail as it reads any prompt, and until then every call to it is refused with `disclosure_required`, mail or not, which replaces the earlier mail-only question (§2.8, §6.4). | owner, decided |
| Q-MAILCAL-6 | §23 | Do calendar reads taint the run? | (a). An invitation from anyone can land in a calendar, and `ORGANIZER` is a property any writer sets, so (b) cannot be checked; the cost is that "what is on tomorrow, and add X" asks for approval, which the person gives once for the batch. | peer review |
| Q-MAILCAL-7 | §23 | Is a calendar write from an untainted run W or O? | (a). An untainted run carries out only what the person asked for, as §7.8 reasons for `agent_send` and `ssh_exec`; invitations are mail to other people, so they always wait. | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-8 | §23 | May the person approve part of a batch? | (b): the decision names the events approved (`ApprovalDecision.selected`), so one wrong event does not cost the rest a second request. | peer review |
| Q-MAILCAL-9 | §23 | May an enclave's agents read mail or use the calendar? | (b), decided by the owner (CO-42), in the form CO-43 gives it for the initial version: the person's enclave is one of their devices (§11.4), so it reads their mailbox and calendar links as their other devices do, with no `EvsShare` to file (23.6), and its agents use the mail and calendar tools there under the taint and approval rules any run has, and the `private` mark (§7.8). | owner, decided (CO-42) |
| Q-MAILCAL-10 | §23 | May a link reach a calendar inside the network, such as a Nextcloud or Radicale at home? | (b). The person, not an agent, chose the host, and neither discovery nor a redirect may move into the overlay, so no injection or server can aim it; self-hosted CalDAV is common. A private name has no public certificate, so the device pins the server's at save, or speaks plain `http` to a sidecar, whose overlay flow is encrypted end to end (23.7); LAN addresses outside the overlay stay refused (§22.4, R-FETCH-5). | peer review |
| Q-MAILCAL-11 | §23 | Do external harnesses get the calendar tools? | (a). DESIGN §16.5 already gives them `mail_list` and `mail_read`, a harness's taint is kept by DESIGN §16.6's hooks for what it reads through `ur` and its web tools, though not for what it reads by itself, so its writes count as a tainted run's (23.9), and the link stays in the daemon either way. | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-12 | §23 | Should a summary run on its own, as a morning digest? | (a). A scheduled run has no person at hand to acknowledge a disclosure (§2.8) or approve a batch, and scheduling agents is not yet designed; the digest follows that design (Later). | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-13 | §23 | How does a Google calendar connect on Android, where Google offers an app no OAuth redirect and keeps refresh tokens off the device? | (a). (b) uses one platform's client on another, against Google's policy of a client per platform, which its verification checks; (c) puts a calendar credential on a server, which the directive rules out. The cost is that an Android device links Google on itself, with the Google account it holds, while every other form and platform reads the link from EVS. | owner, confirmed (CO-35) |
| Q-MAILCAL-14 | §23 | May `mail_read` give an agent an invitation's `text/calendar` part, the event a meeting invitation carries? | (b). Invitations are the commonest mail that carries an event, and their part states the time, zone and recurrence exactly where the text may not; the parser is the one the calendar tools already run on providers' answers, vendored, fuzzed and capped (23.7); the fields reach the model between the untrusted-data markers, as the body does, and the duplicate check (23.8) keeps an invitation the provider already placed from being added twice. (c) stays Later with attachments. | owner |
| Q-MAILCAL-15 | §23 | Should sign-in codes and reset links be withheld from models outside the device or an A1 or A2 TEE? | (b). Burner mail is largely codes and magic links, and a call to a `none` provider reaches its gateway and the machine that serves it, at SayGM a miner and the upstream it calls, any of which could use a password-reset link while it is valid; the skill's instruction binds only the model, after the provider has the text. A deterministic filter in the daemon takes nothing a summary needs, since a summary names codes without copying them and the apps show codes themselves (DESIGN §15.9), and CO-34's disclosure still covers the rest of the mail; AP is included, since there the provider's own code reads the request. The switch leaves the last word to the person. | owner |
| Q-CTXH-1 | §24 | Where is the history kept? | (a). It is the record: the vault already holds Harness runs (§7.7) under the record's chains, erasure, retention, disclosure and I-20's line, and one copy is cheaper and simpler than two; the agent repo is readable by the member's other agents (§20.4), and a new kind would rebuild what the vault has. An agents' enclave reads the vault as its sponsor's device (24.7). | owner |
| Q-CTXH-2 | §24 | Does CO-25 lift §22.7's 64 KiB cap on a fetched page's text? | (b). The record is the person's own and the page their own visit (§22.7), and the cap was a storage choice, not a term anyone set; an agent that continues a run, or a person reviewing it, gets the page that was read, not its first 64 KiB. | owner |
| Q-CTXH-3 | §24 | Does CO-25 override CO-26 on keeping search results? | (b). CO-26 answers Parallel's §2(c)(xi) by not storing results, and a sealed copy in the vault is storage that invites answering a later query from it (§21.11, Q-SRCH-9); the agent's prose, citing what it used, is kept, and if the owner ever allows storage, results become blobs like any part, with no format change. | owner |
| Q-CTXH-4 | §24 | How does an enclave read a run? | (d), since CO-43 makes an agents' enclave one of its sponsor's devices (§11.4): it reads every run from the vault as the member's other devices do. That puts every run on a machine a miner holds (§2.6), which the owner accepted for the initial version and the enclave's disclosure says (§2.8); (b)'s packs are gone with their builds, seals and confirmations (24.7), and (a) and (c) would add a share or a copy for what the enclave reads already. | owner |
| Q-CTXH-5 | §24 | Does deduplication reach across runs? | (a). Bytes shared across runs would let one run's erasure take another's content, and a person could not erase one run without weighing every other; a parent link can only cut a path, which the rebuild names. The cost is a system prompt and tools stored once per run, about 60 KiB for Claude Code. | peer review |
| Q-CTXH-6 | §24 | With the gateway recording each call, should the transcript tail stop for runs it covers? | (a). DESIGN §16.7 keeps capture fixed, `record.capture` ignored until a person-only surface exists, and the two say different things: the transcript is the harness's own word, its local commands and its view after its own edits included, and the gateway's entries are what the model received; they differ exactly where the harness rewrote its context, which a reviewer wants to see. The overlap roughly doubles an external run's record (24.10). | owner |
| Q-CTXH-7 | §24 | What retention does the history get by default? | (a). CO-25 says all, and the vault's owner sets its retention: the storage view warns at 80% of the network's storage and names the largest runs, and one command sets the `bulk` class's life. | owner, confirmed (CO-35) |
| Q-CTXH-8 | §24 | How large a part is kept whole? | (b), in up to eight 8 MiB blobs, under DESIGN §16.7's 256 MiB a run-hour. No catalog model reads that much in one call, so a larger part never reached a model whole; past it, the hash and size stand, with the `oversize` gap. | peer review |
| Q-CTXH-9 | §24 | Should the gateway now serve `previous_response_id` from the record? | (a). Codex and Claude Code send full history and need no stored state; serving from the record would make the vault's sync a dependency of every call and the record a cache. It stays Later (§19.5), its data now kept. | owner |
| Q-CTXH-10 | §24 | Is redaction applied though it makes rebuilds inexact? | (a). DESIGN §16.7 redacts before every seal, and a secret in the record is a secret on every device that opens the run and in every export; a rebuild marks each redaction, and a continued agent that needs the secret reads it again where it lives. Email addresses and phone numbers are not secrets of that kind, and `record.redact.pii`'s hashing spares kinds 54 and 55 (Q-CTXH-15). | owner |
| Q-CTXH-11 | §24 | Who may move a run into an enclave? | (b). Since CO-43 the enclave reads every run from the vault, so a move carries no data there that it lacks; but it starts work the person pays for, in an enclave whose agents may reach the internet, and a prompt-injected agent that could move any run would do both unasked, so every move waits for the person: a confirmation in the app or on /dev/tty, never an RPC `ui_response`, which a process could answer, and, from a tainted run or with untrusted nodes into an enclave that reaches out, kind 24's approval on another device, which shows the taint, the egress and `ContextFields` (D-HARN-7, §16.3), since the enclave's daemon would otherwise hold those nodes from its container (§7.8). (c) would cost the person who asks their own bot to move a run the same confirmation with an extra step. A shell is no way around it: `ur harness continue --enclave` refuses a caller with a harness ancestor (24.7). | owner |
| Q-CTXH-12 | §24 | Should session blobs be padded past Padmé, so a part's size says less? | (a). Padmé already bounds what a size says to a few percent, and evs sees no URL, so matching a fetched page by its size needs a candidate list and the push time; (b) costs up to twice the bytes of every blob, against the storage that D-CTXH-8's caps ration. 24.11 discloses the inference, and §18's measurements can reopen this. | peer review |
| Q-CTXH-13 | §24 | CO-25 asks for all history; may it be capped below the network's storage? | (b). Under (a) one enclave that works all day fills Community's 1 GiB within days, and in a Team one member's runs stop every member's mail, which no admin can prune, since a vault is its owner's alone (RECORD.md section 8); (b) keeps everything up to the caps, names what it drops, and leaves the person the storage view, pruning and the `bulk` class to make room. | owner, confirmed (CO-35) |
| Q-CTXH-14 | §24 | Does CO-25 reach a harness that calls its own provider rather than the gateway, such as Claude Code on the person's own Anthropic account? | (a). Only a call that passes through sidecar can be kept as the model received it. (b) reverses Q-GW-4, putting providers outside the catalog's labels, disclosures and budgets behind the gateway and another company's API keys in the daemon; (c) puts a certificate authority into the person's trust store to read their traffic to another company. The Harness's runs, and every call of a harness set to the gateway, which one command does, are kept whole; a harness that keeps its own provider keeps what its transcript shows, and its record says so. | owner |
| Q-CTXH-15 | §24 | Should session history be exempt from `record.redact.pii`'s default hashing, so a run resumes with the addresses the person typed? | (b). Hashing before seal makes every resumed or continued run lose each address and number the person typed or a tool read ("invite bob@example.com" becomes a marker, and so does every attendee a calendar read returned), which a phone meets at every app death, while the vault already keeps them owner-bound, sealed and out of every index; secrets stay redacted, since a secret in the record is on every device that opens the run. `ur harness export` and `ur record export --bodies` hash them in what they write. A disclosure packet proves each body by its commitment, so it cannot hash without breaking the proof: it carries them as sealed, and its confirmation counts them, so the person chooses. This narrows [owner decision 452](DESIGN.md#od-452)'s default for two new kinds. | owner |
| Q-CTXH-16 | §24 | What is a member's default share of the network's storage for history? | (b). Half keeps a one-person network's history to 512 MiB of Community's 1 GiB, one to two and a half months at 24.10's rates, though the 90% cap already keeps room for its mail, and lets one member of a Team of 20 take 100 GiB of its 200; 2/n lets each member use twice an even split, the 90% cap still keeping mail and repos writing. Q-CTXH-13's caps stand as confirmed (CO-35); only the share's default changes. | owner |
| Q-CONN-1 | §25 | Where do service definitions live, and how is a service added? | (b). The policy is signed by the two-person compute-policy key the release key certifies (§5.4), moves only forward and cannot be widened by a server (IC-9), and each release carries the newest one; (a) makes a new or narrowed service wait for every platform's release and store review; (c) would let a breached server point people's tokens at its own hosts. Typed tools still ship in releases, and `service_call` serves a new service until they do (Q-CONN-3). | owner |
| Q-CONN-2 | §25 | May a person add an arbitrary OIDC issuer? | (b) on desktops at launch, in the apps Later, and (c) Later. CO-36 says "generally", and people who run their own networks often run their own identity providers (Keycloak, Authentik, Forgejo, Nextcloud); only the person adds one, its issuer and hosts shown on `/dev/tty`; no one has reviewed its rules, so every write waits for approval as kind 26, and its token reaches only the hosts the person listed. The apps wait because their redirects need the person's provider to register URnetwork's app identities, a long setup on a phone, and a Team's definitions wait for a review step in the config. | owner, confirmed (CO-41) |
| Q-CONN-3 | §25 | Should the generic `service_call` exist at launch, or only typed tools? | (c). Without it, a service a policy adds, or a person's own (Q-CONN-2), does nothing until a release brings tools, against R-CONN-1, and models already know the large providers' REST APIs. The risk is bounded: the token stays in the daemon; calls reach only the connection's API hosts, within the scopes the person granted; reads taint; a tainted run's writes and sends wait for an approval whose card shows the body whole, the safety classifier deciding a write first (CO-40, §27); typed paths are refused, so calendar writes keep kind 25's cards. The cost is approvals of API bodies, which read worse than an event card, so typed tools stay the first choice and `service_call` the fallback, switchable per connection and by a network (§16.4). At launch, with only the calendar's scopes, it adds little on Google and Microsoft; its value is the next service. | owner, confirmed (CO-41) |
| Q-CONN-4 | §25 | Do access tokens stay in memory only, or are they also cached, sealed, in the connection's repo so the member's devices do not each refresh? | (a). The refresh token in EVS already lets every device mint an access token, so a cache adds no reach and saves at most one token request per device an hour; it would write the repo at every refresh, telling URnetwork's servers when a member's agents use a service, which for Google, whose refresh tokens do not rotate, they otherwise never see; Google's tokens are bound per platform client, so a shared cache would need an entry per platform, and an Android device's come from Play services and stay there; and every refresh leaves through the connection's one exit, so separate refreshes look like one client to the provider. CO-37 holds either way: what is long-lived is in EVS, and an access token is derived from it and dies within the hour. | owner |
| Q-CONN-5 | §25 | May an enclave ever get a connection? | (c), decided by the owner (CO-42), in the form CO-43 gives it for the initial version: the person's enclave is one of their devices (§11.4), so it reads their connections, credentials included, as their other devices do, with nothing to file (25.6); its daemon holds and attaches the tokens outside the agents' container, so no token enters an agent's context (I-7), a run that uses one takes the `private` mark (§7.8), and the enclave's disclosure says what it holds (§2.8). | owner, decided (CO-42) |
| Q-CONN-6 | §25 | On Android, how does a service other than Google redirect? | (b). An App Link that a browser fails to hand off is loaded from its host, which would send a code to a URnetwork server, so it is used only where the Auth Tab captures it; a private-use scheme can be caught by another app, but PKCE makes a caught code useless (RFC 8252 section 8.1) and it never reaches a server; Google deprecates (c) for mobile clients, and an app in the background may not be listening. A device with neither uses a connection another device made, since Microsoft's token serves every platform. | peer review |
| Q-CONN-7 | §25 | Is every write from an untainted run W, as the calendar's are, or are some always outward? | (a), decided by the owner (CO-40): "once the oidc is approved, no further approval is needed", so once the person has connected the service, every call from an untainted run is R or W, sends and unclassified calls included, recorded and rate-limited (25.8); and in a tainted run every write and send is kind 26: in auto mode, the default, the device's safety classifier decides a classified write first, and a send, an unclassified call and every call on a person's own definition go to the person (§27.4, §27.7). | owner, decided (CO-40) |
| Q-CONN-8 | §25 | One connection per account, shared by its features, or one per feature? | (a). One consent and one token per account is what the person sees at the provider, and Google counts refresh tokens per account and client; adding a feature asks for the union of scopes, since Google's installed apps have no incremental authorization, and checks that the account is the same. A second account is a second connection. | peer review |
| Q-CONN-9 | §25 | May a connected service's data reach a model without a TEE? | (b). CO-18 makes the model the person's choice, and the provider's disclosure already informs it (CO-34); but Google's Limited Use rules confine its data, and data "derived from" it, to the user-facing feature the user consented to and bar people reading it, and its Workspace API policy forbids training a model beyond the user's own (25.3), so a provider that trained on it, kept it or let staff read it would put URnetwork's verification, and every user's Google connection, at risk. So Google's definition is `limited_use`: a read marks the run, the mark follows what the run writes, launches and sends, and its context goes only to local models and to models of any label, AP included, since at AP the provider reads plaintext, whose provider's gate recorded such terms (25.10, §4.7); a harness whose model calls do not pass the gateway gets no such data over MCP. (c) would refuse providers whose terms meet the rule, and admit an AP provider whose terms do not. | owner |
| Q-CONN-10 | §25 | Should the person's sign-in at the provider also go through the egress? | (a). The provider already knows the person's address from their everyday use; their browser holds their session and passkeys; a sign-in from an exit's address could be flagged as an anonymous one; and sidecar does not control the system browser's routes. Everything after the sign-in, the code exchange included, leaves through the connection's exit. | owner |
| Q-CONN-11 | §25 | Should devices refresh idle connections to keep them from lapsing? | (a). A grant nobody uses should lapse (Microsoft's 90 days after its last refresh, Google's after six months unused), which shrinks what a lost device exposes; the screen shows when one will, and reconnecting takes a minute. | peer review |
| Q-CONN-12 | §25 | Do external harnesses get the connection tools? | (a). DESIGN §16.6's hooks keep a harness's taint for what it reads through `ur` and its web tools, the token stays in the daemon either way, and the calendar's tools are already there (Q-MAILCAL-11); `connection_request` stays out, since only a person in the apps or at the terminal can answer it. | owner |
| Q-CONN-13 | §25 | How does a device use a connection another platform made, such as a Google connection made on a desktop and used from an Android phone? | (b). (a) makes a second consent, repo and connection for one account, against Q-CONN-8; (c) uses one platform's client on another, against Google's policy (Q-MAILCAL-13). Under (b) the person signs in once per platform that keeps a token (Google's desktop and iOS), an Android phone shows Google's consent only where Google asks for it, and the `sub` check keeps a token for the wrong account, which Android's result does not name, from writing into the person's calendar. | peer review |
| Q-CONN-14 | §25 | Does CO-40's rule for a run that has read nothing untrusted reach an MCP session, whose taint misses what its harness reads by itself? | (b) at launch. An external harness is tainted only by what it reads through `ur` and by hooks on its web tools (DESIGN §16.6): a cloned repo's files, a package's README or its own shell's output taint nothing, so its untainted run has not shown that it read nothing untrusted, which is what CO-40's rule rests on; under (a) an injected coding agent writes 20 events a call into a shared calendar, or sends mail through a connection, with no card. (c) spares taps but lets the classifier judge an action whose cause it never read, which §27.4 refuses elsewhere; the bench can measure it for a later release. The Harness keeps CO-40's rule whole, since every input of its runs passes its tools (§7.8). | owner |
| Q-CONN-15 | §25 | Should a Team's audit reader, or a device of another platform, ever hold a member's live tokens? | (b). An audit reader that holds live tokens acts as each member at their provider, an iCloud app password opening their mail too, which no audit needs, and it still sees each connection's record; under (a) a lost phone holds the desktops' Google token as well, so Replace must revoke both; and a member who leaves has no device left to run Disconnect, so a personal Google token would stay live for months. The cost is a re-seal a device does as it opens its entry, and a device of a platform with no entry yet waiting for another to seal it one. | owner |
| Q-CONN-16 | §25 | May a connected service's calls, and a calendar link's, leave by the device's own route where the person or the network chooses? | (b). The privacy exits buy here is small: the provider knows the account and sees the person's own address at every sign-in (Q-CONN-10), and no URnetwork server takes part either way; while each exit change is a new address at the next refresh, which Entra ID Protection may read as a stolen token and answer by revoking a work account's sessions, and a Conditional Access policy that judges the token request's address refuses an exit it does not trust. `auto` stays the default until the gate's 30-day exit test (§19.2) says otherwise. | owner |
| Q-CONN-17 | §25 | Should an enclave hold an OAuth grant of its own, so that revoking it when an incarnation ends touches no other device? | (a) at launch, (b) Later. Clean revocation does not need (b): a stop ends the VM, its memory and its ReaderKey, and the tokens it held go with them; only a breach, which the owner accepted for the initial version (CO-43), could have kept a copy, which a compromise revocation answers with Replace as for any device (25.7). (b) would narrow Replace to the enclave's own grant at Google, but Microsoft revokes no single token, so it gains nothing there, and it asks the person to sign in again for each enclave; (c) would ask at every incarnation, which unattended restarts cannot do (§11.7). | owner |
| Q-LSTN-1 | §26 | Who sees whose listeners? | (a). CO-38 decided it ("any client on the network") and CO-39 confirms that the design supports the use case whole; (b), the earlier default, kept most people's services off the list until they opted in. A person keeps a service or a device to themselves by hiding it, after reading `listeners:publish`, which their devices wait for; admins may narrow who publishes with the document's `listeners` block, never widen past the default. | owner |
| Q-LSTN-2 | §26 | Who may reach a listed entry by default? | (a), as CO-38 says: "any client on the network" sends to `ip:port` and reaches the service, and CO-39 asks for the whole use case. The consequence, said in `listeners:publish` and in 26.15: every service a device serves on every interface, a development server or a database with no password among them, is open to every device and every enclave agent of the network, a prompt-injected one included, unless its person hides it or an admin narrows the rule; what is open is exactly what is listed, so the person sees it. Reach opens only by people's acts: a person's devices once that person acknowledges the text and confirms each desktop's first list on it, tagged sidecars' entries and the implicit document's rule once an Owner or Admin acknowledges it for the network (Q-LSTN-8, Q-LSTN-9); an enclave whose egress is `none` reaches listed services too, and so counts as reaching out (§7.8); and a flow the rule admits reaches the service as the network's, never as localhost (Q-LSTN-11). | owner |
| Q-LSTN-3 | §26 | Which repo holds the lists? | (a). Every admitted sidecar must read every list and each write its own alone, the directory's shape: (b) lets only config writers write, through heads; (c) holds only runs (I-20), only in Teams, and the vault reaches no other member and no tagged sidecar but the member's own enclaves; (d) reaches only as far as each document's grants, the implicit document giving tagged sidecars no read. A kind fixes its readers, as the directory's are (D-ACL-24), so no document narrows the network's view below CO-38's. | peer review |
| Q-LSTN-4 | §26 | Does the listeners rule open forwards too? | (a). A forward is a grant to one sidecar for its own use (R-BRIDGE-6); opening its local port to every client would let each reach the target through that grant, past whatever the target's own rules say. The service a forward reaches is listed by its own host, where the listeners rule opens it to every client once that host publishes (26.6), delivered there as the network's traffic (Q-LSTN-11). | owner |
| Q-LSTN-5 | §26 | Are sockets bound to loopback alone listed? | (a). A loopback bind is a program's or a person's choice to serve this machine alone: a browser's debugging port, which runs any script it is sent, a local admin panel, a database set to `localhost`; (b) would open them to every client and, at `127.0.0.1`, skip the host's firewall and pass their "allow from localhost" checks. A person who wants to offer one maps it (`ur bridge expose :<port>=127.0.0.1:<port>`, or "map it" in the apps), an approved act of theirs whose map is then listed, and opened, as any. | owner |
| Q-LSTN-6 | §26 | Are UDP sockets listed? | (b). The overlay carries UDP and rules 1 and 3 map it (DESIGN §17.6), so a DNS, WireGuard, game or QUIC server is a service CO-38 covers; UDP has no listen state, so a fixed port below the ephemeral range is what marks a server, and (c) would list every client's resolver and QUIC sockets. | peer review |
| Q-LSTN-7 | §26 | May the local Harness open a listed service, as `web_fetch` of an http entry? | (a). The local profile reaches the network only through sidecar's own transports and `web_fetch` only public addresses (IC-7, IC-16), so a prompt-injected run cannot send requests into the person's network; the person opens an entry in their browser, and an enclave's agents, which run programs, dial as any program there, within the enclave's reach. No new outward kind is needed. | owner |
| Q-LSTN-8 | §26 | Does the release open the listeners rule anywhere by itself? | (a). A document is its admins' signed statement (I-4), which no release rewrites; a network with no document takes its rules from the release, so a rule it gained at an upgrade would open services to every CI runner, cloud agent and enclave's root agent of the network with no one who may decide for the network having acted, as (b) and (c) do; so the implicit document's rule waits for an Owner's or Admin's acknowledgment, as tagged sidecars' publishing does (Q-LSTN-9). Until the acts, such a network's entries show `blocked` or `waiting` with the fix, so the list stays honest. | owner |
| Q-LSTN-9 | §26 | Must someone acknowledge `listeners:publish` before a tagged sidecar publishes? | (c), as CO-41 settled for tagged sidecars' disclosures (Q-CTRUST-3): no person sits at a server, a CI runner or an enclave, so one who may decide for the network reads the text for them. (a) opens every tagged host's services to every client at the upgrade with no one having read anything; (b) needs a sponsor's act per machine, and an admin's servers have no sponsor who reads. In a network with no document the `compute` block sits in a config record that sets no reach, which keeps it under DESIGN's allow-all. | owner |
| Q-LSTN-10 | §26 | Is a new entry open at once, or only once its person has seen it? | (a). CO-38 asks the bridge to keep the list current, and a confirmation for every development server started would leave the list behind the machine; the person reads `listeners:publish` once and confirms each desktop's first list on it (26.6), then sees each new entry with its program's name and hides what should stay theirs. | owner |
| Q-LSTN-11 | §26 | How does a host deliver a flow the listeners rule admits? | (b). (a) shows the service a local peer, so Redis' protected mode and every "allow from localhost" panel answer; skips the host's firewall, which does not filter loopback, opening what it keeps off the LAN, such as SMB on a Windows laptop; and can reach a loopback-only socket that shares the port, as a test on macOS showed, where Docker's published `*:5432` would expose a private `127.0.0.1:5432`. (b) keeps the firewall and the peer's identity where `ur tun` runs and never reaches loopback elsewhere, the firewall's gap there said in `listeners:publish`; (c) would close every desktop that runs no `ur tun`, which needs root, against CO-38's "any client". | owner, confirmed (CO-42) |
| Q-SAFE-1 | §27 | Which model? | (a). It has the best published detection of the small classifiers, 81.2% of AgentDojo's attacks prevented at a 3% utility cost for the 86M against 22.2% for Protect AI's, by Meta's measure; a tokenizer refined against the spacing attacks that broke its predecessor; a multilingual 86M; and a 22M that fits a phone. (b) is English only, archived and nearly three times the 22M's size; (c) resisted adaptive search better (71% against more than 90%) but is 0.2B on an English base, and the bench can swap it in by release if it serves better; (d) classifies hazards, not injection; (e) is the agent's own model in a local run, open to the same text. The Llama 4 Community License asks for its copy and "Built with Llama", both in the release's notices, and "Llama" first in a derived model's name, which the exports' names keep. | owner |
| Q-SAFE-2 | §27 | Which runtime? | (a) at launch, and (b) when a conversion passes the bench, which drops a runtime. ONNX exports of these models exist and ONNX Runtime ships for every platform here, a few MB each when reduced; no DeBERTa-v3 conversion to LiteRT is published, and its disentangled attention would be URnetwork's own port to prove; (c) would run in wasm, but costs a hand-written encoder and its speed without SIMD. | peer review |
| Q-SAFE-3 | §27 | Should the classifier also decide DESIGN's own taint-driven refusals, such as `mail_send` from a tainted run to recipients already approved, which would amend I-8 and I-9 through Appendix D? | (c), so (a) at launch. CO-40 answers Q-CONN-7, a question about this document's kinds; DESIGN's outward actions mostly reach other people or the network (mail, publishes, grants, DNS), which §27.7 would send to the person anyway, so (b) buys little now while amending invariants frozen with `record.proto` at M3 (owner decision 142); an owner decision beside 142 can extend it later, with the records to judge by. | owner |
| Q-SAFE-4 | §27 | Does CO-40's rule for clean runs reach the calendar's invitations, which §23.9 sends to the person in any run? | (a). CO-40 answers Q-CONN-7, which asked about `service_call` and set it against the calendar's own rule; an invitation is mail the provider sends from the person's account to other people, which DESIGN asks about in any run for a first recipient (R-CTX-26); one rule for a tool across its links is what a person can learn; and one tap approves a whole batch. Under (a) a clean run's raw `service_call` send goes without a tap while a typed invitation asks, which the owner may settle by (b) or (c). | owner |
| Q-SAFE-5 | §27 | Does auto mode wait for the person's acknowledgment of `approvals:auto`? | (b). CO-33 asks that the person read what could be exposed, and that an automatic check may let an injection act is such a fact; the person is at that first card anyway, and the setting's default stays `auto` (CO-40). | owner |
| Q-SAFE-6 | §27 | What threshold, and who sets it? | (b). A miss costs an injected action and a false alarm a tap, so doubt should ask; calibration on URnetwork's own corpora fits the threshold to agents' traffic rather than to Meta's set; (c) would let a person, or an agent that misled them, lower the protection without a release's review. | peer review |
| Q-SAFE-7 | §27 | Should the classifier also judge whether the action follows from the person's requests, as LlamaFirewall's AlignmentCheck does? | (a). AlignmentCheck's published gain comes from a large model reading the whole trajectory; a phone's model is the agent's own or one as weak, takes seconds and reads the same injected text; (c) sends the run to a provider for each check, and charges for it. The bench measures (b) on LiteRT-LM's models each release, and a stage that passes joins under §27.6's fixed-prompt rule; meanwhile the person's requests name the destinations that count as known (§27.7). | peer review |
| Q-SAFE-8 | §27 | How many automatic approvals, and does one ask end them for the run? | (b). A miss should cost little and be seen: 10 covers a run's ordinary fetches and writes, and 50 a busy person's day; ending auto after an ask stops a run from trying phrasings until one passes, at the price of a tap for each later action in a run already suspect. | owner |
| Q-SAFE-9 | §27 | May the classifier decide a tainted run's `send` through `service_call`, as CO-40's "if the classifer approves, go ahead" could be read? | (a). A send reaches other people, whom the daemon cannot read from an arbitrary API body, so it cannot tell a first recipient (§27.7), and an injected send harms them, not only the person; DESIGN asks even a clean run before mail to a new recipient (R-CTX-26). Writes, to the person's own data, are where the classifier spares taps; (b) can follow once typed tools name their recipients. | owner |

## Appendix C. Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| A1, A2, AP, none | labels (§4.3): verified TEE; verified TEE with custody of the machine; TEE with the provider's platform inside the boundary (Chutes' inference; Hippius', Lium's and Cathedral's enclaves); no TEE, by the person's choice (CO-18) |
| Approvals mode | a person's `auto` or `ask`, for every kind and per kind, in their harness config's `approvals` key; `auto` by default (CO-40, §27.10) |
| Attach | a Harness driving another Harness's session over the bundled SSH with Pi's RPC (§7.10) |
| Automatic approval | a taint-driven approval of kinds 23-26 that the device's safety classifier gave: an `ApprovalDecision` on channel `auto`, signed by the device, recorded with its verdict, never a person's approval (§27.9) |
| Broker | `computeservice`'s part that relays remote calls and holds the balance (§6.6, §14.2) |
| Calendar link | a saved credential with which sidecar's calendar tools read, and where its form allows write, one calendar: CalDAV with an app password, a secret ICS address (read-only), or a Google or Microsoft connection (§25); kept in a `secret` repo, never in an agent's context (§23.6) |
| Canonical name | a model's one name, `<provider>-<model>-<effort>` (§6.3) |
| Catalog | every model, shape and search endpoint a device may use (§6.3) |
| CO-n | an owner statement of 2026-11-23 (front matter, §20.1) |
| Compute balance | a network's prepaid USD balance for remote inference, enclaves and web searches (§9) |
| Connection | a person's link to their account at an OAuth or OIDC service: a `Connection` record and every OAuth credential it holds, in its own owner-bound `secret` repo, used by sidecar's tools and never by an agent (§25.6) |
| Container socket | the one socket mounted into an enclave's agents' container, serving MCP's tools, `ur gateway token` and `ur hook` to the harnesses that run there, every call a tainted run's (§11.10) |
| Context history | everything a Harness or gateway model call read and wrote, kept in the author's vault as session entries and blobs (§24) |
| Credit | one US dollar of compute balance, as bought (§9.5) |
| Direct path | a call to a model without a TEE, from the device to the provider, with a btauth/1 signature the broker makes over the request's hash (§6.6) |
| Deposit (gamma) | gamma minted under a hotkey on one subnet, spent by that hotkey at a service (§10.2) |
| Disclosure | a service's or provider's plain statement of what stays private and what could be exposed, by id and version in the signed policy, its summary line on every card of the service; web search, models without a TEE and enclave providers ask the person to acknowledge it before first use, and again at a version that changes a fact; for the network's tagged and cloud sidecars an Owner or Admin acknowledges for the network (§2.8) |
| E2E path | a provider's request encryption to a key generated inside its TEE (Chutes: ML-KEM-768) |
| EPC | the enclave platform contract (§11.3) |
| Enclave | a TEE VM at a provider that is also a tagged sidecar of the person's network; an agents' enclave is, for the initial version, one of its sponsor's devices, with their access and none of their authority (§11.4) |
| Engine process | `ur-engine`, the desktop's out-of-process LiteRT-LM, a separate executable the OS confines (§6.5) |
| Event batch | the events one calendar write call carries, which one kind-25 approval covers, each event switchable (§23.9) |
| Feature (connection) | a named use of a service, such as `calendar`, with the scopes it needs and the typed tools that use it (§25.4) |
| FetchedPage | the structure `web_fetch` returns: metadata, outline, text, links, tables, data (§22.3) |
| First release | M11, M13a, the listeners track and Codex on local models through M12a's gateway: what a person can use with no outside party's act (§19.3) |
| Gamma | a subnet's USD-valued, non-transferable service credit in the Subtensor runtime (§10.2) |
| Harness | sidecar's embedded agent harness (§7) |
| Hidden entry | a listener entry its person keeps off the network's list (`ur listeners hide`), which the listeners rule then stops opening; the person's own devices see it by asking live (§26.6) |
| Incarnation | one VM of an enclave; the enclave's identity outlives it (§11.4) |
| Indexer enclave | a network's one enclave designated as its indexer; members grant it their mailbox (§11.10) |
| Keeper | an always-on device of an enclave's sponsor that may start a new incarnation alone, on a machine an earlier incarnation used or an A2 one, else paging the person; for the indexer enclave, an Owner's or Admin's, which may also take any machine its Where row allows, at most two new ones a week (§11.7, §11.10) |
| Limited-use mark | what a run takes from reading a service whose definition's model rule is `limited_use`, Google's: its nodes, pushes, messages, children and continuations carry it, and its context then goes only to the models that rule admits (§25.10) |
| Known destination | a site, enclave or calendar that the member's record shows an untainted run or a person's approval reaching in the last 90 days, or that the person's own words named; an automatic approval never makes one known (§27.7) |
| Listed URL | a URL the person gave, or one that appeared in this run's search results or fetched links (only a page's first 16 once the run is tainted), or in a trusted inbox message or EVS version; fetchable without approval (§22.5) |
| Listener entry | one line of a device's list, `ip:port (description)` beside its private name: a socket, a port map, a forward, a socket name, a TLS name or an enclave's SSH server, with its protocol and its end (§26.4) |
| Listeners rule | the policy rule granting `dial` on `listener:<selector>`: each listed socket and map entry of the subjects named; the implicit document carries it for tagged sources once an Owner or Admin has acknowledged `listeners:publish` for the network, and Team's starting document and every new document for every client; it delivers a flow as the network's traffic, never at `127.0.0.1` (§26.6, §26.7) |
| Lot | one credit of the compute balance with what is left of it (§9.4) |
| M12a, M12b, M13a, M13b | the two parts of M12 and of M13: part a needs nothing new from another company, part b holds what waits on one, each with its own exit (§19.1) |
| Management link | the attach link's mode for a whole Harness, `ur harness rpc --manage`: one SSH session per device and enclave, reaching every agent there (§7.10) |
| MRTD, RTMR, MEASUREMENT, HOST_DATA, MRCONFIGID | TDX and SEV-SNP measurement and launch-data fields a verifier checks (§5.3) |
| Origin | who a command on an attach link comes from, the person or a run with its taint bit, signed by the caller's sidecar over the session in an `origin@ur.io` request (`SIGNED_ATTACH_ORIGIN`), which the enclave's SSH server verifies outside the agents' container; the receiver trusts it as §20.7 trusts a push's provenance (§7.10, §12.5) |
| Outcome class | a search's result without content, `ok`, `provider_error`, `timeout` or `refused`, which devices report and the broker counts only hourly across all networks (§21.8) |
| Policy (compute) | `compute-policy.json`, the signed list of roots, TCB floors and measurement profiles (§5.4) |
| Private mark | what a run takes from reading its person's mail, calendars, connected services, mailbox, vault files or marked nodes; in an enclave that reaches out, a marked run uses no tool of the agents' container, and a run that used one makes no such read, but by the person's kind 24 (§7.8) |
| Promotion code | a code URnetwork makes for a campaign, redeemed by a person who may buy for a lot of at most $10 that pays for inference and enclaves, never search, and lapses 30 days later (§9.11) |
| Provider adapter | the one interface every provider is reached through (§4.6) |
| Reference provider | Google Cloud's TDX confidential VMs and a SEV-SNP host URnetwork runs itself, for building and testing enclaves, never for users (§11.3, CO-21) |
| Report data | the 64 bytes in a quote or report that bind a nonce and a key (§5.5) |
| recURd skill | the instructions and tools every Harness agent starts with (§20.9) |
| Safety classifier | the small model, Llama Prompt Guard 2, that reads what tainted a run and what an action would send, on the device or in an enclave's daemon, and allows the action or asks the person (§27.5, §27.6) |
| Service definition | a service's issuer, URnetwork's public clients and redirects per platform, its features and scopes, its API hosts and `service_call`'s rules, signed in the compute policy's `services` (§25.4) |
| Setup statement | an indexer incarnation's sponsor's signed word for what its device installed over SSH, binding the incarnation's evidence, keys, B and payload, on which members' devices seat it (§11.7, §11.10, CO-41) |
| Session tree | a run's session entries linked by parent, Pi's tree; a call's context is the path to its input node (§24.5, §24.6) |
| Sign-in mail | a message in which the mail component finds a one-time code or a sign-in, password-reset, verification or magic link, withheld from models outside the device and A1 or A2 TEEs unless the person allows it (§23.4) |
| Spend view | where a network's credits went: each service's total since the first charge and its last 7 UTC days, by provider and model, enclave and member, and over the 7 days by agent too, net of refunds (§9.13) |
| Thread | a conversation between agents, or a person and agents, as a dir of messages in an inbox (§20.7) |
| Track | a team that builds its part of M11-M16 beside the others, in §19.3's order (§19.4) |
| Web search | the `web_search` tool, in the Harness, through MCP and as `ur search`, backed by Parallel's Search through its keyless gateway, `parallelmpp.dev` (§21) |
| Workspace | a local agent's temp directory, its only file system (§7.5) |
| Written commitment | a provider's written undertaking to build what its gate asks, which starts its adapter (§19.3, D-CPHASE-2) |
| x402 authorization | a one-search USDC transfer authorization (EIP-3009) that the broker signs to the payee named in the challenge of Parallel's gateway, and the device presents with its search (§21.5) |

## Appendix F. Use-case coverage

CO-39 asks that the design fully support the use cases. Each owner statement's use case is walked through below, end to end: what the person does, on which surface, and what their device, URnetwork's servers and the providers or peers do, each step with the section that designs it. "Supported once G-…" marks a use case whose design is complete on URnetwork's side and waits on an outside party; §4.7 and §19.2 say what each gate needs and what users get meanwhile, and §19.6 shows, use case by use case, what a person can use with no outside party's act, what waits, and what each outside party must do first. Where a use case holds only under a condition, its status says so. Statements that are process instructions (CO-13, CO-14, CO-39) say where the document honors them.

## Appendix G. The owner's open decisions, by what they block

Every question in Appendix B carries an answer, which stands as the design unless its decider overrides it (CO-14), and every decision in Appendix A stands unless the owner says otherwise. Of the questions whose decider is the owner, 100 are open; the owner has already settled 49 others, in CO-31, CO-35 and CO-40 to CO-43 (Q-CCTX-1, Q-CCTX-2, Q-CTRUST-3, Q-PROV-1, Q-PROV-2, Q-PROV-3, Q-PROV-5, Q-PROV-7, Q-PROV-10, Q-ATTEST-4, Q-ATTEST-5, Q-BAL-1, Q-BAL-2, Q-BAL-3, Q-BAL-4, Q-BAL-5, Q-BAL-6, Q-BAL-13, Q-BAL-14, Q-BAL-15, Q-GAMMA-1, Q-GAMMA-2, Q-GAMMA-3, Q-GAMMA-4, Q-ENC-4, Q-ENC-9, Q-ENC-10, Q-ENC-11, Q-CACL-2, Q-CACL-4, Q-CPHASE-1, Q-CPHASE-4, Q-CPHASE-5, Q-SRCH-1, Q-SRCH-5, Q-SRCH-13, Q-SRCH-14, Q-SRCH-15, Q-FETCH-1, Q-MAILCAL-5, Q-MAILCAL-9, Q-MAILCAL-13, Q-CTXH-7, Q-CTXH-13, Q-CONN-2, Q-CONN-3, Q-CONN-5, Q-CONN-7, Q-LSTN-11). G.1 puts first the decisions that cost money, bind URnetwork to another company or are hard to undo, each with its options, the answer recommended and its price; G.2 indexes every open owner question by the first milestone or gate it blocks. Everything else stands unless the owner says otherwise.

By CO-44 the owner let the recommended answers of the questions in G.2 stand, each to be changed only where the owner flags it; G.1's were all answered one by one (CO-42): each as recommended, but Q-CPHASE-4 (none of §19.7's deferrals taken) and Q-CONN-5 with Q-MAILCAL-9 (connections and mail shared with enclaves), which CO-43 then widened to an enclave's full access as its sponsor's device.

## Appendix I. Residual risks the design accepts

The design accepts the residuals below. Each is stated where it arises; approving the document accepts them as a set. "Accepted by" names the owner statement that accepts one, or the design, whose acceptance stands unless the owner says otherwise.

| Residual | Who can use it | What it costs them | What it yields | Where | Accepted by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
